value.claim: Nothing in this repository reads what a bash call spent. Every bash call an agent made appended one row beside its seat's page, carrying the wall time, the child processor seconds and the peak memory of that call. Five closures put every reader out of reach of those rows, two of them by construction rather than by inspection, and the fifth holds even for a reader pointed at the right file. The writer has since been taken away. The two files left over their ceiling were divided by hand at `206db9e58eb`, since taking a writer away divides nothing.
value.evidence:
THE WRITER, NOW GONE. The rows came from an exit trap in `bash-call-weighing.shell-script.shell.sh`, and `weigh-bash-call.agent-hook.code.ts` settled before the call which file each row went in. The hook stopped wrapping the command at `1a6f6cd4597e44a4545af388bcf1cfc1afc17a98` and the script went at `952a5640db0b09ded010e82cff055ad760718df7`. Line numbers into either are no use now; read them at the first of those commits.

ONE. `check-cost.module.code.ts` exports `opening`, `closing`, `costOf`, `costSpawned`, `lineFor`, `fillingAt`, `costRecorded`, `recordCost` and three `/proc` parsers, and no reader. Every one of its eleven production importers takes a writer symbol.

TWO, BY CONSTRUCTION. Every entry-file reader in the tree routes through `entriedAmong` at `page-entries.module.code.ts:20-26`, which keeps only `pageTypeSlug === ENTRY_PROPERTY`, and that is `page-property-entry` at `index-entries.module.code.ts:58`. `entries` is `file-property/entries`, declared on the base page type at `page.page-type.ts:18`. The four `entriesAt` callers each name a different property: `SYNC_RUNS`, `TRACKS`, `LISTENS`, `NOTIFICATIONS`. Every `rowsOver` and `entriedValue` caller passes that gate.

THREE. The one check that reads entry bodies, `page-matches-its-type`, reaches them at `entry-reasons.module.code.ts:287` through a loop opened at `:281` with `entriedAmong`.

FOUR, AT THE SERVER RATHER THAN THE BUNDLES. `file-answering.module.code.ts:39` refuses an uncommitted file property by name. Independently, `bytesAt` at `page-file-body.module.code.ts:46` composes with `besideAt`, the committed name, so it would look for a file that is not there.

FIVE, THE PHASE FILTER, WHICH HOLDS ALONE. Every row is `phase: "bash"`, over all 20,204 rows of one seat's file. `check-measuring.module.code.ts:277` admits `AUDIT` or `CHECK`, `change-measuring.module.code.ts:63` admits `CHANGE` or `APPLY`, and `command-measuring.module.code.ts:73` admits `COMMAND`. A reader pointed at the right file would drop every row.

THE EDITOR EXTENSION, SEARCHED. `code/editor/extension` is what `akasha.domain.ts` links at `linkedAt`. It names no `.entries.` path and composes no uncommitted name; its own `entries` are Claude Code transcript entries, and `command-server.module.code.ts:47-53` composes `besideAt(one.path, CODE, TS)` alone.

WHAT IS GIVEN UP. The wall time, the cgroup processor seconds and the peak memory of every bash call, which was the only place bash-call cost was measured anywhere. It was given up because nothing read it, rather than because it was not worth reading. A reader was one filter from done: `heldIn` in `check-measuring` would have to take a page type other than `check-code`.

MEASURED AFTER, AND THE WINDOW WAS TOO SHORT. The seat's entries file grew about 400 bytes a second before the hook landed and took no append in the three minutes after, while the entries beside `block-biome` kept growing, so dispatch and the other bash guards ran throughout. That observation names no file, and a seat's rows go to whichever part is filling, so which file it was over cannot be recovered; at least one seat's entries file took appends inside that window. Counting the trap's own rows finds twelve appends across six seat files in the three minutes after 14:25:52Z, five of them to `athena.seat.entries.part3.uncommitted.jsonl` between 14:25:52.629Z and 14:26:05.354Z. The trap had not stopped. Its last append beside a seat's page was 2026-09-12T15:04:12Z, 38m20s after the hook stopped wrapping and 31m47s after the script went, because `trap __akasha_shut EXIT` binds a function the shell has already sourced, so unlinking the file it came from changes nothing for a shell that holds it. The longest-lived row carries `wallMs` 13,837,255, three hours fifty minutes, and its `ran` is an `export` of an agent id, so it is a session shell's row written at teardown rather than a call finishing. It is not the last row: four rows land within 28ms of one another at 15:04:12Z and this is the second of them, with three more landing together at 15:03:28Z. The rows cluster because sessions end. A trap row is told from a `recordCost` row by `childCpuSeconds`, which the trap prints through `%s.%06d` and `toFixed(3)` cannot emit.

NOT ESTABLISHED. Readers outside this checkout were not searched, so anything under `~/.local/state/` opening a seat's file by path would not have been found. No audit was run over either landing.

A row written before `137ed2adbee8` may state that a peak was measured where nothing measured it, so a reader of what is already written must discount `peakMeasured` before that commit.

value.claim: A change is allowed 300 processor seconds and spends 1.6 at the ninetieth percentile, so the ceiling is about a hundred and ninety times what a change wants. Over 40,586 runs in three and a half days the median change spent 0.74 processor seconds, two runs ever crossed 300, and no change page states a ceiling of its own, so every change is on the default. Memory is the dimension running hot and is held to nothing: the same runs have a median peak of 345 MiB, a 99.9th percentile of 8.3 GiB and a maximum of 29.8 GiB, and no code reads the number.
value.evidence:

A line carries wallMs, cpuSeconds, childCpuSeconds, peakBytes, residentBeforeBytes, peakAddedBytes, readCalls, writeCalls, readBytes, pathsChanged and refusals. The seconds here add cpuSeconds and childCpuSeconds, the second of which is above zero on 647 lines of the 40,586.

Dearest kinds by their highest run, with the p90 and the count of runs beside it: remove-folder 1333.4, 5.6, 69. move-folder 490.4, 9.2, 1367. move-pages 120.0, 43.3, 42. change-file 116.1, 1.6, 23007. remove-property-from-every-page 114.1, 70.6, 174. add-page-property-types 97.9, 58.0, 92. rename-page-type 94.3, 59.2, 45.

value.claim: `akasha change apply` runs the tests beside the files a change carries, and no others. A test fixture is imported by tests outside its own folder, so a change that moves what a fixture writes lands green while every test importing that fixture goes red, and nothing says so. The deploy is the only backstop, because it judges every changed file between its last success and HEAD rather than the files one change carries. That makes the gap show up hours later, in someone else's run, over a range holding many agents' commits — so the agent who is there reasons from their own recent changes and names the wrong cause. The cost is not the red tests, which are quick to mend once seen. It is that the signal arrives detached from the change that caused it.
value.evidence:
`8ff4d48d0b4` landed 2026-09-12 at 08:32 local, moving `shapesAt` from the value index onto `shapes/page-property/<page-type>.jsonl`, and migrated the fixture that files those lines in `page/index/modules/reading/index-reading.module.test-fixtures.ts`. The apply that landed it reported `5 test files` beside what the change carried, holding 101 tests, while the change carried 11 files across `page/index/modules/filing`, `indexing`, `property-shaping`, `reading`, `settling` and `shapes`. Three other fixture worlds write the same index and were not among those five: `grounded` and `declaring` in `page/index/modules/entries/index-entries.module.test-fixtures.ts`, the local `entryShapes` and `oneOfRecords` in `page/index/modules/reaching/reaching.module.test.ts`, and `filed` in `page/service/modules/kinds-gathering/kinds-gathering.module.test.ts`. Each files `value/<kind>.jsonl` and nothing else, so `fileKeysAt` at `index-entries.module.code.ts:158`, `uniquePropertiesAt` at line 401, and `knownIn` at `reaching.module.code.ts:93` each read an empty map. Nineteen tests went red at 08:32 and were red until 09:04.

That it is the fixture and not the deploy was settled by reproducing it outside the deploy. `akasha change apply` refused a fold at 15:01 UTC with 6 of 35 failing in `index-entries.module.test.ts`, `grounded()` in every frame, on an overlay apply builds itself from kept edits over the live checkout. `3a8627eb8ac` and `dc823372301` file the shape beside the value through one exported `keptFiled`, and both folds then landed green.

The mis-attribution is the part worth keeping. Dalla mended the deploy's own check overlay, which had been mixing bodies from two commits, in `8c9a570f4be` at 08:46:31 and `46f6d4c68ec` at 08:53:44, then read the remaining refusals as residue of that mend and asked whether the six were mine. Both mends were already in the run that showed those six, which finished about 08:57, and it failed anyway. The fixtures landed at 09:03:21 and 09:04:26 and the green deploy began at 09:18. Dalla checked the same times and withdrew the attribution. A second one ran the same way in the other direction: four peak-memory assertions were put down to the overlay mend when `76c37d27c3c` of Aine's, landed 09:18:09, twenty-one seconds before that run began, is what cleared them. Two agents, two wrong causes, one afternoon, from the same source — red arriving far from the change that made it.

The same shape had already run once that day. `854b492cc52` moved page type descent onto the relation index, landed green beside its own tests, and left `kindsUnder` answering a subset in every fixture world, which surfaced as `page-type-renaming.module.test.ts:71` in two other agents' deploys before it was reverted in `c2b8840546795`.

A second casualty of `8ff4d48d0b4`, which landed at 14:32:17Z, outlived that mend by seventy-eight minutes. `check/code/pages/identifier-names-one-page/identifier-names-one-page.check-code.check.test.ts` reaches the same fixture through `check/modules/scratch/check-scratch.module.code.ts`, was not among the five test files the landing ran, and was not among the nineteen mended at 09:04. Its own per-run ledger brackets the cause to the minute: `refusals` 0 at 14:31:44Z and 1 at 14:38:16Z, then 1 on every run until 15:49:48Z. What the detached signal cost here was not the red test. It reached a live sweep: two folder-moving batches refused on it, an audit refused it, and a bisect spent an evening moving folders one at a time on the theory that a move had broken it, when any batch rewriting that file would have refused and the next folder due to move would have produced a false confirmation. Mended in `87f84da9b3ea`.

What would close it is not running every test on every change. The narrower fact is that a `test-fixtures` page is imported across folders while a change's test net is drawn by folder, and the importers of a changed file are already filed: `importersOf` in `page/index/modules/reading/index-reading.module.code.ts` answers them from the import index in one read. A change carrying a `test-fixtures` file could run the tests beside every importer of it, which for `8ff4d48` would have been four more test files rather than the whole repository.

value.claim: A landing runs a page type's type generator off the checkout, so a change writing that generator's own code composes from the code as committed rather than from the code the change leaves. `generatingIn` in `page/type/modules/type-generating/type-generating.module.code.ts` loads the generator with `createRequire` off `change.root`, and `turnsFor` reads the committed index, so the written type lands one commit behind its generator and a check proving the two match refuses the landing that would mend them. `group-writing` had the same shape and no longer has it. A second, narrower half is that `withheld` in `change/modules/shadow/change-shadow.module.code.ts` holds back only a `replace` or an `append`, so an `add` onto a path a machine writes is kept and lands, and nothing says the machine will write over it.
value.evidence:
`group-writing` had the first half of this and no longer has it: `writingIn` takes the body the change leaves at the group's own path and loads the code from that body through a `Bun.plugin` onLoad claim, landed as dfafc5b6eec. Drafting one character of `registry-gc.shell-script.scripting.code.ts` and applying refused on 2026-09-11 at `registry-gc.shell-script.scripting.test.ts:21`, the diff showing the composed line against the committed one, and the landing said nothing about the group at all. The same draft landed as bd9b09ea888 after the mend, rewriting `registry-gc.shell-script.shell.sh` in that one landing, and was put back as bf5352278f8. `type-generating` keeps the old shape line for line: `generatingIn` at line 51 loads through `createRequire(join(root, at))`, `typedOver` at line 96 hands it `shadow.codeAt(beside)`, and `codeOver` in `page/modules/shadow/shadow.module.code.ts:126` answers the path on disk for a rewritten file and null for a new one. Closing it wants the loader `group-writing` now has, which wants that loader lifted into a module both can import.

The silent drop is closed where the agent names the path rather than in `withheld`, as eb3b4a20173. `akasha change draft change-file` naming `registry-gc.shell-script.shell.sh` now exits 1 and names the `bodyIn` to change instead; before that it exited 0, printed that the edits are kept, and `akasha change list` then answered that none were. `withheld` is unchanged and should be: `reach` calls it on every change's answer at line 169, and a mechanical sweep passing over a generated body relies on being dropped. The mechanical runner names 118 changes and none is a `change-agent` address, so nothing mechanical reaches the new refusal.

What is left of that half was measured by reaching `reach` over a world whose bodies replay. A `replace` on `registry-gc.shell-script.shell.sh` comes back with no edit and `refused: null`. A `replace` on the group's own code comes back with its edit. An `add` at a path in that folder a group would write comes back with its edit, because `withheld` holds back only a `replace` or an `append`. So `add-file` onto a file a machine writes is kept and lands, and the machine writes over it later with nothing said. Refusing that as well would shut the route that lands a generated file beside its generator in one change, which type generators still need while they run off the checkout, so it waits on `type-generating`. The loader `group-writing` now has is being lifted into a module of its own by another agent, and that lift is where this half closes: once `type-generating` composes off the change the way `group-writing` does, no change needs to land a generated file beside its generator by hand, and the `add` can be refused where the `replace` already is.

The refusals this shape drew on files the change never named are closed separately, as 5b47ad203a8: `unfresh` in `command/modules/change-freshness/change-freshness.module.code.ts` drops a path a group writes from both the commit it was read against and the reading recorded on disk, because a hand edit to such a path is now refused outright and the group composes that body again from the index at each landing. Reproduced by running against `bootstrap-namespace.shell-script.shell.sh` and `deploy-functions.shell-script.shell.sh`, which refused before and no longer do, while `bootstrap-namespace.shell-script.scripting.code.ts` beside them still refuses in both halves.

value.claim: A check judges outside the landing hold, so every store it reads may move under it. Two of the three stores are now fastened: `2d6f58fc98b` gave a change the commit it is judged against and reads the page bodies and the folder tree there, and `5d074c8c60f` reads the command tree from the index the change leaves. The third cannot be fastened the way those were. `.gitignore:18-23` keeps `import`, `listing`, `path`, `rule`, `shapes` and `value` out of every commit, so no commit holds those six to be read from, and one folder judgement read 38 such files beside 617 that are committed. Cost is not what stops it: 655 reads through the batched `git cat-file` reader cost 0ms once the tree is cached. Fastening only the committed 617 would make the remaining window rarer without closing it, and a rarer window is a harder one to catch.
value.evidence:
Run rather than read, 2026-09-13, against HEAD as it moved through `bbaf02dc770`, `2d6f58fc98b` and `5d074c8c60f`.

THE WINDOW, MEASURED. `command/modules/landing/landing.module.code.ts:324` judges and `:345` then opens `holding(root, ...)`, so the judging is outside the hold. Polling `.git/akasha-landing.lock` every 20ms for two minutes caught three other landings holding it 1.85s, 1.13s and 0.95s, against about 20s of wall time for an apply of eleven paths. 182 commits landed in the hour around that, 103 of them touching `.index/`.

WHICH READS CANNOT BE FASTENED. A folder judgement over `agent/modules` was run with the index reading wrapped, and each path it asked for was tried against the base commit through `bodyAt`. 655 index files were read. 617 were readable at that commit, all under `identity`. 38 were readable at no commit: 27 under `shapes`, 9 under `path`, 2 under `value`. None of the three is incidental. `shapes` carries the property shapes `shapesAt` and `uniquePropertiesAt` answer from; `path` carries which page claims a file, which `claimedIn` in the folder-shape decision asks for every file in a judged folder; `value` carries the page-type values the declaration source is built from.

WHY THIS IS NOT A TORN READ. `page/index/modules/keeping/index-keeping.module.code.ts:59-60` writes beside and renames, so a reader sees one whole version or another, never half of one. What a reader can see is a version later than the commit its bodies came from. That is the same two-instants fault the two mends above closed, in a third store.

WHAT CLOSING IT WOULD TAKE, NONE OF IT BUILT. Commit the six indexes, and every landing carries derived files it now leaves alone, `.index/value/domain.jsonl` being 480KB and written again whenever any domain page moves. Or answer from the pinned bodies, walking `identity` to find them, which rewrites the read path every reader in the repository goes through and turns one file read into one read per page for a wide type. Or hold the landing lock across the judging, which `the-landing-lock-orders-landings-and-orders-nothing-against-a-reader` argues against from the authors' own scoping, and which `landing-concurrency-needs-a-read-set` reads as serializing the gate; on today's figures it would stretch a 1-2s hold to about 20s against a landing every 20s.

A SECOND LIMIT, LEFT AS IT IS. The fastened tree reading subtracts what a later commit first carried, so a path another landing added is left out. It does not put back a path another landing took away: such a path is gone from the disk listing though the base commit still carried it. A folder emptied that way is read as holding nothing and is judged by no shape, so that direction is quiet rather than refusing, which is why it was left.

WHAT IS NOT ESTABLISHED. No wrong refusal has been traced to the index read. The two that were traced came from the tree and the body reads, both now fastened. The 38 is one folder judgement over one change; a wider change or an audit reads more.

value.claim: A check measures a run with the copy of the run harness its own process loaded at start, so a change to the measuring machinery is judged by the machinery it replaces, and a long round keeps judging by that for as long as the round lasts.
value.evidence:
`costsKept` at `check/code/pages/tests-pass/tests-pass.check-code.decision.code.ts:213` writes one row for every test file of every run, carrying `peakBytes`, `peakMeasured` and whether that file came back clean. For `util/run/modules/running/running.module.test.ts` those rows are at `util/run/modules/running/running.module.entries.uncommitted.jsonl`, and they hold the whole of this.

`24e4d308f02` landed 2026-09-12T14:52:29Z. It put a run in a leaf of the group made for it, so a run started inside finds that group as the nearest one it may write in and makes its own group underneath, where before it made one beside. In the same commit it added an assertion that an inner allocation's peak exceed 250 megabytes, which holds where an inner run's group is beside the ceilinged group and not where it is under it.

Its own run of the tests was 16 seconds earlier, at 14:52:13.062Z, and recorded 88006656 bytes with no refusal. Every recorded run of that file before the commit lies between 88006656 and 91480064. Every run from 14:56:08.523Z onward lies between 134545408 and 136081408, against the 134217728 the ceiling states, and carries a refusal. The split is the commit, and the commit is on the near side of its own judging.

The audit that produced the verdict naming `559bd5b46fb` is the exception that shows the mechanism. Its process began 08:50:49-06:00 and ended 09:09:15-06:00, so it was 100 seconds old when the commit landed, and its test phase measured 14:56:54.460Z to 15:07:26.601Z — entirely after. That run covered 1664 test files and found ten unclean, which are the ten its verdict names. Its row for this file reads 91398144 bytes and no refusal: the figure from before the commit, recorded eleven minutes after the commit, while separate processes minutes on either side recorded about 135 megabytes and a refusal for the same file over the same bodies. A deploy gate at 09:10:42-06:00, a fresh process, refused `dc68b09c3006ca6f5bfbd810b59122bf97233920` with four tests failing in that file.

The overlay carries the change's bodies to the test file on disk and the test file's own import reaches them. What it cannot reach is the harness already in memory. `budgetAt` walks up from the calling process's own group, so where a process was put decides where every group below it is made, and the process was put there by whichever copy of the harness the check loaded when it started. A change to the run harness is therefore judged by the harness it replaces, and a round that opened before such a change goes on judging by the older one until it ends.

This is why reading the two routes side by side finds nothing: the audit and the deploy gate reach the same `runsIn` at `code/running/modules/code-tests/code-tests.module.code.ts:279`, both over an overlay, both under the same stated ceiling. Nothing in either verdict says which harness did the measuring, and two rows for the same file in the same ten minutes differ by 44 megabytes and by their verdict with nothing on the page to tell them apart.

No mend is made here. Proposed rather than built: a recorded cost that named the harness the run was measured by would tell those two rows apart, and a round that reopened its harness when the tree beneath it moved would not carry a stale one for eighteen minutes.

value.claim: `experimental: true` on a check page takes that check out of every phase on its own: `check/modules/checking/checking.module.code.ts:118` hands back no phases for it whatever the four `runsOn` flags say. The property means one thing, whether a check has landed and does not yet judge, and the mechanism lets it carry two: a check that never judged, and a check taken out of service. The page reads the same either way. `Alan Approves Checks` asks approval for adding a check and frees widening one, and says nothing about narrowing one to nothing; the page type's invariant about switching a check on has no counterpart for switching one off. Eight of 66 checks state `experimental`, and not one of them ever judged. The only check ever taken out of service this way was put back the same day, so no instance is live now, and the audit command names all eight together as not yet judging.
value.evidence:
`check/modules/checking/checking.module.code.ts:118` is the whole mechanism: `judgingOn` hands back an empty phase list where `experimental` is true, and the four `runsOn` booleans it was handed are dropped. `check/modules/checking/checking.module.ts:30` states it as an invariant, that a check whose page states `experimental` is gathered on no phase. So one optional property, required by none and absent from most check pages, takes a check out of change, worktree, deploy and audit at once. The four `runsOn` flags stay on the page and stay readable as intent while nothing consults them.

The one check ever in that state by a change rather than by never having judged was `module-sits-under-a-modules-folder`. Commit `646246f5568`, Aine <aine@alanwalton.com>, Sat Sep 12 08:23:59 2026 -0600, one file, four `runsOn` flags from true to false plus `experimental: true`. Its message says the modules-folder check is experimental and judges at no phase, and gives the reason: it ran at change over every module page, 6,672 module folders were not under a modules folder yet, and it refused any change to a page the nesting migration had not reached. At `runsOnChange: true` that left most of the repository unwritable, so the scale it answered was real. The flags went back the same day in `100671f6447`, Akasha, Sat Sep 12 20:17:11 2026 -0600, which judges at every phase again. The state lasted twelve hours, and no check is in it now. Nothing here is an objection to either change; those two messages are a good record, and they are the only record.

Eight of the 66 check pages state `experimental: true`, and not one of the eight ever judged. `folder-matches-a-shape`, `identifier-matches-its-place` and `invariant-statement-is-plain` were born 2026-09-03 and marked by Thea on 2026-09-10, the day the property itself landed in `b519b9ba51e`, giving a check an `experimental` property saying the check has landed and does not yet judge. `folder-matches-a-shape` gained `runsOnAudit: true` in the very commit that marked it, so the marking raised its stated reach rather than lowering it. `no-unparsed-boundary-read` was marked the same day. `command-takes-its-arguments-through-one-reader`, `invariant-restated-on-a-part-narrows-it`, `parts-list-is-sorted` and `no-unused-exports` were each born and marked on 2026-09-12. Not one of those eight judged and stopped, and with the modules-folder check judging again there is no live instance anywhere in the tree. That bounds the claim: the fault has happened once and has been undone.

`check/code/check-code.page-type.ts:177` carries the rule `Alan Approves Checks`, whose act at line 181 is to add a check to akasha only where Alan has approved that check, warranted because a check binds every writer on every change and a wrong one costs more than what it guards. Its four aids settle the neighbouring cases: approving the initiative is not approving a check, a check replacing an old one still needs approval, widening what an approved check reaches needs none, and how an approved check reads needs none. Every one of them runs in the adding direction. Taking an approved check out of service is not among them. The page type has weighed the on direction elsewhere too, at line 133, where an absence invariant covers a change that switches a check on, so that the check does not judge the change that switched it on. There is no matching line for a change that switches one off.

The vocabulary has room for only one of the two states. `check/code/properties/experimental.boolean-property.ts:8` defines the property as whether a check has landed and does not yet judge. The page type says at line 125 that a check running on no phase has landed and does not yet judge, and at line 129 that the landing is how a check states its rule before that check binds anyone. Before, and not yet. A check that judged and stopped has no words of its own on the page.

Something does report it, in those same words and in one place. `command/pages/audit/audit.command.code.ts:82` builds a notice that an answer leaves out a count of checks not yet judging, naming each with the phases its page states. It runs at audit, and only where no check was named on the command line, so a change never meets it. While `646246f5568` was in force, because it set the four `runsOn` flags to false as well as setting `experimental`, `waitingOn` at line 76 found no stated phases for `module-sits-under-a-modules-folder` and printed it as a bare slug, while the checks that never judged printed theirs as waiting at change or at audit. In the one notice that told anyone any of this, the check that had been taken out of service was the entry that looked least like it was coming back.

What this informs rather than decides: whether taking an approved check out of service is Alan's the way adding one is. There is an argument that it should not be. The rule's warrant is the cost of a wrong check falling on every writer, and against that warrant the off direction is the safe one, which is why widening is free and narrowing goes unmentioned. The argument the other way is that an armed check guards something Alan approved, and the warrant weighs the cost of a wrong check without weighing the cost of a right one that stopped. If the answer is that it should be Alan's, the mend is one aid on `Alan Approves Checks` rather than any code, saying that taking an approved check out of service needs approval as adding it did. If the answer is that the reporting is the fault rather than the permission, a check could refuse a change that sets `experimental: true` on a check page that did not carry it before, which is a two-version comparison the change phase already holds the inputs for.

value.claim: A check's cost log counts refusals and never records that a judgement threw, so a round a check could not run reads exactly like a round it refused once. The only place the difference survives is `unrun` in the verdict store, and that store keeps one verdict per check, replaced each round. Nothing on disk says how often a check could not run over time, so that rate has to be inferred from the code path rather than read. It is why `lint-clean` falling short in two rounds of five went unremarked for days: the log that would have shown it was counting those rounds as findings.

value.claim: `namingOver` in `check-reaches-a-path-through-the-index` draws the page-file name tails it judges by from `shadow.listed()`, and the tree search folds into that every ignored path whose name holds `.uncommitted.`. A tail a tmux attach wrote minutes ago is in the set, and another agent on the same commit may not hold it, so the LISTED verdict at change depends on transient state rather than on the commit. Two agents on one commit can disagree, and nothing afterwards says which of them read what. This was masked while the tails came from the listing index. A tail is not a fact about which files are there: `.module.code.ts` and `.seat.uncommitted.attachment.json` are what page types declare, through their file properties and file-property groups. Built downward from the pages the set is a function of the commit alone.
value.evidence:
Measured 2026-09-14 against HEAD as it moved through `90667a3ffc4` and `e3d626f8481`, over the 51,180 files this check judges.

That tail is in the set only because a tmux attach left a mark on disk. The module writes those marks from a shell function keyed by pid and process start time and reads them back by listing, and the index answers for none of them. It is judged a false positive and left as it is, evidence rather than an exemption: this check's page carries no exemption list, and exemptions elsewhere are page properties on the file exempted.

WHAT IS NOT ESTABLISHED. No disagreement between two agents has been seen, only the mechanism that would make one. The 860 and the 845 are one checkout at one moment, and another checkout gives other numbers, which is the finding rather than a caveat on it. value.claim: `move-folder` rewrites path strings inside a finding's prose and never the line number beside them, so a repoint can leave a citation resolving to the wrong lines rather than failing loudly. That the repointing happens is verified. That it has ever produced a wrong line number is not, and no instance was found. What the measurement shows instead is the plainer fault beneath it: of 216 path citations that resolve, 110 carry a line number, and 8 of a sample of 30 point at something other than what the sentence around them says. All 8 were right when written, all 8 drifted with the cited path unchanged and so were never repointed, and 6 of the 8 were written the same day they went wrong.
value.evidence:
Measured 2026-09-12 at `4228b13044` over the 298 pages under `domain/finding/pages/`. HEAD advanced 92 commits to `01c4efe8ce1` while the measurement ran, so every count here is as of `4228b13044`.

WHAT WAS COUNTED. Every backticked span in the two text properties of each page, 4,555 of them, kept where it holds a `/`, carries no whitespace, and ends in an extension once a trailing `:NN` or `:NN-MM` is taken off. That leaves 517. Globs, absolute and home paths, URLs, a git revision and a container image take away 41. A further 126 name a top folder that has never been one of this repository's and are citations into other repositories. 350 akasha path citations remain, on 109 of the 298 pages. `akasha/X` is ambiguous and both readings are accepted: `node_modules/akasha` is a symlink to the root, and a literal `akasha/` folder was there until `b18329f1c34`. Reading it one way alone had inflated the count of citations wrong at writing by 32.

WHAT RESOLVES. 216 of the 350 resolve and 134 do not. Of those 134, 54 have the same basename elsewhere and 51 of those have exactly one candidate, 68 name a file no basename search finds, and 12 name a basename never in this repository's history. Pinning each stale citation to the commit that introduced its text with `git log -S`, 101 were right when written. The other 33 were read by hand and none is invented: past-tense sentences naming a file the sentence says is gone, ephemeral files, and files the prose says sit outside akasha.

WHY THE SWEEP IS NOT THE CAUSE. 8,024 commits and 12,651 renames landed in the 24 hours before the measurement, and ten citations broke in that window, one of them after midnight. Citations on pages landed that day were 2 of 109 stale, against 132 of 241 on older pages. `move-folder` repoints path strings inside page bodies rather than inside imports alone: `480dd741d95` rewrote the evidence of `a-ratchet-collects-where-the-fix-is-smaller-than-the-edit-that-trips-it`, and that commit's own message says it did.

WHAT THE REPOINT LEAVES, AND WHAT IT DID NOT CAUSE HERE. A repoint carries the path and never the `:NN`, so a repointed citation keeps whatever line number it was written with. That this has actually put a citation on a wrong line is not shown by this measurement, and the sample says it did not. 110 of the 216 resolving citations carry a line number, on 36 pages. Reading a random 30 against the lines they name, 22 land on what the sentence names and 8 do not. Each of the 8 was right when written, checked by reading the cited file at the commit that introduced the citation. Each of the 8 carries today the same path spelling it was written with, so none was repointed. The cause in every case is the cited file growing or shrinking under later edits. Six of the 8 were written on 2026-09-12 and were wrong by 09:46 that morning, one within 25 minutes: `command/modules/change-acting/change-acting.module.code.ts:59` was written at 09:21:34 with `noPageSaid` on line 59, and that function is now on line 60. The two largest are 27 lines: `change/modules/answer/change-answer.module.code.ts:161`, whose quoted `const first = text.indexOf(one.contentFrom)` is now at 188, and a command page whose level name was at 76 and is now at 103.

WHAT A READER CONCLUDES. 66 pages carry at least one stale citation and 19 carry three or more. On 45 of the 109 pages carrying akasha path citations, every one of them is stale. A page whose every address reaches nothing reads as a page whose evidence was made up.

WHY NO MECHANICAL MEND IS OFFERED HERE. `move-folder` already does the repointing, so a second sweep over finding pages would repeat it. 68 of the 134 name a file with no successor to point at. And many of the 51 unambiguous moved ones are past-tense prose about where a file used to be, where repointing makes the sentence untrue while keeping its address live. `a-retirement-orphans-prose-and-the-repair-is-a-rewrite-not-a-repoint` already argues this.

LIMITS. The 8 drifted citations measure line drift from any cause. None was traced to a repoint, so the rate is not a rate of repoint-induced drift and should not be read as one. About 20 path citations written outside backticks are not in these counts. The 12 said never to have existed rest on basename absence from `git log --all --name-only`, so a file that only ever existed untracked would be counted wrongly. The line-number rate is a sample of 30 out of 110. Folder citations carrying no extension were not measured at all.

value.claim: A command stopped at the ceiling its page allows is killed with a signal it cannot catch, so every cleanup it had waiting is skipped and the records that would hold it back are never written.
value.evidence:
`watchOf` at `command/modules/stopping/command-stopping.module.code.ts:29` builds the watchdog as `process.kill(pid, "SIGKILL")`. A SIGKILL cannot be caught, so a `finally` does not run and no last write lands. This is the stop every command with a `timeout` on its page shares.

Measured on `akasha deploy`, whose page allows 300 seconds. Four calls were stopped that way on 2026-09-12, at 07:15:07, 07:21:05, 08:13:11 and 08:18:21, each of them putting up `service-workstation`.

Two kinds of cleanup are skipped. The hold taken in `heldWhile` is released in a `finally` at `command/pages/deploy/modules/holding/deploy-holding.module.code.ts`, so the hold file is left behind; that one heals itself, because `heldNow` reads a hold whose process is gone as no deploy running and the next taker clears it. The records do not heal. Every ending in `deploy.command.code.ts` lands through `noting()`, which calls `recordedRefusal` and `recordedEnding` at lines 245 and 246 and 272, and those write `deployEndedAt` and `deployRefusedAt` beside the service page. A killed call reaches none of them.

That unwritten ending is a loop. `cooledBy` at `infrastructure/service/modules/deploy-choosing/deploy-choosing.module.code.ts:26` reads `if (one.deployEndedAt === null) return true`, so a service whose deploy was killed is cooled the moment it is looked at, and `waitedBy` keys the 600 second refusal wait off `refusedAt` matching `deployEndedAt`, which is also never written. Both brakes live in the code the signal skips. The service is chosen again on the next tick and burns the ceiling again: the gap between the first two kills was 358 seconds and between the last two 310 seconds, which is the ceiling plus one tick.

It also makes debris. The only scope collision in the journal, `Unit akasha-deploy-service-workstation.scope was already loaded or has a fragment file`, is at 07:15:09, two seconds after the kill at 07:15:07: the scope the killed call was running inside was still loaded when the next tick took that unit name.

The loop no longer re-chooses a killed service, because the tick now keeps that ending itself from the exit code it already holds. That is local to one caller. Every other command with a ceiling still loses whatever it had waiting.

A command stopped at its ceiling runs the cleanup it had waiting, and a command that will not stop is stopped anyway.

value.claim: A workstation watch service caught in a crash loop reads as well. `brokenIn` calls a unit broken on three counts alone: systemd knows no such unit, `ActiveState` is `failed`, or a service that is not scheduled sits outside `active`, `activating` and `reloading`. A loop restarting every five seconds hits none of them, because it oscillates between `active` and `activating` with `auto-restart`, and `activating` is in the well set. Only `failed` would catch it, and the only thing that puts a fast loop there is systemd's start rate limiter, which the akasha watch services turn off deliberately with `StartLimitIntervalSec=0`. `Result` is read and quoted back but never tested, so `Result=exit-code` never reaches the verdict on its own. Measured today: a unit carrying the real block restarted 17 times in 136 seconds and never once entered `failed`, and the repository's own health code answered well at every sample after the first.
value.evidence:
`services/workstation-services/service-health/service-health.module.code.ts:9` states `const WELL = new Set(["active", "activating", "reloading"])`.

`brokenIn`, lines 59 to 67 of that file, has three routes to broken and no fourth. Line 60 answers where systemd knows no unit. Line 61 answers where `activeState === "failed"`. Line 66 answers where a service that is not scheduled is outside WELL, after line 64 lets every scheduled service through. `state.result` is read at line 54 and quoted back at line 62, but no line tests it, so a unit whose `Result` is `exit-code` is not broken for that reason. The published verdict is exactly this one: `wellIn` at `services/workstation-services/service-wellness/service-wellness.module.code.ts:11` is `one.broken === null` and nothing else.

`activating` counting as well is meant. `service-health.module.ts:33` states that a service still coming up is well rather than broken. A unit in `auto-restart` is `activating` too, and nothing separates coming up for the first time from coming up for the seventeenth.

What removes the last route is the unit text. `services/workstation-services/unit-writing/unit-writing.module.code.ts:9` sets `DEFAULT_RESTART = "always"`, lines 86 to 88 emit `StartLimitIntervalSec` where a page states one, line 129 emits `Restart=`, and lines 130 to 132 emit `RestartSec=`. `StartLimitBurst` occurs nowhere in the repository, so the burst is always systemd's default of five. `StartLimitIntervalSec=0` disables the rate limiter outright. Without it, a loop restarting every five seconds trips five starts inside ten seconds and lands in `failed` with `Result=start-limit-hit`, which line 61 would catch. With it, that route is gone, and looping alone can no longer reach `failed`.

Four service pages state `startLimitIntervalSeconds: 0`: `alan/harness/alan-readouts/day-readout-watch-service/day-readout-watch-service.workstation-service.ts:15`, `alan/harness/inbox/count-watch-service/inbox-count-watch-service.workstation-service.ts:17`, `temper/watcher/workstation-services/temper-watcher.workstation-service.ts:17` and `page/service/workstation-services/page-service.workstation-service.ts:15`. The first three are watches. The day readout watch states `restart: "on-failure"` at line 13 and `restartDelaySeconds: 5` at line 14, and carries its own invariant at lines 22 to 24: repeated starts are counted over no window. The inbox count watch and the temper watcher carry that same sentence at lines 26 and 35. So this is chosen rather than overlooked.

On this workstation today, `systemctl --user cat day-readout-watch-service.service` shows `StartLimitIntervalSec=0` in the unit section, then `Type=simple`, `Restart=on-failure`, `RestartSec=5`, `SuccessExitStatus=143 79` and `RestartForceExitStatus=79`. `systemctl --user cat code-editor-data-watcher.service` shows `Restart=always` and `RestartSec=5` with no `StartLimitIntervalSec` line at all, so that one keeps the limiter and can still reach `failed`. The akasha watch services are the ones that cannot.

The measurement, 2026-09-10. A throwaway user unit was written carrying that exact block, and a child that crashes. At each sample the real `systemctl --user show` output was fed through the repository's own `statesIn`, then `brokenIn`, then `wellIn`, with `scheduled: false`. Two runs, 136 seconds, 17 restarts. The unit never entered `failed` once. It oscillated between `active` and `activating` with `auto-restart`. In the run where the child exits nonzero immediately, which is the realistic crash loop, the unit read `activating` at 22 of 23 samples. `well` was true at every sample after t=0, and the only false reading was at t=0, before the first start.

The same shape arrives with nothing wrong at all. The wrapper leaves on `RESTART_EXIT = 79` (`unit-writing.module.code.ts:16`) whenever a file the service reaches moves, returned at `services/workstation-services/service-wrapping/service-wrapping.module.code.ts:139`. `SuccessExitStatus=143 79` makes that exit read as `Result=success` while `RestartForceExitStatus=79` starts the service again anyway. So a repository being edited quickly produces the identical oscillation as a crash loop, and neither the verdict nor `Result` tells the two apart.

Not verified: no akasha watch service was made to crash. The oscillation is measured on a throwaway unit carrying the same block, with the verdict computed by the repository's own code.

value.claim: A watch service that dies and restarts forever is never called broken. `service-health` counts `activating` among the states that are well and calls a unit broken only where systemd says `failed`, while every watch unit states restart on failure, a five second delay, and no window over which starts are counted. So systemd never gives up and never rests in `failed`, and a watch dying every five seconds spends most of each cycle in `activating`. This matters more as the readouts move from timers to watches, because a reading judged current by whether its watch is well would then rest on a signal a crash loop passes.
value.evidence:
`services/workstation-services/service-health/service-health.module.code.ts:9` holds the well states as `active`, `activating` and `reloading`. Line 58 is the only way a running unit reads as broken, and it asks whether the active state is `failed`. The module page states it plainly: a service still coming up is well rather than broken.

All three watch services carry the config that keeps a failure from settling. `inbox-count-watch-service` states restart on failure, `restartDelaySeconds` 5 and `startLimitIntervalSeconds` 0, with the invariants that repeated starts are counted over no window and that a watch failing all night keeps on. `temper-watcher` states the same. `day-readout-watch-service` was modelled on the first.

systemd holds a unit through its restart delay as activating rather than failed. With no interval over which starts are counted there is no state in which systemd stops trying, so `failed` is passed through rather than rested in.

`service-watching` runs on `*:*:00` with five seconds of jitter, so it samples about once a minute against a five second cycle.

The restart count is no help, which looking settled rather than reasoning. `inbox-count-watch-service` is `active` with a restart count of 498. The wrapper starts a service again whenever a file that service reaches changes, and this one follows 180 files, so a restart here is ordinary rather than a symptom. The journal carries one at 10:16:29 saying that `code/running/modules/code-tests/code-tests.module.code.ts` moved and it was restarting to run on what is there now. A count climbing all day for a well unit tells nothing about a looping one.

What keeps this from being worse is that a watch takes every reading as it opens, so a restart re-takes rather than leaving a gap. That also means an actively changing checkout beats these watches for free, which is an accident rather than a design, and which would stop on the day the repository went quiet.

Not verified: no crash-looping unit was run, so what systemd reports through a real loop, and what `service-health` makes of it, are still unobserved. This rests on the state set the code holds and on the config the unit pages state.

value.claim: Three exported functions across two modules are capabilities the `@akasha/page-service` migration cut away and left as tombstones: a body of one `throw` under a declared return type that promises a value. `loadSave` says `Promise<IdleSave | null>` and returns nothing, ever. I built the transitive import closure over literal specifiers, including `import type` and literal `await import()`, resolving `akasha/...` against the repository root, from every `.ts` under a given entry folder. From the 880 files under `command/pages/` it reaches 3,259 files; from `alan/web/routes` it reaches 1,402. It would also miss a dynamic `import()` whose specifier is computed, a defaulted seam or an injected dependency, and any entry that is not TypeScript.

The check that was considered and rejected. Parsing all 84,136 `.ts` and `.tsx` files with the TypeScript compiler API found 14 exported functions whose body is one `throw`, and 41 counting those not exported. A syntax rule cannot make the distinction its own case rests on: `syntax-rule.page-type.ts:64` and `:70` state that a rule is handed one file already parsed and reads no index of its own, so it has no import graph and would refuse a live route-reached tombstone and an orphan alike. value.claim: A deploy places every Secret its manifests demand before the workload reading them is applied. `appliedWorkload` hands `putUp` a callback that runs once the namespace-opening manifests are up and before the rest, and that callback calls `placeSecrets`, which walks the plan for every `secretKeyRef`, `secretRef` and `volumes[].secret.secretName`, finds the secret page answering each, decrypts the sops sidecar beside that page, and applies one `Opaque` Secret per resource name. A demand no secret page answers is reported and the deploy carries on. Two pages placing a value under one resource name and key, a sidecar that is missing, and a sidecar carrying no `value` each refuse the deploy.
value.evidence:
Read 2026-09-14 in the akasha checkout.

Where the placing is called. `infrastructure/service/cluster/modules/workload-applying/workload-applying.module.code.ts` `appliedWorkload` calls `putUp(plan, placingBetween(root, report))`. `placingBetween` calls `placeSecrets(root, plan)`, pushes a report line for each Secret placed and for each demand no page answers, and hands back the runs `placeSecrets` made.

The ordering. `infrastructure/service/cluster/modules/workload-deploying/workload-deploying.module.code.ts` `putUp` applies the manifests `opensTheNamespace` picks out, runs what comes between, and only then applies the rest and waits on the rollout. A run that comes between and exits non-zero stops the apply where it is. The ordering is the point: a pod cannot start against a Secret that is not there yet.

Which tree the pages are read from. `placeSecrets` is handed `root`, the checkout whose pages are read, rather than `codeAt`, the tree pinned at the commit being deployed. The manifests come from the pinned tree and the secret values from the checkout.

What refuses and what is reported. `placeSecrets` throws `DeployRefused` where two pages place a value under one resource name and key, where a page's sops sidecar is missing, and where a sidecar carries no `value`. `appliedWorkload` catches that around the apply and answers `OPERATIONAL` with what the refusal said, keeping the report built so far. A demand no secret page answers is a report line instead, because a cluster may already hold a Secret placed by hand, and refusing would stop a deploy that works.

Nothing is placed on a dry run: the dry-run branch answers before the apply.

What is proved. `workload-deploying.module.test.ts` drives `putUp` with a fake kubectl: what comes between runs after the namespace manifest and before the rest, a run between that exits non-zero stops the apply, and a `putUp` handed nothing to come between applies every manifest. `workload-applying.module.test.ts` proves the two report lines and drives `placingBetween` over a plan demanding `api-token` from `cloudflare-api-token`, in a checkout whose pages answer that demand with nothing: nothing is placed, nothing is refused, and the demand is reported.

Not measured: no deploy was run for this. No test here reaches a cluster, so what `kubectl apply` makes of the Secret this builds is unproven here.
