value.claim: A landing lock admits one apply at a time, so applies are ordered. Nothing reserves the bodies a draft read, so a draft is refused where any other landing touches one file the draft carries. The wider the change the likelier that is, and a mechanical repoint is the widest change there is: it rewrites the import line of every importer and lands whole or not at all. A repoint over 6854 module pages was refused five times in a row on that alone, each refusal arriving in seconds against a repository where a dozen seats land continuously. It landed on the sixth attempt, and only because a peer seat stopped ten of its own agents by hand. A change that cannot reserve its text can win only by being faster than the tree moves, which is luck rather than mechanism.
value.evidence:
Read and measured 2026-09-10 on the akasha checkout.

What the change carries. `akasha change draft add-page-type-types` over `code/module/module.page-type.ts` answers 6854 changes: one type file added beside the page type, and the import line rewritten in every `*.module.ts` in the repository. `move-code-export` repoints every importer in one change because a half-repointed tree does not compile, so the landing is whole or nothing.

The five refusals. Each came back as `nothing was written — read them again against what is there now`, naming module pages read against the commit the draft read at. One named `page/service/modules/page-listening/page-listening.module.ts` and `services/workstation-services/service-health/service-health.module.ts` against `1729dd8a6cc`. A later one named four, among them `alan/web/modules/alan-app-shell/alan-app-shell.module.ts` and `change/modules/shadow/change-shadow.module.ts`. Every refusal printed six lines and returned within seconds, so no check ran and the cost was the draft rather than the judging.

What moved underneath. `c7526fd1f26` rewrote `uuid-version-7.module.ts`; `d2a63e1ccd7` rewrote two module pages; a swarm of eleven agents was rewriting invariant statements inside `*.module.ts` pages while this ran. Those changes and this one touch the same files on different lines.

The attempt that landed. A peer seat stopped ten landing agents and ended a read-only audit. Drafted inside that window, the same change reached the checks, ran for minutes and committed as `092fddfb09adce378f4e4d6e7fc0f7a63fa7c6af`. The peer measured her own seat at 106 commits per ten minutes before the hold and one per two minutes during it, near ninety percent of the repository's traffic; four or five seats she has no authority over went on landing.

Where the gap sits. `.git/akasha-landing.lock` admits one landing at a time, so two applies never interleave. That orders applies and reserves nothing for a draft. The draft records the commit each body was read at, and the apply compares; a body that moved on any line refuses the whole change.

What I did not verify. Whether a draft could be carried onto the newer bodies instead of refused, and what that would cost to judge. Nothing here says the comparison is wrong, only that it is whole-body where the two changes were on different lines.

value.claim: A fenced argument keeps the newline on its last line, so an `old` passage ending mid-line matches nothing and the change refuses with `holds no such passage`. That sentence names the file, so it is taken for a body that moved under the reader, and the reader re-extracts the passage from a file that never changed. Two agents met it five times in one session and neither revisited the diagnosis; one retyped about three thousand characters of a one-line property twice, having concluded that only a passage ending at a line's end could anchor. The rule is written down, and printed in another gate's own closing line. What misroutes the reader is a refusal naming the body rather than the fence.
value.evidence:
The mechanism sits at two sites, both verified 2026-09-09.

`change/modules/answer/change-answer.module.code.ts:161` is `const first = text.indexOf(one.contentFrom)`, refusing on line 163 where that is negative, and refusing again on line 165 where the body holds the passage twice. Nothing there is line-aware, so the matcher is not what rejects a mid-line passage.

`command/modules/argument-reading/argument-reading.module.code.ts:3` is `const OPENS = /^([a-z][a-z0-9-]*) (\S+)( no-newline)?$/`. Every fenced argument keeps the newline on its last line unless its opening line closes with `no-newline`, and because the key in that pattern is a generic `([a-z][a-z0-9-]*)`, the modifier is not special to `body`: `old HEREDOC-OLD no-newline` parses exactly as `body HEREDOC-BODY no-newline` does. So a passage handed in without it always ends in a newline, and matches only where the body has one in the same place.

None of this is undocumented. `command/modules/argument-reading/argument-reading.module.ts:33-44` states it three times over: a line in a body keeps its newline, a body whose opening line closes with `no-newline` drops the newline off its last line, and a passage ending mid-line is said that way and no other way. The `block-combined-akasha-calls` gate prints the modifier in the closing line of its own refusal text.

Five instances in one session, by two agents working in different folders.

One is mine and I verified it directly. Drafting into the `evidence` field of a landed finding, the passage `The remedy is a positive control` was refused with `holds no such passage`. That field is one source line, so no passage inside it ends at a newline at all. The identical draft opened `old HEREDOC-OLD no-newline` was kept. I had filed the underlying rule that same morning and still read the refusal as a stale body before I read it as a fence.

Four are reported by the lane working `seat-system` and are that agent's own count, which I cannot read from outside its session. It met `holds no such passage` four times, diagnosed a stale read every time, and re-extracted the passage rather than closing the fence. Its own words are that it could not have been fewer than four because it never revisited the diagnosis. The last of the four cost it roughly three thousand characters of a single-line property retyped verbatim, twice, on the conclusion that the only workable anchor was one running to the end of the line.

What makes the misreading systematic rather than careless is that the true cause and the common cause produce the same sentence. The refusal names a path. In a repository where several agents land in one folder at once, a body that moved under you is the usual reason a passage stops matching, and agents are told to expect exactly that. So the reader is handed a sentence that fits the frequent explanation, with nothing in it pointing at the fence.

Under that is a second layer, and it is what separates the four instances from the one. The rule is complete and correct, and it sits on `argument-reading.module.ts`, the page of the module that reads arguments. Both agents were using `change-file`. The one that met the refusal four times had no reason to open the argument reader and never did, so the only copy of the rule that ever reached it was the closing line of the `block-combined-akasha-calls` refusal, arriving as a footnote to a different problem. Being written down and being reachable from where it goes wrong are not one property, and here they came apart. The reader that did know the rule still read the refusal as a moved body first, so knowing it is not sufficient either.

The cost falls hardest on any property whose value is one long source line, where the failure is total rather than occasional: a finding's `evidence`, a page's `definition`, any text property written as one line has no interior newline, so every passage inside it needs the modifier. That is also where the retyping is most expensive, which is why the one instance with a measured price is of that kind.

Two things would each have been enough. A refusal that tried the passage without its trailing newline and said so when that matched would name the fence outright. Short of that, a reader meeting `holds no such passage` has one cheap test before re-reading anything: ask whether the passage ends where a line ends.

value.claim: A finding can argue against a mend, and the premise that argument rests on can stop holding with nothing marking the page stale. The claim still reads true, so the page is not retired, and the next reader trusts the reasoning and re-derives the whole evening. Worse, one change can undo the objection and destroy the alternative the finding prescribed in the same stroke, leaving a page that forbids the mend now possible and prescribes one now impossible. The page type retires a finding whose claim has gone false and says nothing of a finding whose reasoning has.
value.evidence:
Measured 2026-09-12, on a page retired the same evening.

THE INSTANCE. `a-seats-cost-file-passes-its-ceiling-because-the-size-read-and-the-append-are-two-steps` held that a seat's cost file passed its ceiling because the size read and the append were two steps. It argued against both mends in reach. Of a lock: `Neither a roll margin nor a lock is the mend while there is no reader, because a lock held across the window would be held for the whole bash call and so serialise the hottest path in the tree`. Of the alternative: `Picking the file in the trap rather than in the hook is the only mend that closes the window without a lock`. The text is only in git now, at `206db9e58eb`.

BOTH HALVES FELL TO ONE CHANGE. The window was a whole bash call because `weigh-bash-call.agent-hook.code.ts` picked the file before the call ran and a shell trap appended at exit. The hook stopped wrapping the command at `1a6f6cd4597` and the trap script went at `952a5640db0`. That left one window, two adjacent statements inside `recordCost`, where a turn costs one stat and one short append rather than a whole bash call, so the objection to a lock stopped holding. The same change took the trap away, so the mend the page called the only one that closes the window without a lock could no longer be written at all. From then the page forbade what was possible and prescribed what was not. Nothing marked it. The lock landed at `104ee41a59b` against the page's own advice, around a `fillingAt` identical to the one `edits-keeping` had been locking all along.

WHY NOTHING CAUGHT IT. The reason-expired shape is recorded for other carriers and for no finding: for code at `a-sync-run-record-was-ablated-on-a-premise-that-has-since-turned-false`, for refusal prose at `a-refusal-explains-itself-by-a-fact-the-day-migration-turns`, and for a hook invariant at `the-root-tsconfig-names-no-file-and-the-hook-guarding-it-still-says-that-run-exits-zero`, whose evidence says the hook's warrant expired a day before and the hook still refuses on it. Three directives circle it and each is scoped to invariant entries: Move When It Turns at `invariants.record-property.ts:35-46`, Move When False at `design.invariant-group.ts:9-19`, and Resolve When Found at `intent.invariant-group.ts:9-19`, whose warrant that a stale entry sends someone at a gap already shut is the nearest statement anywhere of the consequence. `finding.page-type.ts` carries no directives.

PRIOR ART, REMOVED. `a-reversal-outlived-the-reason-it-was-taken-for` said it one level up, of decisions rather than findings: the failure is not a wrong decision but a right one whose premise expired unobserved. It went at `7bcf60fc202` because every instance it named was undone. `finding.page-type.ts:43-47` files an observation that comes up again fresh rather than restoring the page that had it.

NOT ESTABLISHED. One instance was read end to end and no sweep was run. How many findings in the tree argue against a mend was not counted, and no reading tells a live warrant from a spent one. A second instance the same evening, over a refusal for a path naming no page, was reported rather than read here.

value.claim: A fold rewrites the TypeScript specifiers naming the package it folds away, and leaves untouched every specifier spelled as data in a file the rewriter never parses. Nothing judges those. `d63348fafea` folded `testing-system` into the root, took `@akasha/testing-system` out of the dependency list of both web packages, and left both `bunfig.toml` preloads still naming it. A preload that does not resolve ends the run before any test file loads, so it reads as every test in the package failing rather than as a missing module at one call site. An unrelated landing in `temper/` being refused is what surfaced it. The same shape had already shipped four times over two earlier folds, in shell scripts reaching a module through `bun -e`.
value.evidence:
The two lines. `temper/web/bunfig.toml:2` and `alan/web/bunfig.toml:2` both read `preload = ["@akasha/testing-system/modules/dom-registering"]`. Commit `d63348fafea`, 2026-09-09 19:04:15 -0600, wrote 89 files: it deleted `testing-system/package.json` and took `"@akasha/testing-system": "workspace:*"` out of the `devDependencies` of both `temper/web/package.json` and `alan/web/package.json`. It touched no `bunfig.toml` at all. So the fold updated both dependency lists and left the two preloads that were the only remaining readers of the name.

Why nothing caught it. The rewriter reads TypeScript, and a `.toml` is not TypeScript, so the preload was never a specifier the fold could see. `tests-pass` does not cover it either: the check runs only the tests beside the files a change carries, and no test is beside a `bunfig.toml`. Measuring an apply carrying only `temper/web/bunfig.toml` answered `nothing it carries sits beside a test, so nothing landed`. The one file that decides how every test in a package loads is a file whose edit runs no test.

The failure mode. The preload is handed to the runner as `--preload`, so a specifier that does not resolve kills the process before the first test file is read. It presents as the whole package failing, with `error: preload not found "@akasha/testing-system/modules/dom-registering"`, rather than as a missing module reported at the line importing it. `node_modules/@akasha/testing-system` is still a symlink onto `testing-system/`, so the name still lands on a directory; it is the deleted manifest, and with it the `./dom-registering` export key, that leaves the subpath unresolvable. The stale link makes the error say less than it would say if the link had gone too.

The respelling. The deleted manifest mapped `./dom-registering` to `./dom-registering/dom-registering.module.code.ts`, so the code file is what that key named. The root manifest states the name `akasha` and exports `./*` to `./*`, and `node_modules/akasha` links to the root, so `akasha/check/test/modules/dom-registering/dom-registering.module.code.ts` reaches it. `code-tests.module.code.ts:179` passes a preload through untouched unless it opens with a dot, and `runsIn` at line 255 runs with the repository root as the working directory, so a root-spelled preload resolves from the bunfig of a package. The root `bunfig.toml:3` had already been respelled this way for `dom-guard-setting`, in `9bf4e377ecb`; the two package ones were not. Repaired in `e750ddd6c09`. A measured run of `alan/web/routes/no-such-route/no-such-route.route.test.ts` and of `temper/web/modules/cli-link-failure/cli-link-failure.module.test.ts` each came back clean, at 0.8 and 0.7 processor seconds.

Four siblings, from two earlier folds. A search for `@akasha/` across `.toml`, `.json`, `.yaml`, `.md`, unit files and shell scripts, read against the 84 names the manifests in the tree actually state, found four more live specifiers naming a folded package, every one of them in a `.sh` file calling `bun -e`: `@akasha/ci-benchmark/toolchain-manifest` at `infrastructure/machines/provisioning/scripts/provision-workstation/provision-workstation.shell-script.shell.sh:72`, and `@akasha/mobile-cli/ios-program-components` at `render-harness-run.shell-script.shell.sh:57` and at line 18 of the `decode-harness-run` script of each of the two iOS apps. `6f6afa51973` and `3ef0fdb1e13` folded those two packages, and each old manifest mapped the same key to the same `.module.code.ts` shape. Repaired in `17f0f0abe82`. Reading the provisioning script rather than running it, that substitution is assigned under `set -euo pipefail`, so provisioning looks to have been dying at the ast-grep step since its fold; that is inference, not a run.

What a mend would need. `specifier-names-a-package` runs on change, deploy and audit, and reads TypeScript, but refuses nothing while the one manifest in the tree is named `akasha` rather than a scope. Nothing reads a specifier out of a `.toml`, a `.sh` or a value in a `.json`. Either a fold searches every body for the name it retires whatever the language of the file, or a check judges package-shaped strings in non-TypeScript files against the manifests. This is the class the two root-spelled-specifier findings closed today, `640862bdaac` and `92f59b43a48`, name from the import side; this is the same class seen from the data side.

Not measured. The refusal in `temper/` that surfaced this was reported to me rather than observed, and no reading was taken of the time between the fold and that refusal. No count was taken of how many bodies in the tree name a package that is live now and will not be after the next fold.

value.claim: `~/.local/bin/akasha` is a symlink to a script inside the checkout, placed by `setup-symlinks`, which is run by hand. A change moving the folder that script sits in repoints every import in the tree and leaves the symlink naming a path that is gone. Nothing in the change rewrites it, nothing refuses the change for it, and nothing on the machine notices; `akasha` stops being a command for every agent and every shell until someone runs the provisioning script again. What a shared launch path costs is `a-move-leaves-the-pinned-tree-every-unit-runs-from-behind-including-the-deploy` (`cafe3ff0856`) rather than this.
value.evidence:
`infrastructure/machines/provisioning/scripts/setup-symlinks/setup-symlinks.shell-script.scripting.code.ts:49` places the `akasha-launcher` page at `$HOME/.local/bin/akasha`. The link on the workstation reads `/var/home/walton/.local/bin/akasha -> /var/home/walton/repos/akasha/infrastructure/machines/provisioning/scripts/akasha-launcher/akasha-launcher.shell-script.shell.sh`, an absolute path into the checkout. `setup-symlinks` is a provisioning script; no change act and no `akasha deploy` runs it.

Commit `ce98adcdbdc` at 14:02:21 MDT on 2026-09-11, `provisioning moves under infrastructure with the machines it sets up`, moved `machines/provisioning/` under `infrastructure/`, carrying the launcher's script with it. Three agents converting workstation services hit the gap on their own and said so unasked, over roughly ten minutes. One found `akasha` was not a command for about a minute and waited it out. Two others could not reach it at all and finished their work by calling the launcher's new path directly; one of those answered `day=2026-09-11 tasks=1 temperTasks=13` as expected. None of the three repointed the link, each saying it sat outside the repository and outside its brief. The link's own mtime is `Sep 11 14:02`, the same minute as the commit, so it was mended by whoever ran the move rather than by the change.

The history holds the same shape rather than a new one. `d9b9074b789`, `move the dispatcher to command/modules/cli, the launcher and the extension naming its new path`, and `cc1f55ea5f8`, `the akasha launcher says where it now is and keeps its executable bit`, are both commits whose whole subject is a path inside the launcher catching up to a move that already landed.

How far this reaches rests on `infrastructure/service/workstation/modules/unit-writing/unit-writing.module.code.ts`. Line 102 writes `Environment=PATH=%h/.bun/bin:%h/.local/bin:/home/linuxbrew/.linuxbrew/bin:/usr/local/bin:/usr/bin:/bin` into every unit, so a bare `akasha` in an `ExecStart` would resolve through `~/.local/bin`; `execLines` at line 53 builds the `ExecStart` lines from the service's `runs` instead. Those `runs` are no longer each page's own. `infrastructure/service/workstation/modules/service-reading/service-reading.module.code.ts:23` holds one constant `RUNNER = "module/service-running"`, and line 78 composes every workstation service's start from it with the page's slug as the sole argument; no `service-workstation` page states a `runs` of its own. All 51 units under `~/.local/state/workstation-services/`, each symlinked into `~/.config/systemd/user/`, now carry the same `ExecStart` naming `service-running.module.code.ts` and differ only in that trailing slug, 19 of them behind the `set -a; . ~/.secrets.env` preamble `shelled` adds at line 47 for `needsSecrets`. So the reach has inverted rather than shrunk: a move breaking that one path breaks all 51 units at once, not one apiece. `a-move-leaves-the-pinned-tree-every-unit-runs-from-behind-including-the-deploy` (`cafe3ff0856`) and `service-watching-shares-one-launch-path-with-every-service-it-reports-on` (`c3b0d454a0c`) hold that shared path and what it costs. The most recent outage bore it out: 31 distinct units were seen failing in the journal, which counts the units that had a tick due in the window rather than every unit naming the file.

value.claim: A folder move rewrites the import specifier in every file reaching into that folder, so the bodies it reads are spread over the tree rather than gathered in the folder. Every one of those reads is held to freshness at the apply, and one landing by any other seat inside the window refuses the whole change. A wide move is therefore held back by how much of the tree it has read rather than by how long it takes, and it lands or is refused on whether another seat happened to touch one of those files in the minute the apply took.
value.evidence:
Measured 2026-09-10 moving `readouts` to `alan/harness/readout`, where `alan-harness.domain.ts` already declares `domain/readout` a part. 179 files move and the draft answers 191 moves over 323 edits, in seconds, since `facingIn` went lazy.

Three applies in a row were refused, each by a different pair of files, none of them a file being moved and all of them files whose specifier the move rewrites:

1. `alan/web/modules/attribute-stoplights/attribute-stoplights.module.test.ts` and `alan/web/routes/inbox-stoplights/inbox-stoplights.route.test.ts`
2. `alan/harness/cost/modules/reading/cost-reading.module.code.ts` and `alan/harness/sleep/modules/reading/sleep-reading.module.code.ts`
3. `alan/harness/capacity/modules/reading/capacity-reading.module.code.ts` and `alan/harness/surplus/modules/reading/surplus-reading.module.code.ts`

What was landing meanwhile. `git log` over the same 25 minutes answers 17 commits touching `alan/harness/*/reading`, among them `read AKASHA_ROOT through optionalEnv in sleep-reading` and the same for `surplus-reading`. One seat was going through every reading module in turn, landing about every ten seconds. A drop, a redraft and an apply cost about four minutes, so the move lost the race three times.

What the fourth try answered. The same move, drafted and applied an hour later on 2026-09-10 with the swarm landing about ten commits a minute across `alan/`, landed first try as `7c56ece3b30905e388a7f9b7d95ebbf971625df9`. So a wide move is not held back for as long as any seat is busy; it is held back only while a seat is going through the very files the move rewrites, and it wins as soon as that seat moves on.

What the remedy costs. A refused apply keeps its edits, and redrafting over kept edits reads a world where the move already happened, so each retry needs a drop first. That is recorded at `a-refused-apply-leaves-edits-that-make-the-redraft-refuse-for-the-wrong-reason`.

What I did not settle. Whether a specifier rewrite needs holding to the same freshness as a body the change composed. The rewrite is derived from the path rather than from what was read, so deriving it again against the newer body would land the same text; nothing here proves that is safe for every edit a move makes.

value.claim: `move-folder` rewrites relative import specifiers and a manifest's `exports` targets. It does not rewrite a folder path spelled as data — a string in a page's property, a path in a JSON deploy file, a constant in a module body outside the moved folder. `folder-not-left-named` does not catch these either, because it judges only bodies the move writes, and a speller outside the moved folder is a body the move does not write. So a folder move lands green while leaving stale paths behind it. This has already shipped a container command pointing at a directory that is not there.
value.evidence:
The guard's reach. `move-folder.change-mechanical-folder.ts:79` gives the invariant as `A body the move writes still naming that folder refuses the move`. `movedInto` at `move-folder.change-mechanical-folder.code.ts:28-37` builds the move from `world.under(at)`, so the bodies the move writes are the files inside the moved folder plus the importers whose relative specifiers it respells. A file that names the folder as data and neither sits inside it nor imports from it is in neither set.

Already shipped, before this session. Commit `970930951e2` moved `infrastructure/auth-proxy/auth-proxy-server` to `.../server`. `infrastructure/network/auth-proxy/deploy/dockerfile-extensions.json` carried `runtime_cmd` naming `auth-proxy-server/`, a JSON string in a file the move did not write. It was not respelled and the move landed. The container command has pointed at a path that is not there since. Repaired this session in `45dd3fe67f9`.

Hit again, twice, this session. `infrastructure/backup-retention` moving under `infrastructure/storage/backup/` left `infrastructure/dockerfiles/built-images/gfs-promoter/gfs-promoter.built-image.ts` spelling `folder: "infrastructure/backup-retention"` — a page property whose whole value is a repository path. `infrastructure/auth-proxy` moving under `infrastructure/network/` left `auth-proxy.built-image.ts` the same way. Both moves landed green. Repaired in `1e1b644c0d2` and `9f422941a50`.

The shape of the spellers. Three kinds appeared, none reachable by import rewriting: a `folder` property on a `built-image` page whose value is a path; a `runtime_cmd` string inside a JSON deploy file; and a module constant such as `const REPO_PAGES = "infrastructure/git-repos/repos/pages"` at `page/modules/checkout-roots/checkout-roots.module.code.ts:10`, which the `git-repos` move left stale and which is stale yet, because editing that file draws `no-index-path-spelled` on its `readdirSync` at line 33.

What a mend would need. Either the move reads every body in the tree for the folder path spelled as a string literal and refuses or respells, or a check outside the move judges path-shaped string literals against the tree. The second was there once: `the-check-for-stale-path-literals-was-ablated-hours-before-it-was-needed` records `repo-paths` being ablated on 2026-09-03 with its scanner `ts-path-literals` kept and unread. That finding is about the ablation. This one is about `folder-not-left-named` being unable by its shape to cover the gap the ablation opened, since it reads only what the move writes.

Not measured. No count was taken of how many stale path literals the tree currently holds, and no reading was taken of whether `ts-path-literals` still runs correctly. Four of these were found by hand, one per move, by grepping the old path after each landing.

value.claim: A folder move that lands while writers are running leaves those writers resolving the old path and writing fresh files at the folder the move vacated. `763256c3212` moved the seat pages out of `seat-system/` at 04:47 on 2026-09-12 and a seat entries file was born at the vacated path at 09:04; `9c808e72ac0` moved `alan/attribute/points` at 09:20 and its sidecar was appended at the vacated path minutes after. Each writer holds the path it resolved for as long as its own cycle runs, so none reads the move again. `file-has-its-page` names these files correctly, at a layer that cannot act on them: the move carried the git-ignored sidecars along with the pages and the writers re-created them behind it, so the check is right and the tree is wrong. Clearing them would throw away lines a running writer is still writing.
value.evidence:
Read 2026-09-12 at HEAD, and read again at 14:11 the same day.

The paths the check refuses, every one an uncommitted sidecar under a folder holding no page file: `seat-system/seat/pages/ryn/ryn.seat.entries.uncommitted.jsonl`, `seat-system/seat/pages/athena/athena.seat.entries.uncommitted.jsonl` and the `.part2.` file beside it, and `alan/attribute/points/attribute-points.module.entries.uncommitted.jsonl`. The two `lines` files under `seat-system/seat-log-days/pages/oauth-proxy-console-athena-2026-09-12/` that this page first named are no longer in the tree; that folder is now empty.

The seat move. `763256c32122a1b944bc3694d901fd00622000f3`, dated 2026-09-12 04:47:38 -0600 and titled `apply 118 files`, renamed the athena and ryn seat pages from `seat-system/seat/pages/` to `agent/seat/pages/`. Nothing is tracked at HEAD under `seat-system/seat/pages/`.

The sidecars were carried by the move, not left behind by it. `agent/seat/pages/athena/athena.seat.subagent-edits.uncommitted.jsonl` is at the new path with a btime of 2026-09-11 22:46:02, hours before the move, and btime survives rename on this filesystem. The mover walks the directory itself: `move-folder.change-mechanical-folder.code.ts:28-30` calls `world.under`, wired at `change-shadow.module.code.ts:244` to `treeUnder` at `change-shadow-tree.module.code.ts:10-17`, which calls `walkedUnder(at, () => true, entering)`; `walkedUnder` at `tree-reading.module.code.ts:15-34` is a `readdirSync` recursion, and that `() => true` takes every file whatever git thinks of it. Git is read only by `missing` at `move-folder...:32-37`, which refuses a move that would leave a tracked file behind. So no move drops a sidecar, and a folder left holding one was written into after the move rather than skipped by it.

What is at the vacated seat path is new. `seat-system/seat/pages/athena/athena.seat.entries.uncommitted.jsonl` has a btime of 2026-09-12 09:04:12, four and a quarter hours after the move commit, so a writer created it at a folder the move had already emptied. The `.part2.` file beside it was carried across the move, btime 04:47:38, and was appended to in that same second, 09:04:12. Only the ryn file truly stopped with the move, at 04:47:39. The live side ran on throughout: `agent/seat/pages/athena/athena.seat.entries.part3.uncommitted.jsonl` was born 08:08:25 and was still being written at 09:54.

A third writer, with no calendar day in it. `9c808e72ac0b58fba28a619ec1031d665da11d91`, dated 2026-09-12 09:20:59 -0600 and titled `apply 249 files`, renamed `alan/attribute/points/attribute-points.module.*` into `alan/attribute/modules/points/`. The new-path sidecar `alan/attribute/modules/points/attribute-points.module.entries.uncommitted.jsonl` is 47407 bytes with a btime of 2026-09-11 15:14:25, carried by the move, and was still growing at 13:11. The old-path one is 756 bytes, born 09:20:57, two seconds before the commit, and last written 09:23:28, two and a half minutes after it. That writer holds a module's path rather than a day's, so a once-per-calendar-day closure does not account for it.

Why, for the writer this page first found. `agent/seat/log-day/modules/log-day-writing/log-day-writing.module.code.ts` builds an appender only when the calendar date changes, at `:302-305`, and `appenderFor` at `:200` resolves `dayPathIn` at `:206` once, keeping the page path and the part path in closure variables for the rest of that day. A writer that started before 04:47 holds the old folder until the date rolls over. That is one instance of the wider shape rather than the whole of it: a path resolved once and then held for as long as its holder's own cycle runs.

Counts. 1826 directories tree-wide hold `.uncommitted.*` sidecars, and 5 of them hold no page file. Three are the vacated old paths named above. The other two, `alan/harness/code-editor/code-editor-terminals/pages` and `alan/harness/code-editor/terminal/pages`, hold only `.uncommitted.attachment.json` files, 403 of them, and neither side of that rename holds a page, so they are a separate fault and not this mechanism.

The condition a mend would meet: a path a writer holds is read again after a landing moves it, rather than held for the length of that writer's own cycle, so a move landing under running writers leaves no append going to a folder its page has left.

value.claim: A folder move respells the path inside a message's body, so a record of what an audit said becomes a record of what the audit never said.
value.evidence:
`move-folder` reads every path in the index through `spellersIn` and repoints each file whose text holds the moved folder's name, `move-folder.change-mechanical-folder.code.ts:125`. A message's `body` is text somebody wrote, and it is respelled the same way. Drafting a move of `agent/claude-code/session/modules/session-jsonl` rewrote `agent/messaging/message/pages/message-09d8897d3fee.message.ts`, whose body records an audit at `58eb1e896c1a` refusing that folder, into one naming `agent/claude-code/session/modules/session-jsonl`, a path that folder did not have at that commit.

The record was measured by one check and is held by another. That message's body is the audit's own words, and what they ask for is a folder named `session-jsonl-schema` rather than `jsonl-schema` — what `session-jsonl-schema` calls its folder. They name no `modules` level. The check that wrote those words is `folder-matches-a-shape`. The check refusing the rename now is `module-sits-under-a-modules-folder`, which wants a `modules` segment in the folder chain and judges only a path a change writes, so it is invisible until the file moves. Satisfying the second check is what nests the folder, and nesting it is what respells this record. Three folders named in that message are unmoved for this reason: `agent/claude-code/modules/claude-launch-args`, `agent/claude-code/session/modules/session-jsonl` and `agent/claude-code/session/modules/session-jsonl-schema`.

value.claim: A mechanical folder move rewrites a test fixture's example literal wherever that literal names a real package or path, and leaves the invented literals beside it alone, so the test reads a rewritten example against an untouched one and fails.
value.evidence:
`change/modules/package-naming/package-naming.module.test.ts` set a package rename up with `BODY` naming `@akasha/code/code-source` and `RESPELLED` naming `@akasha/kode/code-source`. Moving `code/code-source` to `code/reading/modules/code-source` rewrote the first, because `@akasha/code` is a package the index answers for, and left the second, because `@akasha/kode` is invented. The test then read `@akasha/kode/source` where it wanted `@akasha/kode/code-source`, and the failure refused a landing of 204 changes that had nothing to do with it.

The same fixtures already carried `akasha/code-system/code-system.workspace-package.ts`, a path no file has had since the `code-system` folder moved, left by the same mechanism on an earlier move. So this has happened twice in the one file.

Mended at `f3442fea3f3` by making every package and path that test names invented, and by putting `No package or path this module's test names is one this repository has.` on `change/modules/package-naming/package-naming.module.ts`. That mend reaches one file. Nothing refuses the next fixture written with a real name, and a check could, because the index answers for exactly the literals at fault.

value.claim: A `workstation-service` page's `runs` value spells its module's path as data. `move-folder` repoints imports and leaves that value; the systemd unit is rendered from it and nothing a move does rewrites the unit. So a folder move lands green, and the service it names crash-loops from its next restart until someone reinstalls the unit by hand. Today `temper/temper-watcher` moving to `temper/watcher` stopped the temper watcher for fourteen minutes, and `service-system` moving to `services` the day before had already stopped `service-watching`, the service that tells a persona a service is broken, for twenty-five hours: the alarm for this fault is the first thing this fault silences. Six more service pages were stale the same way, three of them running old code held in memory and one restart from dying.
value.evidence:
`28323e26913` at 17:19:26 on 2026-09-09 moved `temper/temper-watcher` to `temper/watcher` and respelled the paths inside it, including `runs` on `temper/watcher/workstation-services/temper-watcher.workstation-service.ts`. The unit at `~/.local/state/workstation-services/temper-watcher.service` still read `bun temper/temper-watcher/watcher-running/watcher-running.module.code.ts`; the journal shows `Module not found` and `Scheduled restart job` every five seconds, the wrapper first waiting sixty seconds each cycle for a file that does not parse because it is not there. `akasha infrastructure service install temper-watcher` rewrote the unit at 17:33:40 and `restart` brought the worker up at 17:34:03. The unit's restart counter read 13,886, a lifetime figure; at a five-second delay the fourteen minutes were near 170 of them.

`8941ab3a799` on 2026-09-08 at 16:06 carried `service-system` into `services`. `service-watching.workstation-service.ts:10` kept `bun service-system/workstation-services/service-watching/service-watching.module.code.ts`. Its journal shows the last `Finished` at 16:06:04 and `Failed with result 'exit-code'` from 16:07:02 through 17:40:02 the next day, every minute. The page was repaired in `7c09c207e76`, the unit rewritten, and at 17:41:10 it ran green and told `amy` about `overdue-rolling`.

The sweep. Grepping every installed unit for a `.module.code.ts` path and testing each against the tree found 13 stale paths across 11 units. Four units, `ci-orchestrator`, `main-pipeline-creator`, `pages-system-service` and `sweep-editor-pages`, have no page and no link under `~/.config/systemd/user`, so they are staged files an older renderer left rather than installed units. Of the other seven, `temper-watcher` and `memory-reaper` had correct pages and stale units, repaired by the reinstall alone; `alan-email-worker`, `inbox-count-watch-service`, `inbox-tracking-poll`, `monarch-sync`, `service-watching` and `surplus-fall-notifier` had stale `runs` values, repaired in `2b9cb2a6d9b` and `7c09c207e76` and reinstalled. `alan-email-worker`, `surplus-fall-notifier` and `inbox-count-watch-service` read `active` throughout, because a process started before a move keeps the old file in memory; each would have died at its next restart. `inbox-tracking-poll` is on a timer and had failed at every tick; at 17:45:02, on the corrected unit, it ran green.

The survey that comes back clean and is still wrong. Surveying `alan/track/days` on 2026-09-09 across every extension, hidden files included, with `~/.local/state/workstation-services` swept too, found nine files spelling the literal and four spelling it as a constant. It missed `alan/chess/game/chess-game.page-type.types.ts:4`, which spells the same folder `../../track/days/properties/played-at.instant-property.ts`. A literal-path search and a relative-import search are two different questions of the tree, and a folder a sibling reaches upward answers only the second. So a clean literal survey says nothing about relative importers, and the file at the centre of the `alan/track/days` deadlock was reachable only by the search that was not run. A sweep for stale spellings owes both.

The read that hides it. `service-wrapping` waits up to sixty seconds for a file that does not parse before running on, so `systemctl is-active` reads `active` through about sixty of every sixty-five seconds of a crash cycle. A status check that samples once sees a running service.

The mechanism. `runs.text-property.ts` is plain text with `nameFormat: null`, and nothing reads the path out of it. `a-folder-move-leaves-a-path-spelled-as-data-stale-and-no-guard-reads-it` names three shapes of speller; this is a fourth, and the one with a running process on the other end. The command page for `infrastructure-service` states `An install restarts no service whose units are unchanged`, so a reinstall after a move is cheap and idempotent, and no move runs one. A check that every `runs` value naming a `.ts` file names a file in the tree would have refused all six landings; none exists, and `repo-paths`, the check for path literals, was ablated on 2026-09-03.

value.claim: `fork` is a SessionStart source the client raises, and `clear-reads-on-context-replaced` does not name it, so a forked session keeps the whole read record and the day-old stale sweep does not run either. That is right where a fork copies the whole transcript, because both sessions then hold the bytes. It is a warrant that lies where a fork is taken from an earlier point, because the forked session holds fewer bytes than the record claims while sharing the record file. Which of the two the client does is not settled here.
value.evidence: Alan states in 6681b35d813 on 2026-08-31 that the client raises SessionStart for startup, resume, clear, compact and fork alike. Verified by running against the hook's own exports on 2026-09-12: `replacing("fork")` is false where it is true for startup, clear and compact; a payload of `{hook_event_name: "SessionStart", source: "fork"}` parses, `sourceIn` reads `fork` out of it, and `agentIn` names the seat; and `cleared(root, seat, "fork")` returns `{agent: 0, stale: 0}`, which is `NOTHING_SWEPT`, because `cleared` returns before reaching `sweptReadings`. So a fork takes neither the agent's own readings nor anyone's readings older than a day. A fork keeps the seat's `AGENT_ID`, and a reading is keyed by path and then by agent, so the forked session and the session it came from share one record file rather than getting one each. The hook's SCOPE already files `a source this does not name` under NOT REACHED and says the absence of a record from that list is not a finding that it survives a replacement. No line is written to `.git/data/reads/clearings.jsonl` for a fork, because the hook writes one only for a replacing source, so the log cannot say how often a fork has happened. value.claim: A move rewrites the relative specifiers of every body importing what moved, and `generated-file-not-written` refuses the change where any of those bodies is generated. value.claim: A module property group whose code will not load leaves the file that group writes exactly as it was, and the landing says so and commits. That much is stated design on `group-writing.module.ts`: a group that breaks is said rather than refusing, and nothing there refuses a landing. What carries it further than it reads is how the code is reached — a group's own body comes from the change, while the imports in that body resolve against the checkout, where a move the same change carries has not landed yet. So a fold that moves anything a group imports makes that group unloadable for exactly the landing that needed it to run, and the file it would have written stays as the move left it until some later change happens to touch it. Nothing tells the writer which of the two they got, because a group whose body was going to be identical and a group that could not run at all are said in the same breath and neither refuses.

WHY THE RESOLUTION SPLITS. The same page states that a group runs off the body the change leaves rather than off the checkout, and that is true of the group's own file. It is not true of what that file imports: `heldOver` loads the body, and the loader resolves each specifier against the checkout as it is on disk at that moment. A fold applies its moves and then composes the derived files, so during that window a specifier naming a moved module reaches nothing. Every group importing anything the fold moved fails together, and the bigger the fold the more of them.

WHAT MAKES IT WORSE THAN IT READS. The file a group writes is the kind nothing re-derives on its own, so a stale one waits for a change that happens to touch the same page. `A file no change names is written again where what a group reads turned` is a departure on the same page, which is the promise this breaks: the thing that would have written it again is the thing that could not load. NOT MEASURED. How many groups import a module that a fold of ordinary size would move. Whether any derived file in the tree is stale right now for this reason. What it would cost to compose the derived files before applying the moves, or to resolve a specifier against the change rather than against the checkout, which is what every other reader in a landing already does.

THE CALL THIS INFORMS. Whether a group that cannot load refuses the landing, or the loading is mended so a move cannot break it. Refusing is the smaller change and reverses a stated departure, which needs no approval but would refuse a landing wherever any group breaks for any reason. Mending the loading is the larger change and leaves the departure true.

value.claim: A check whose process was killed apart answers `died on SIGKILL apart, so it judged nothing —` with an empty error stream, and nothing there or anywhere on disk says which sender signalled it. Only the memory reaper can be ruled out from a log, since it signals SIGTERM first and names what it took. The round that would settle it records no cost, because a check's cost is written by the child that died. So a killed check under memory pressure reads as the reaper harvesting it when the check's own ceiling is as likely, and the mend each reading asks for is the opposite of the other.

Read 2026-09-14.

THE INSTANCE. 2026-09-13 at 15:55, with thirteen agents landing at once: 13 `akasha change apply` processes, 13 `tsc` processes holding 16.0 GB between them, and 141 `bun` processes holding 19.6 GB. No kernel OOM kill and no oomd kill fired; the swap absorbed it, which is why the machine went slow rather than dying. Forty minutes later, with the applies drained to one, the same readings were load 18.28 and `some avg10=3.51`.

THE GUARD HAS THREE CALLERS AND APPLY IS NOT ONE. Read 2026-09-13, every call site of both entry points in `util/system/modules/memory-guard/memory-guard.module.code.ts`:
  dev-server-running.module.code.ts:95        enforceMemoryGuard(KIND)
  spawn-seat.module.code.ts:99                enforceSpawnAdmission(worker name)
  supervisor-child-spawn.module.code.ts:37    admitSpawn: given.admitSpawn ?? enforceMemoryGuard

This is the other side of that: the most expensive thing an agent starts does not pass through it.

NOT MEASURED. What one apply costs on its own, and how many can run together before the machine is worse off than running them in turn.

value.claim: A landing can refuse because its test overlay carried none of the change's bodies, and that refusal reads as a test failing rather than as a run to make again.
value.evidence:
An `akasha change apply` over eighteen kept edits refused on 2026-09-13 with `the fold is undone`, the refusal filed by `tests-pass` with the verdict `short`: `3 of the 4 test files named ran, so the ones that did pass say nothing about the rest`. Running the identical `akasha change apply` again, over the same kept edits, folded every file and landed them as `41fcb52788c9defd54c5a62e086eaba9b159d2fc`. Nothing between the two runs changed the edits.

What the first run measured was the tree before the change. The four test files named are the tests beside the files that change carried. The three that ran reported 37, 17 and 6 tests passing. Those are the counts the three files held before the change: `change-imports.change-mechanical-file-content.test.ts` held 37 tests and the change replaced it with a file holding 2, `move-folder.change-mechanical-folder.test.ts` holds 17, and `file-carrying.module.test.ts` holds 6. The fourth was a file the change added, and bun answered `Test filter "./change/modules/import-repointing/import-repointing.module.test.ts" had no matches in --cwd="/var/tmp/akasha-overlay-ji1CCT/merged"`. A merged tree holding the old bodies of three files and none of a fourth is the lower layer alone, so the upper layer carried nothing.

The upper layer is built by `bodiesOf` at `check/code/pages/tests-pass/tests-pass.check-code.decision.code.ts:199`, which walks `change.carried ?? change.changed` and asks `change.after` for each body, and `refusalsOver` at line 246 hands the result to `ranOver`, which mounts it over the checkout. `changeOf` at `command/modules/landing-change-composing/landing-change-composing.module.code.ts:80` is what sets `carried`. Worth knowing while reading that line: `[] ?? held` answers `[]` in JavaScript, so a `carried` that came back empty would silence the whole upper layer rather than falling back to `changed`. I did not verify that this is what happened, and the second run leaves no artifact to read.

What makes it worth writing down is how the refusal reads. `short` names the count of files that ran, never that the bodies it ran were the old ones, so the natural reading is that a test is missing or a new test file was misnamed. The change that drew it was adding a module and a test beside it, which is exactly the shape where `had no matches` reads as `you named the file wrong`. The mend that reading invites is renaming a file that was already right. Running the identical apply a second time costs one call and tells the two apart.

The commit is in `git log`; the answer said it was not. value.claim: The command server writes its lease refusal to fd 3 with `writeSync`, and that write can throw EPIPE. When it does, the refusal never reaches the caller, the server dies of an unhandled rejection, and the client refuses the ask with `gone` rather than `lease`. The test `a server past its lease refuses rather than answering from the runtime it has held` fails exactly that way, and only in a run of many test files; alone it passes. Because an apply runs the tests beside what it carries, this refuses landings with nothing to do with the editor extension, and it is the one thing now blocking the seat-system package fold. Why the caller's read end is already gone 22ms before the caller sees that pipe end is not established.
value.evidence:
The probe. `onNoise` logging and two `console.log` lines were put into `command-server.module.test.ts`, landed as `54819265bed`, run under a fold apply carrying 133 changes across 128 importers, and taken back out as `e8c4e78c7f8`. That run printed:

  asking at 2405ms, first pid 90721
  noise 2406ms: stderr: ... EPIPE: broken pipe, write   fd: 3, syscall: "write", errno: -32, code: "EPIPE"   at writeAll (.../command-server.module.code.ts:164:21)   at pump (.../command-server.module.code.ts:301:13)
  noise 2428ms: protocol ended pid=90721
  noise 2433ms: protocol closed pid=90721

How that becomes `gone` instead of `lease`. `serve` at `command-server.module.code.ts:231-238` sets `leaseOver` and calls `refuse`, which is `say` at :170-172, which is `writeAll` at :161-168, a `writeSync` loop on fd 3 whose write is line 164. So what throws is the lease refusal itself, and the refusal is never written. The throw escapes the loop in `pump` at :298-302, where line 301 is `await serve(ask)`, so the `void pump()` at :353 rejects with nothing handling it and the runtime dies. The client then reaches `child.on("exit")` at `command-server-client.module.code.ts:184-194`, which sets `went` and calls `lose` on a `setImmediate`, and `lose` refuses every waiter with `REFUSAL_GONE` at :286. The test asserts `REFUSAL_LEASE`, so it reads `gone`. `pump`'s `finally` still calls `finish()` at :306, arming the goodbye timer on a process already unwinding.

What the pipe did. The client destroys its read end only in `closePipe` at :291-296, reached from `lose`. A destroyed `Readable` emits `close` and no `end`. The probe shows `end` at 2428ms and `close` at 2433ms, in that order, which is what a pipe whose writer went away emits rather than what a destroyed one emits. So the read end was still open in the client's own accounting 22ms after the server had already met EPIPE writing to it, and `closePipe` is not what shut it.

The shape of the failure. Alone, the test passes. It passed alone after `163892bb20b` took the `.unref()` off the goodbye timer in `finish()`, which was a real and separate fault, and it passed alone again with the probe in. It fails in the run of 32 test files that an apply carrying the seat-system fold puts up. Four fold attempts narrowed seven failures to this one.

Not established. Why the read end is gone is not established. I found no call that closes it, and the `end`-before-`close` order says `closePipe` did not. I did not test whether a child another test file in the same run spawned can reach fd 3 of this one, and I did not read how bun test shares one process across files, so reading this as a race over the fd table is a guess rather than a finding. I did not measure how often it comes up beyond seeing it on four applies out of four.

value.claim: A `lint-clean` audit falls short in about two rounds of five, and the cause is a landing moving a path while the linter reads the live tree rather than any fault in the code being linted. A round that fell short judges nothing about lint quality, so a real lint fault can sit unseen across several rounds. It is not silence: the audit names a check that could not run apart from a check that refused, every time it happens. That is why it went unremarked. A check answering nothing reads the same as a check answering something until the answers are counted.
value.evidence:
Read 2026-09-12 from `check/code/pages/lint-clean/lint-clean.check-code.audit.logs.uncommitted.jsonl`, which holds one row per audit round carrying `ranAt`, `wallMs`, `cpuSeconds` and `refusals`, and from the audit service's journal.

How often. 70 rounds from 2026-09-10T17:10Z to 2026-09-12T13:47Z, every one of them logged, and every round the journal names has a row, so the check ran in all of them and was never skipped. Rounds answering one refusal: 19 of 70 overall, 17 of 46 since 2026-09-11T21:00Z, and 16 of 37 on 2026-09-12 UTC. The rate rose as the swarm got busier.

Why that one refusal is the fall rather than a finding. Since 2026-09-11T21:00Z every non-zero round is exactly 1, seventeen times running, never 2 and never 3. The earlier era answers 14, 15, 24 and one round of 926, which is the shape real findings take. The check's own page says every path the linter could not open is answered as one run that fell short, and that a run that fell short says so rather than naming a file at fault.

The round that shows the cause. The round beginning 2026-09-12T12:10:38Z ran 71 seconds and fell short. Twenty-three commits landed inside that window. Two of them renamed folders that reading was holding: `bfc3edc40b7` at 12:11:07Z moved `page/index/index-keeping` to `page/index/modules/keeping`, 29 seconds in, and `3dd26386629` at 12:11:39Z did the same for `infrastructure-calls`. The path list was right when it was gathered and stale half a minute later.

Not a timeout. Wall times across these rounds run 56 to 76 seconds against `audit: { maxCpuSeconds: 180 }`, and `cpuSeconds` is under one second in every row.

Not silence. `check/modules/audit-verdict/audit-verdict.module.code.ts:64` answers clean only where a check neither fell short nor refused, and `check/modules/audit-asking/audit-asking.module.ts:73` states that a check that could not run is named apart from a check that refused.

What the design already reaches, and what it does not. `lint-clean.check-code.audit.code.ts:29-38` gathers the folders of every page type stating it is mortal and skips them, because the check's page says a page that can go while the tree is read is judged by no reading of the tree. That covers pages that go. It does not reach an ordinary module folder renamed by a landing, which is what these rounds lose.

Running the check again is not a rule this repository already applies. `check/modules/audit-asking/audit-asking.module.code.ts:71-90` asks for two rounds at most, but `unansweredIn` at `:37-49` counts a check answered as soon as a verdict exists at or after the commit, and a round that fell short does write a verdict, carrying `unrun: true` from `check/modules/audit-serving/audit-serving.module.code.ts:124`. So a check that could not run is never asked again, and nothing in `check/modules/checking` or `check/modules/audit-serving` runs a check a second time either. Teaching `asked` to re-ask an unrun check contradicts its own departure that a check every verdict already answers for is owed no round, and changes what all fifty-nine checks cost.

The skip is not the level this mends at. `9dba20d137a` landed the mortal-page skip at 2026-09-12T11:29:58Z for this very fault, and the rate did not move: 12 of the 29 rounds before it that day fell short, and 5 of the 10 after it. The cause had changed shape beneath it, from mortal pages going to ordinary module folders being renamed, which that skip cannot reach by construction.

What a mend reaches for instead is the constraint at `lint-clean.check-code.ts:95-97`, that the tree an audit reads is live. A verdict naming `925a06af5ef` was taken over a tree four commits further on by the time the reading ended. An audit reading a fixed snapshot at the commit it answers for, a worktree or an archive at that sha, takes the race away from all fifty-nine checks at once, makes a verdict honest about which commit it describes, and retires the mortal-page skip entirely. It also changes what an audit round is and costs a snapshot a round, so it is Alan's call or the check champion's rather than a fault to mend in passing.

Two measurements bear on that call. The race window is the wall time, so the rate follows it: these rounds ran 8 to 12 seconds on 2026-09-10, 55 to 60 overnight, 65 to 88 on 2026-09-12, and 122 seconds run by hand at 14:43Z. And `code/running/modules/code-lint/code-lint.module.code.ts:39-45` caps the linter at two rayon threads, which lengthens its own reading and widens its own window.

The same fault sits at the other end in `a-repeat-run-ends-the-same-way-whether-the-change-had-nothing-left-or-a-batch-was-refused`: here one reader drops a distinction the type carries, there one writer does. `unrun` sits on every verdict and `audit-verdict.module.code.ts:64` honours it, while `unansweredIn` alone does not consult it. There `refusing` and an answer holding no edit and no refusal already part blocked from done, and `nest-modules` alone answers `refusing` for done. Each is a distinction the type carries and nearly every site honours, dropped at one site, unread here and unwritten there, and each is a one-line mend.
