The sweep is unfinished: forty-one subagent pages are tracked under the new root and six under the old, new ones are still born under the old, and my own page moved at 09:28:47 while this was written, so the window is still open.

HOW A DRAFT GOES TO THE OLD PATH. Draft, list and apply are three processes, each resolving the agent's page afresh: `change-draft.command.code.ts:77`, `change-list.command.code.ts:15`, `change-apply.command.code.ts:43` and `apply-running.module.code.ts:146` all call `agentPathOf`, which falls through at `warranting.module.code.ts:365-367` to `subagentPathOf` at `:352-363`, reading `listedAt(root, "subagent", slug)[0]` and never the disk. `editsAt` at `edits-keeping.module.code.ts:41-47` derives the sidecar name from that page path, no disk either. `keptEdits` at `:273-290` locks the derived path and `mkdirSync(dirname(full), { recursive: true })` at `:281` remakes the folder the move emptied; `heldIn` at `:283` then reads nothing there, so `had` is empty and `settled` at `:249-261` appends the new row alone. A later list calls `listingKept` at `change-acting.module.code.ts:261-267`, reading `editsIn` at the path the index now names. Neither compares what it found against anything asked for. The one signal is `keptSaid` at `change-running.module.code.ts:328-330`, printed at `:421` and `:433`: the answer names the path the edits are kept at. It is a path in prose, and the exit is nought.

THE RESIDUE AND ITS TIMING. Three sidecars sit at the vacated root whose ids' pages are now under the new one. Each was written one to two seconds after the commit that moved its own page, and each holds exactly one row — what an empty `had` produces. Under `seat-system/subagent/pages/`: `ember-ae9e180fbf0bb2cd1`, 1426 bytes, 09:15:34.74, against `c347f5d2b31` at 09:15:33; `athena-ab5c1d7ca25d6c244`, 721 bytes, 09:16:41.72, against `8b463329fe0` at 09:16:41; `athena-a498c748bb4ee1a35`, 771 bytes, 09:17:21.66, against `0d482ad901c` at 09:17:20. No edits sidecar sits beside any of the three at the new root.

EACH HOLDS WORK THAT LANDED OR WAS OVERTAKEN. The ember row's `contentTo` is in `temper/lost-treasure/modules/lost-treasure-item-cache/lost-treasure-item-cache.module.code.ts` now, landed by `5736a590bc7`. The athena-ab5c row adds a test to `command/pages/change/draft/change-draft.command.test.ts`, and that test is in the file now. The athena-a498 row empties the intents of `athena-command-modules.initiative.ts`, a page removed whole at `26bd524ff65`. Two were re-drafted and landed, one overtaken; none needs re-landing and nothing was cleared.

THEY ARE ORPHANED RATHER THAN PENDING. `subagent.page-type.ts:51-55` says the edits a subagent leaves unlanded move onto the seat that dispatched it as its page goes. That carry is `movedOnto` at `subagent-recovering.module.code.ts:74-88`, reading `linesIn(root, subagentPage)`, where `subagentPage` comes from `subagentPagesStanding` at `agent-page-reading.module.code.ts:39-53`, which walks the index. The carry reads the same resolved path the loss stranded the edit away from, so a stranded sidecar migrates nowhere. Read rather than run.

WHAT IS LIVE AT THAT ROOT, AND IS NOT RESIDUE. Subagent pages are tracked there too, born after the sweep began and not yet swept, one of them with an edits sidecar that was growing while this was written. Those are working agents the sweep has not reached, and the set turns over by the minute.

THE SECOND SITE, READ AND NOT OBSERVED. An agent reports an apply that landed a real commit and left all twelve edits listed, its next draft then refused because edit one no longer fit its body. I did not see that run. The code holds a second silent return of the same shape: `undone` at `apply-running.module.code.ts:122-128` clears the kept edits through `droppedFirst` after `applying` has committed, and `droppedFirst` at `edits-keeping.module.code.ts:222-239` re-reads the sidecar from disk and returns without a word twice, where `held.length < went.length` at `:229` and where any of the first `went.length` lines differs at `:230`. A clear that did not happen is reported as a landing that did. That is the clear after a landing rather than the resolve before a draft, filed here because the absence is one.

WHAT I DID NOT VERIFY. I did not reproduce the loss; the window had closed. Its evidence is two independent agent reports hours apart plus the code path and the residue above, not an observed failure. I did not see a listing answer four where five were drafted; that count is one agent's report. The tree does not say how many rows those three ids held at the new root when their pages moved, so it does not say how large any one loss was. I did not establish that the fourth agent's uncleared edits came from a move, only that both of `droppedFirst`'s returns are silent.

NEAR PAGES THAT DO NOT BIND THIS. `a-folder-move-leaves-a-running-writer-appending-to-the-path-it-already-resolved` has the same occasion and stops at the tree being wrong rather than at an edit going missing.

THE CONDITION A MEND WOULD MEET: a call that keeps edits says how many it holds, and a later call can tell a smaller number apart from a smaller draft. Described rather than built.

value.claim: The page store answers a malformed read and a refused one with the same 400, so a check that names the payload key wrongly reads exactly like the guard working. Whoever verifies the secret guard by status code alone gets a green having tested nothing.
value.evidence:
Found by making the mistake. Three probes were sent to `/read` carrying `filePath`, which the endpoint does not read; it takes `paths` as a list, or `pages`. All three came back 400. One asked for an ordinary page, one for a `.sops.` tail, one for an `.uncommitted.` tail, and the two meant to be refused were refused — but so was the one meant to succeed, and every body said the same thing: `a read carries at least one path or one page`. Read by status alone that is a guard turning away secrets. It is a request the endpoint never parsed.

Re-run with `paths`, the four answers separate properly: an ordinary page 200 with its body; a `.sops.yaml` path 400 with `holds a page's secret values, and this hands out no secret`; an `.uncommitted.json` path 400 with `holds a page's uncommitted values, and this hands out no uncommitted value`; and a path under `shared/` 400 with `stands outside akasha/, and this answers for akasha alone`. So the guard does hold, and this finding is not that it is broken.

What it is: the guard cannot be verified by status code, and the obvious verification is the one that lies. `refusalIn` returns its message before anything places a path, so a request naming no key and a request naming a secret are turned away by the same line. The messages differ and the codes do not.

This matters because that guard was closed against a real exposure: a pod in an unrelated namespace, holding no grant, was answered 200 with a real body, and all 113 running pods stand in the caller set. A guard closing that is worth re-checking, and the re-check costing one line is the one that cannot fail.

The call I took: file this rather than change the endpoint, whose callers were not surveyed. Whoever verifies this next asserts on the refusal's words rather than its number.

value.claim: A new page's id comes from one of two places depending on the kind of file it is, and nothing anywhere says so. A markdown page takes a uuid version 5 worked out from its own address, `repo:relPath`. An akasha TypeScript page takes a minted version 7, and that minter cannot reach a markdown page at all. Neither wrong choice is refused: the version 7 check reads TypeScript only, and the name format judges the shape while naming version and variant as no concern of its own.
value.evidence:
`idDerivedFrom` at `akasha/file-page-identity/file-page/file-page.module.code.ts:21` is a uuid version 5 over the RFC 4122 OID namespace, hashing the page address. `idOfFilePage` at `:33` is `stated ?? idDerivedFrom(at)`, so it only ever fills a blank. `withId` at `tools/lib/page-write-compose.ts:22` fills it for a new markdown page. Measured by calling it: `akasha:pages/refusal/command-help-parser-unread.refusal.md` works out to `c290df61-98e5-5a8c-ba58-31a09479c521`, the id it now carries. 365 of the 54604 markdown pages match their own address, all recent, so this is live, not historical.

The version 7 half cannot reach markdown. `insertedInto` at `akasha/command-system/value-minting/value-minting.module.code.ts:66` walks a parsed file's statements for a variable holding an object literal and answers null otherwise, so it never inserts an id into a `.md` file. `statedIn` in `id-is-a-uuid-version-7.check-code.decision.code.ts:43` reads the same way, so the check that would refuse a version 5 reads no markdown. `lower-uuid.name-format.ts` names as an absence that a uuid's version and variant are not judged there. That is why 109 of the 110 documents under `pages/refusal/` carry a version 5 and land, and why a hand-minted version 7 lands beside them and is wrong for life.

I made this mistake an hour ago, which is the reason to write it down: I minted a version 7 for a new refusal document because the convention in front of me was version 7 and a sibling carried one. Corrected at `5968f067f6`.

The legacy ids cannot be recovered here. None of the 110 matches `idDerivedFrom` over any of the 124309 paths that have ever existed in this git history, nor any of 12437536 combinations of 777346 candidate namespaces by 16 name forms. `temper-pages-lose-the-deterministic-ids-their-slugs-used-to-work-out` records that the old generator worked an id out from the slug and is gone; this adds that the recipe is unrecoverable here, so a legacy id is a stamp now whatever it once was.

value.claim: `landedMechanically` does not only format what it lands, it applies lint fixes, and one of them changes behaviour. A `function () {}` handed in as the target of a `new Proxy(...)` lands as `() => {}`. An arrow function is no constructor, so `new` through that proxy throws `TypeError: not a constructor` where it used to answer. The landing reports this as `formatted ... as it landed — what stands there is not what was handed in`, which reads as whitespace. A change-mechanical landing runs no check, so nothing else looks.
value.evidence:
Measured 2026-09-03 in this repository, carrying `tools/extension-panel-stub.mjs` in as `akasha/editor-extension/vscode-stub/vscode-stub.javascript-module.javascript.mjs` at commit `d6313506`.

WHAT WAS HANDED IN, at line 17 of the body: `new Proxy(function () {}, { get: ..., apply: () => anything(), construct: () => anything() })`. WHAT LANDED: `new Proxy(() => {}, { ... })`. Confirmed by diffing the body handed in against the file on disk. The whole rest of the 367-line diff is tabs to spaces, single to double quotes, line wrapping, dropped semicolons and a sorted `export {}` list — all inert. This one line is not.

THE BREAK, PROVED WITH A CONTROL. Two proxies were built under node, one over an arrow and one over a function expression, both carrying the same `construct` trap. Arrow-backed: `TypeError: make(...) is not a constructor`. Function-backed: `new () -> function`. So it is the target and not the trap.

THE STUB'S OWN ARMS, four of them, three of which had to fail. Subject, the landed file after repair: TreeItem kept its label, the status bar slot kept its text, and `new` through the proxy stood. Control, the same file with an arrow behind the proxy: `TypeError: reached is not a constructor`. Control, the same file whose fallthrough answers undefined: `Cannot read properties of undefined`. Control, the same file whose tree item drops its label: `TreeItem lost its label`. All three fired, so the subject passing is sighted.

WHY IT MATTERS HERE. This stub is what an extension activates against when a panel is read back. Every member the extension reaches that the stub does not name falls through to that proxy, and a `new vscode.Something()` on the fallthrough is ordinary. The failure would have read as the extension throwing rather than as the harness being broken.

WHAT WAS DONE. The proxy now stands on a named `function nothing() {}` declared above it. `useArrowFunction` rewrites function expressions and leaves declarations alone, and the repair landing drew no `formatted` line, so the shape survives a second pass.

WHERE THIS BITES BEYOND ONE FILE. Any migration carrying a file in byte-for-byte is carrying it in through this rewriter. A `function` expression standing where a constructor is needed is the shape at risk, and `new Proxy`, `Object.create` and anything reflective over `.prototype` are where it stands. A landing reporting `formatted` says a file changed and does not say how.

NOT MEASURED. Which rule set the landing applies, and whether any other behaviour-changing fix is in it. Only `useArrowFunction` was caught, and it was caught by reading the diff rather than by anything reporting it.

value.claim: A file landed mechanically enters akasha unjudged, and the gate then refuses the next agent-authored change to it on debt that agent did not write. The debt is whatever the gate refuses in that file, from prose restating a page to plain lint; restatement is only its commonest family. It is invisible until someone tries a gated edit, and the cheapest way out is another mechanical landing, so the file is never judged and the debt compounds. Migrating a package by mechanical batch hands every later toucher that same choice. A mechanical folder move is itself a gated write to every file importing the folder, so the debt surfaces on the mover rather than on the author, and it has to be landed first, alone, before the move is drafted at all. Going first is cheap: finding it late costs the fold rather than the line. Drafting in parallel is safe only where no file is written twice: two drafts touching one file race, so edits sharing a file go one at a time whatever act made them.
value.evidence:
A one-line import repoint in `akasha/alan/web/modules/alan-auth-provider/alan-auth-provider.module.test.tsx` and `akasha/alan/web/modules/device-secret-sync/device-secret-sync.module.test.tsx` was refused by `akasha edit` on twenty-one findings, none of them the change: four constants not in `name-format/upper-snake-case` (`trail` and `fakeSupabase` in the first file, `apiCalls` and `plugin` in the second), fifteen lines carrying prose in none of the code comment forms, and a `no-double-cast` at alan-auth-provider line 126 where an assertion reaches its target through `unknown`.

Every one of those came in with the mechanical move of `alanwalton/web/app` into `akasha/alan/web`. The repoint itself was landed with `landedMechanically`, which is what the migration sanctions and which runs no check — so the debt is still there for whoever edits those two files next.

The same is true of the whole package: `akasha/alan/web` holds 332 files landed the same way. The refusals above are what two of them cost.

Two further shapes the gate named on files nothing claims: `akasha/alan/web/tunnel-routes.ts` is refused as `no page claims this file`, and its exported `routes` constant is refused for not being upper snake case — but `infra/k8s/src/cloudflared/discover-routes.ts:36` finds tunnel files by name and reads that export, so the name cannot change. `akasha/audhdalan/audhdalan-web/tunnel-routes.ts` and the two web apps' `server.ts`, `vite.config.ts`, `.gitignore` and `deploy/secrets.sops.yaml` are unclaimed by any page in the same way.

Four more instances came from one lane's folder work in `akasha/seat-system` on 2026-09-09, none of them a mechanical landing's own debt but all of them paid by the mover. Renaming `terminal-init` to `terminal-shell` was refused on six prose lines in two files the move touched only to rewrite an import: `editor-extension/seat-toggles/seat-toggles.module.code.ts:32-34` and `terminal-seat-stating/terminal-seat-stating.module.code.ts:3-4,9`. Moving `tick-deadline` out of `supervising` was refused on `tick-deadline.module.test.ts:56`. Moving four modules into `messaging` was refused on a JSDoc line at `supervisor-claimed-redelivery-decide.module.code.ts:24`. In every one the comment restated an invariant already on that module's own page, so deleting it lost nothing.

A fifth instance the same day was not a comment at all. Moving ten `memory-reaper-*` folders into `seat-system/memory-reaping` was refused on `memory-reaper-owner.module.code.ts:12`, where `const UUID_RE = /^[0-9a-f]{8}-[0-9a-f]{4}-[0-9a-f]{4}-[0-9a-f]{4}-[0-9a-f]{12}$/` respells the shape that `page/name-format/pages/lower-uuid/lower-uuid.name-format.code.ts` owns. The gate's own words were `a name format's shape belongs to its own page, reached by importing it`. The remedy for that family is always the same: import the owning page's function and delete the local respelling. Here that was `lowerUuid` from `@akasha/pages/name-format/lower-uuid`, with `UUID_RE.test(value)` becoming `lowerUuid(value)`, landed alone as `f037eb129f690c9d7f4814d768c4fd1382ea36bb`, after which the ten folders moved without a refusal as `c25e3915f0c35ab33f2fd98ffd479f8ce5e6f893`.

A third form is not restatement at all, and no import clears it. A landing in `check/code/pages/folder-matches-a-shape/` was refused on `lint/nursery/noShadow` at `properties-of-the-type-above.folder-shape.test.ts:26` — plain lint, owned by no page. The first fix moved the shadow rather than clearing it, so it cost two folds, and neither refusal named the next.

The ordering is what costs a cycle to rediscover. A failed apply does not drop its draft, and a kept `move-folder` refuses every later draft naming a file it touched, so the debt cannot be mended on top of the kept move. The fold has to be dropped, the debt landed alone, and the move drafted again. Each of the five cost that full round trip.

The asymmetry is the practical point. The fifth instance's fix was a single line; rebuilding its dropped fold took ten `move-folder` drafts made one at a time, the new domain page, ten `parts` edges and a service path no act rewrites. Going first is not worth it because the debt is expensive. It is worth it because finding the debt late costs the fold rather than the line.

Can these be drafted in parallel? Only where no file is written twice. Two drafts touching one file race, and the hazard belongs to the shared file rather than to the act that made the edit, so it is answered by asking which files each draft writes and not by asking what kind of change it is. Folder moves are the common trap, because a move rewrites every importer and sibling folders share importers. Nine folder moves into `agent/seat/self-healing` and seven into `agent/seat/oauth-proxy` each rewrote importers several of them had in common: `supervisor-monitors-wire`, `supervisor-lifecycle` and `supervisor-interactive` were each rewritten by three separate moves. Those moves were drafted one at a time for that reason, and the ten into `seat-system/memory-reaping` were too. The `parts` edges in the same landings write only the two domain pages, so they are safe in parallel: a `change-domain-parent` batch of seventeen and two of ten and eight all came back complete, each checked against the drafted body before applying.

Debt is not spread evenly, which is what makes the ordering rule cheap rather than punitive. The five `seat-system` refusals sat in five separate files, and three of the landings between them, moving nineteen module folders in all, drew none. One clearing landing can unblock a whole area, so going first is paid for once rather than per move.

value.claim: A mechanical rename over refusal prose lands claims nothing judges. One sweep on 2026-09-08 repointed ten hook files from the pre-split `akasha change`, which landed and ran the checks, onto `akasha change draft`, which lands nothing and runs none. Seven passages were rewritten across five hooks; three were false at the keystroke rather than stale later, a sentence true of the command that landed reattached to the one that keeps edits. Each was then pinned by a test asserting the new wrong string by name, so the test preserved the fault and read as coverage for four days. Prose is the part of a refusal no check reaches: the typecheck and the linter see a string literal, and the test sees the string it was told to expect. Renaming a command inside prose rewrites claims about what that command does, and each has to be re-read against that command's own page. Build no gate: nobody can check prose for truth.
value.evidence:
The sweep is `ec928bd0d1d`, Amy, 2026-09-08, `point the hook refusals at akasha change draft and akasha change apply`. It touched ten files: the code and test of `block-biome`, `block-bun-test`, `block-destructive-git`, `block-git-writes` and `block-subagent-audit`. The split it was catching up to had already landed as `f1f48017d2a` the same day.

The three false ones.

First, `block-bun-test`. Before: `The tests run at the change. akasha change and akasha apply run every test beside what that change carries`. After: the same sentence with `akasha change draft` in place of `akasha change`. A draft runs no test. `change-draft.command.ts` carries the absence invariant `No check runs over a draft`, `draft-keeping.module.ts` carries it again, and at `ec928bd0d1d` itself the draft page already read `no check runs over a draft, and the checks run where the edits land`. It was not stale. It was wrong on arrival. The test pinned it at `block-bun-test.agent-hook.test.ts:29`.

Second, `block-biome`, same commit, same shape: `akasha change draft and akasha change apply run biome over what that change carries`. A draft runs no linter. Pinned at `block-biome.agent-hook.test.ts:36`. This one was found by re-reading the file rather than by searching for the first: its true half, `akasha formats every body it lands`, had been quoted as useful two rounds earlier without the false half two lines above it being noticed.

Third, `block-git-writes`: `Say akasha change --help for the changes it runs` became `Say akasha change draft --help for the changes it runs`. The old command's page at `f1f48017d2a^` carried `The changes the help lists are read off the index rather than named on this page`, so the help did list them. `akasha change draft --help` does not: run today it answers what a draft does and what it takes, and says only that `A call naming no change is refused` and `That refusal names every change a draft runs`. Pinned at `block-git-writes.agent-hook.test.ts:16`.

The four that were true, and why. A sentence naming a route survived the rename; a sentence naming an action did not. `block-destructive-git` says `akasha change draft remove-page or remove-file, then akasha change apply` and `To change what a commit says, draft another with akasha change draft and akasha change apply` — both name the pair as the road and attribute nothing to either half. `block-git-writes` says `akasha change draft keeps the edits, and akasha change apply lands them as one commit`, which the sweep improved from `akasha change drafts the edits`. `block-subagent-audit` says `A change landing through akasha change draft and akasha change apply is checked`, whose subject is the change landing through the pair, with the checking attributed to the landing.

The rate: ten files, seven passages, five hooks, three false. Two were found by being refused and reading the refusal; the third only by auditing the commit, and nothing about it would have surfaced from ordinary use.

The true text now: the tests and the linter run at the apply, a draft keeps edits and runs no check, and the checks judge the whole set of edits kept rather than the draft that went last, which is `change-apply.command.ts:55`. Landed as `8ac8337` and `ff14ea5`, with each hook's reach left exactly as it was.

value.claim: A message page written through the pages service over HTTP is committed whatever its `to` names, so a message addressed to a name no seat has lands in the folder messages are drained from and the writer is answered as though it were delivered. `message-to` states that such a message is refused rather than written, and the in-process writer enforces that. The HTTP writer does not. The two write roads disagree, and the road every writer in the cluster must take is the one that does not hold the invariant. A message written that way waits in a directory nothing drains, which is the outcome the in-process writer names as its reason for refusing.
value.evidence:
Proved against the live store on 2026-09-11. `POST /write` to `127.0.0.1:8787` composing a `message` page with `to` set to `jenny` answered `{"commit":"51325ca567b5484205e7c5c20f6c919e87d72d1d","wrote":["agent/messaging/message/pages/message-bf79450c319f.message.ts"]}`. No seat holds that name: `POST /ask` for the `seat` page type answers akasha, alan, amy, aranya, astra, athena, dalla, ember, nimue, olwen, ryn, thea. The page was taken away again in commit 5a11c05e856a7f2bf194be64ca34b6a75ea560b0.

agents/messaging/message/properties/message-to.relation-property.ts:10 declares `targetPageType: "page-type/seat"`, and its invariant at line 14 states `A message addressed to a name no seat has is refused rather than written.`

agents/messaging/modules/message-file/message-file.module.code.ts enforces it: `unknownRecipient` at line 75 reads `akashaSeatIdForName(to)` and `writeMessage` at line 98 refuses before composing, with the reason `no seat holds the name ... so a message written there would wait in a directory nothing drains. Refused rather than landed, because a send nobody receives must not answer as one that arrived`. The module page states the same at line 29: `A message is refused where it is addressed to no seat the seat index knows.`

The general laxity of the endpoint is already bound by the finding `the-page-store-takes-a-write-from-anything-on-the-tailnet`, which records that `page-serving` refuses a write only for a missing writer or a missing message, and that the pages service states `A write is not gated by the checks`. This finding is narrower: a page-type invariant that one write road holds and the other does not, and the loss that follows from it.

The same corpus shows the pattern is not confined to messages. `page-domain.relation-property.ts` declares `targetPageType: "page-type/domain"`, and live finding pages carry `page-type/seat`, `page-type/model-test`, `command/audit` and one bare `change-agent-file-content`.

What it cost here: the inbound SMS route at alan/web/routes/alan-web-api-sms-webhook writes to the handler seat a sender's relationship names. The two enrolled senders name `jenny` and `ki`, and neither is a seat. Had the route trusted the store to hold the invariant, every text from them would have been committed to an undrained folder and Telnyx answered 200. The route checks the seat itself before writing, so a missing seat becomes the refusal notice to `alan` that `handle-inbound` already knows how to send.

One path behind every unit. All 50 `.service` files under `/var/home/walton/.local/state/workstation-services/` carry the same `ExecStart`, differing only in the trailing slug: `/usr/bin/env bash -c 'exec bun /var/home/walton/repos/akasha/.git/trees/service-workstation/infrastructure/service/workstation/modules/service-running/service-running.module.code.ts <slug>'`. Nothing per-service is spelled on a page. `service-reading.module.code.ts:23` holds `RUNNER = "module/service-running"` and `:78` composes every start through `commandOf(root, { code: RUNNER, arguments: [slug] }, codeAt)`; `run-composing.module.code.ts:115` is the `join(codeAt, run.path)`; `service-putting-up.module.code.ts` passes `codeAt` down; `unit-writing.module.code.ts:53` writes the line. The design says so: `service-putting-up.module.ts:16-19`, 'The code a unit runs is spelled under the tree the deploy pinned rather than under the checkout.'

What advances the worktree. `deploy-tree-pinning.module.code.ts:11` names the path and `:19` moves it with `git reset --hard`, which is what the worktree reflog records. Its only caller is `deploy.command.code.ts`, so `akasha deploy` is the one thing that advances it. On a schedule that command is reached only through the `*-deploying` services, which launch through the shared module like everything else, and `deploy-looping.module.code.ts:93` then runs the deploy CLI at `join(tree, run.path)`, out of the same worktree. The repair path sits inside the window twice over.

What a move can reach. `move-folder.change-mechanical-folder.ts:42` repoints a body outside the folder naming a path that moved, `:84` does the same for manifests, `:88` takes the manifests from the index, `:133` judges the listing against the files git tracks. All of it is rooted at the checkout. Ripgrep over `/var/home/walton/repos/akasha/changes/` finds no mention of `.git/trees` or the `TREES` constant anywhere; the only users of that constant are deploy tree-pinning, `code-moving` and `index-surface`. value.claim: A path composed or globbed from string literals is configuration no typecheck reaches, and a rename that is itself correct breaks it silently. Three findings now record the shape and the failure is total rather than partial each time: the thing dies at its next call with nothing connecting the death to the rename, so what varies is only how long until someone calls it. `inference upscale --host workstation` carried a stale path through two moves before anyone ran it. The contrast worth holding is that where the same rule is written as a check the move is caught at once, and where it is written as a composed string it is caught by nobody. What would close the shape is a check resolving each composed path against the tree, and that call is reserved to Alan.

Every link was read out of `git ls-tree` and none is a deletion: the script was never gone, only never where the composer looked. It surfaced only because `akasha inference upscale --host workstation` was called while proving nine commands could land a run row: bash answered `No such file or directory` and the command raised `upscale-up exited with code 127`. Mended at `5adb5909422`, which follows both moves and drops the prefix for the leaf. Its own finding is done and taken away, and this page is where that instance now lives.

A workstation service's `runs` path is never resolved against the checkout, so a rename leaves the service naming a file that is not there and it dies at its next start. Three at once, one of them the constant writing `ExecStart` for every long-running TypeScript workstation service. It took `pages-system-service` down and was reported as a status-bar defect, because nothing joined the rename to the service.

A `@source` glob is path-keyed configuration no build failure can see, so while a package is half-moved its classes are emitted only where a `globals.css` names both halves. Four apps named the shared half alone. The cost there rises as the move finishes rather than falling.

With the upscale composer mended, those two are the whole of the literal-segment shape rooted at `akashaRoot()` in this tree, a number worth knowing for being so small.

What they share is the mechanism rather than the subject: a path held as data that the language never checks, a folder that moves for a good reason, and nothing joining the two. The rename is correct in every case. The break is silent in every case. The interval to discovery is however long until someone calls the thing, which for a command is until a person runs it and for a service is its next start.

The contrast is instructive and landed the same night. `module-sits-under-a-modules-folder` was approved and landed at `16baf1f779e`, and it refused the very next change touching a module page under `infrastructure/inference/run/` — a folder placement left behind by `18e2bf44d7d`. A mend can close an instance and leave the mechanism, and `5adb5909422` did. `akashaRoot()` resolves through `AKASHA_ROOT` or `rootBeside()`, so it carries none of the step-counting arithmetic that `rootOf(import.meta.dir)` was written to retire, and converting it would change nothing. What it keeps is fixed segments below the root, so it is right today and wrong on the next move. There was nothing better to reach for: no resolver answers a page's path from its slug, and `akasha index` offers only `refresh`.

The repair that would close the shape is a check resolving each composed path against the tree at commit time. value.claim: Every workstation unit execs one module inside `.git/trees/service-workstation`, and the pin reaches every `akasha/...` module that entry imports rather than that file alone. The worktree holds no `node_modules` of its own, but it does hold the repository's own `package.json`, whose `name` is `akasha` and whose `exports` is `./*`, so bun resolves a specifier naming the package it is already inside by self-reference, and tries that before walking up to the checkout's `node_modules/akasha` symlink. Command code alone still loads from the live checkout, because `calling.module` loads that by absolute checkout path. A run launched from the worktree therefore holds two copies of every module above that boundary, and module-scope state splits between them.
value.evidence:
MEASURED 2026-09-14, against the worktree itself rather than a replica of it.

BUN RESOLVES INTO THE WORKTREE. `Bun.resolveSync` handed `akasha/command/modules/calling/calling.module.code.ts` and a parent directory inside `.git/trees/service-workstation` answers that worktree's copy; the same call handed a parent directory in the checkout answers the checkout's copy. The same holds for `running`, `run-relaying`, `check-cost` and `command-stopping`.

THE LIVE IMPORT AGREES. Importing the worktree's `command/modules/cli/cli.module.code.ts` and the checkout's `command/modules/calling/calling.module.code.ts` into one process gives two different `calling` functions: the worktree entry got the worktree's copy rather than the checkout's. The namespace objects for `run-relaying` and `check-cost` likewise compare unequal across the two roots.

WHY THE EARLIER READING SAID OTHERWISE. The replica the previous finding rested on gave its pinned folder no `package.json`. Rebuilt exactly as that finding describes and run under bun, the replica prints `LIVE CHECKOUT`. Writing `{"name":"pkgname","type":"module","exports":{"./*":"./*"}}` into the pinned folder, which the real worktree has because the repository's own `package.json` is committed and a worktree is a checkout of it, makes that same entry print `PINNED TREE` with nothing else changed. That one file is the whole of the difference.

WHERE THE SPLIT FALLS. `command/modules/calling/calling.module.code.ts:262` loads command code at `join(root, beside)`, with `root` resolved from `AKASHA_ROOT`, which names the checkout. Everything above that line is the worktree's copy and the command's own imports are the checkout's. `infrastructure/service/modules/deploy-looping/deploy-looping.module.code.ts:92` launches every looped deploy through the worktree's `cli.module.code.ts`, so that split is the ordinary case rather than a corner.

ONE MEASURED CONSEQUENCE. With the worktree's `check-cost` reading the worktree's `spentRelaying()` while the checkout's `running` did the relaying, a run whose relayed child processor time was 0.124s was recorded as 0.070s rather than 0.194s.

NOT MEASURED. Whether a looped deploy relays at all: one real dry deploy through the worktree entry left both copies of the counter at 0.000, so the relay never engaged in that run. I did not read the entry modules of the other five worktree kinds.

value.claim: A scoped address is `<page-type>/<scope>/<slug>`, where the scope segment is the target's own scoping value rather than part of the target's name. An act rewriting that value therefore rewrites every address naming the target. A plural act reads each line against the world the lines before it leave, so one line in a call can bring into existence the address a later line names. Together these mean a plan recording each target's address as it reads today is wrong for exactly those lines whose target an earlier line rescopes, and wrong in the direction of looking right, because every address in such a plan resolves at the moment the plan is written. Validating a plan by confirming every address in it resolves passes the broken plan and refuses the correct one.

value.claim: A check running live at change collects violations where fixing one costs less than the edit that trips it, and stops unrelated work where fixing one costs more. The page type states the collecting case: a file still carrying a violation is refused the next time it is touched, and that refusal is the ratchet working rather than the check misfiring. It states nothing of the other case. Where the fix is a folder move and the edit is four lines of an invariant list, the author is refused for something their edit did not cause and cannot reasonably mend in the same breath, and the work that stops has nothing to do with the rule.

What the ratchet is. `check/code/check-code.page-type.ts:142-155` states it: a check runs at change before the tree's violation count reaches zero, running at change keeps that count from rising while the rest stay fixed, a file still carrying a violation is refused at change the next time that file is touched, and that refusal is the ratchet working rather than the check misfiring. The mechanism is sound and this check is a fair instance of it.

Where the two costs part. Under `no-code-comments` the fix is deleting the comment the refusal names, which is smaller than most edits that trip it, so each author pays a little and the count falls. Under this check the fix is moving the module's folder and every path that reaches it. An agent taking four lines out of an invariant list is refused, and the mend available in that moment is a mechanical move across the page, its code, its tests and its callers.

The cost, once and concretely. An agent editing `temper/command/modules/inventory-rule-calling/inventory-rule-calling.module.ts` was refused for the folder rather than for the edit. It dropped that one path and landed the rest, which left six invariants stated on two pages at once: a page saying what it no longer does, knowingly, because the alternative was a half-made move. What makes this instance survivable. `c72bba02dc9`, six minutes after the check landed, added the `nest-modules` change agent with its code, its tests and its page, wired into the change runner, which moves every module folder at once. value.evidence:
Renaming 249 day pages in five batches of fifty, the fourth batch drafted cleanly and then refused at the apply, because another agent had landed a rename inside one of the pages between the draft and the apply:

`alan/track/days/pages/2026-09-08/wake-day-2026-09-08.day.ts — read against `3f568e9ee2d6d73f95c9af6e8cc6baedc0dab0d5`, and what is at `1090814f5d8bcd7c66957e1338a2dd30fff8aabd` is not what was read`

That refusal is right and its wording is clear. Nothing was written and the fold was undone. The 282 lines of kept edits were left where they were, at `seat-system/subagent/pages/*.subagent.edits.uncommitted.jsonl`.

Drafting the same batch again then refused:

`alan/track/days/pages/2026-07-22/wake-day-2026-07-22.day.ts could not be read, so no page is renamed`

That file was on disk and git-tracked the whole time. A draft reads the world as every edit kept before it had already landed, so it read a world in which `wake-day-2026-07-22.day.ts` had already become `day-2026-07-22.day.ts` and there was no `wake-day-` file left to rename. The message describes the symptom in the shadowed world rather than the cause in the kept edits, and it names no remedy. The remedy is `akasha change drop`, which lands nothing and takes the kept edits away, after which the same draft goes through. A draft that refuses, by contrast, keeps nothing, so only a refused apply leaves this trap.

value.claim: `reaching` resolves a page's key to a relation target through the property page's bare slug, so where two property pages of different kinds carry one slug and one of them is a relation, every page whose own declaration is the other one has a relation edge attempted against a value that names no page. 125 temper inventory snapshots were refused this way: their `locations: "jsonl"` names a rows file beside the page, and the index read it as naming `location` pages. The four other keys claimed by both a relation and a non-relation property escape it only because their two property pages carry different slugs. Giving the rows declaration a slug of its own mends the one instance and leaves the mechanism as it was.
value.evidence:
MECHANISM, traced end to end 2026-09-03. `knownIn` at `akasha/pages-system/index/reaching/reaching.module.code.ts:67-69` fills its `target` map as `target.set(held.slug, named)` — keyed by the property page's SLUG, over every schema the index holds. `carriedFrom` at `declared-properties.module.code.ts:107,114` deliberately bares a qualified declaration (`bare = slugIn(said)`), so `carriedBy` at `reaching:80-82` files the bare slug too. `slugOfKeyIn` therefore answers `locations` for the snapshot page, and `targetOf("locations")` answers `location` — the OTHER property's target. `namingsIn:269` then treats the value as a page name and `reaches` refuses it.

WHAT THE QUALIFICATION DID NOT REACH. `e0e4d31d04` (13:19) qualified the `properties[]` entry to `page-property-entry/locations` and restored the key on 417 location-deal and 162 inventory-snapshot pages. That repair is real and it holds: `propertiesIfNamedOf` answers `kind=page-property-entry` for the snapshot correctly. It cannot reach `target`, which never sees a kind at all. Measured after that commit: `known.targetOf("locations")` = `location`, `known.targetOf("page-property-entry/locations")` = null.

CENSUS, live against the index. Five keys are claimed by both a relation property and a non-relation property: `appSlug` (nav-app-slug against app-slug), `from` (message-from against sent-from), `action` (action against requested-action), `collection` (chess-collection against collection), `locations`. Five page types carry the non-relation side: chess-game, nav, message, temper-rule-template, temper-inventory-snapshot. Only `locations` refused, and the discriminator is that its two property pages carried one SLUG as well as one key. The other four already carry a distinct slug over one propertySlug — `nav-app-slug`/`app-slug`, `message-from`/`from`, `chess-collection`/`collection`. An earlier finding counted the same thing from the other side: of 1,628 property pages, exactly two slugs were held by more than one page, `locations` and `recipes`, both cross-kind, and `recipes` is not a relation pair so it never refused.

THE REPAIR AND ITS PROOF. `snapshot-locations.page-property-entry.ts` carries `slug: "snapshot-locations"` with `propertySlug: "locations"` unchanged, so the key on every page and the `.locations.jsonl` beside it never move. Built the relation and path entries for all 162 snapshots and all 417 location-deals through the index's own `edgeIn` and `claimingIn` before and after: 912 relation entries and 1,566 claimed paths, BYTE-IDENTICAL on both sides, 125 of the claims still the `.locations.jsonl` sidecars, and refusals 125 to 0. The edge was spurious, so mending it neither adds nor removes an entry.

CONTROLS. The harness answered `ok` for the 912 entries it built while refusing the 125, so it was never blanket-refusing. After the repair it still refuses `tracking-value-levels.view.ts` on `daily-tracking`, an unrelated edge left alone, so it is not blanket-passing either. `reaches("class", "collection")` refuses while `reaches("show-class", "collection")` answers, on the same call.

WHAT IS LEFT. The mechanism is untouched. The next property page that takes a slug already held by a relation property of another kind will do this again, and it will present as a refusal naming a value that was never a page name. A reader gets less than it asked for and nothing but the refresh log says so.

value.claim: `add-property-value` and `add-property-values` resolve a relation value to a page before working out any body, and then write the spelling the caller handed in rather than the page they resolved it to. Two spellings reaching one page — the bare `my-projects` and the qualified `alan-book/my-projects` — are written as two different strings, and a reader comparing strings sees only one of them. `sections-of-the-book-above` reads `partOfCollections` raw and tests `.includes(book)` against the bare slug, so the qualified spelling passes the act's resolution, passes the act's duplicate guard, and leaves the shape refusing anyway. The duplicate guard compares exact text, so a page already carrying one spelling takes the other as a new value and ends up naming one page twice under one key, with nothing refused.
value.evidence: Found by the lane flattening `alan/book` rather than by the act's author. That report gave the qualified form in its worked example; the lane read the mechanical change before copying it and wrote the bare slug instead. Had they followed the example, 140 pages would each have taken a value that resolves, passes every check the act runs, and leaves `sections-of-the-book-above` refusing all 140 — a landing that looks clean and mends nothing. The behaviour is older than the plural act: `change-mechanical-file-content/add-property-value` splices `given.value` through `withValue` unchanged, and its duplicate test is `each.text === given.value`. The plural act's own tests hold that verbatim write in place without naming it as a hazard. This is the Ubiquitous Naming warrant playing out inside one property: a second spelling reads as a second thing. Two ways to settle it — write the address the value resolved to rather than the spelling, which changes what every caller gets, or refuse a value whose page is already named under that key by another spelling, which only refuses more.

value.claim: `monarch-relay-service` exits 0 and logs a reading carried to both sites whether or not anything took a fresh one. For eighty minutes it carried the same frozen reading every five minutes and reported success each time, while the service that takes the reading failed every run. The half that was working reported loudly and the half that was broken reported into a unit nobody watches.
value.evidence: Measured on the workstation at 2026-09-01T18:45Z. The relay logged `9 taken 2026-09-01T17:30:26.542Z carried to https://alanwalton.com` and the same to `https://smilingjenny.me`, exiting 0, every five minutes. The timestamp inside those lines never moved: the reading was taken at 17:30:26.542Z and it was 18:45Z. `monarch-reading-service` had failed on every run across that whole window. `akasha/readout-system/readout-categorization/readout-categorization.module.code.ts` refuses a reading older than `STALE_AFTER_MS`, which is forty-five minutes, so from about 18:15Z the route answered 503 `{ok:false,error:"No reading."}` while the relay went on reporting success. The relay does read the timestamp — it prints it — so the staleness was in its own log line, unjudged. What makes this worth writing down apart from the rename that caused it: the relay is the component with the visible output, and its output is a function of what it reads rather than of whether that reading is live, so a reader watching the relay sees health throughout an outage. A carrier that prints an age it never compares against anything is not a liveness check, and the tile going blank was the first signal available to anyone. After `akasha service install monarch-reading-service`, a fresh reading was taken at 18:50:37.103Z and the relay carried that timestamp to both sites. The call taken: filed rather than fixed, because whether the relay should refuse a stale reading or carry it and let the route judge is a design question — carrying it keeps one judge instead of two, and the fix may belong in what watches the reading service rather than in the relay at all.

value.claim: The recreation lost the reading a schedule got when a reminder was written, so a schedule no clock can read is caught on the next run of the service rather than by the write that put it there.
value.evidence: `ops reminder set` read the schedule through `systemd-analyze calendar` before writing the file and refused a schedule that came back unreadable, so a reminder on disk always named a time. A reminder page is written with `akasha write`, which judges the schedule as text under 100 characters and reads no clock. `nextElapse` in `reminder-sending` still reads the schedule the same way and answers `unread` for one no clock can take, and `send-due-reminders` reports that reminder and carries on to the others. The window between the write and the report is however long the service waits, and a reminder in that window is never sent.

value.claim: A rename can leave a sorted `parts` list unsorted without anyone editing that list. The address-restating module writes the new address over the old string literal's own span, so the element keeps the place it had, and a new address that sorts elsewhere parts the list. Nothing repairs it afterwards: `add-property-value` puts a value in sorted position by a single linear scan rather than by re-sorting, so a list already out of order stays out of order however many values are added to it. `parts-list-is-sorted` then refuses a page whose author touched nothing, and names the two adjacent elements rather than the rename that parted them. Mending this is larger than one act, because the act that keeps the position does not know which property key the literal sits under, and the act that knows is never handed the rename.
value.evidence:
`spellingsOver` in `change/modules/address-restating/address-restating.module.code.ts` pushes `{ from: node.getStart(source), to: node.getEnd(), put }` for every string literal whose text equals the old address, so the replacement occupies exactly the old literal's span and no element moves. `rename-file-page` calls that module, and the agent act `rename-page` sits above that, so this is the ordinary route by which a page is renamed.

The module cannot mend this as it is written. Its page says a body spelling an address is restated whether or not that body is a page, and the descent reaches every string literal in every `.ts` body, so nothing there says which property key a literal belongs to. The act that does know is `add-property-value`: `sortedKey(world.index.shapesAt().values(), given.key)` at `change/mechanical/file-content/add/add-property-value/add-property-value.change-mechanical-file-content.code.ts:87` reads the `sorted` flag off the index shape, and `page/index/modules/property-shaping/property-shaping.module.code.ts:35` is where that flag is lifted. It is handed the key; a rename is not.

The second half is why nothing self-heals. `inOrder` at `change/modules/literal-splicing/literal-splicing.module.code.ts:33-36` goes over the elements once and splices ahead of the first whose source text sorts after the new value, falling back to appending after the last. One linear scan, never a re-sort.

What is at stake: `domain/properties/parts.relation-property.ts:10` declares `sorted: true`, and `:22` says a parts list is sorted by the whole `type/slug` a part is written as. A rename changes that whole string, which is the key the order is taken on. Measured over the checkout: 910 top-level `parts` arrays, exactly one unsorted, and that one is test data at `change/mechanical/file-content/change/change-domain-parent/change-domain-parent.change-mechanical-file-content.test.ts`. So the route is live rather than already taken.

value.claim: A rename carries a property's numbered part files under the old page's name, so each names a page that is gone.
value.evidence: Renaming `eso.temper-mine.ts` to `eso-x` carried all 23 `items.partN.jsonl` files and left every one named `eso.temper-mine.items.partN.jsonl`, which the new page claims nothing of. `besideIn` also spells an uncommitted file property's file without its mark. Since `b596d58e80` the guard refuses this rather than orphaning it, so the data is held while the mend waits.

value.claim: A rename leaves behind a page named through a record field whose key more than one property carries.
value.evidence: `addressedIn` resolves a body key through `slugOfKeyIn`, which settles an ambiguous key from the page type's top-level declarations alone, so a key carried inside a record is not settled. Two fields in the repository are ambiguous this way: `frame` on `prose-frame`, also carried by `detail-frame`, and `action` on `request`, also carried by `action`. `fieldOfKey` answers for these, and reaching it asks `addressedIn` to track which record it is walking inside.

value.claim: A repeat run ends when a batch lands no commit, and a batch lands no commit both when the change has nothing left to act on and when a check refused that batch, so a run stopped part way through its work answers as a run that finished its work.
value.evidence: `repeating` in `command/pages/change/repeat/change-repeat.command.code.ts:152` loops until `committedIn` answers null, then answers `told` whenever any batch landed at all, whatever ended the run. The report names what the last batch said, so the reason is on the page; the exit status is success either way, so a caller reading the status alone cannot tell a sweep across 6673 folders that finished from one that stopped at the third batch. Nothing re-asks, because the next act is to confirm it succeeded and it will. A change agent has two ways to end a batch without a commit and the tree honours the difference nearly everywhere: `refusing` at `change/modules/answer/change-answer.module.code.ts:42` means blocked, while an answer holding no edit and no refusal means nothing to do, which is `NOTHING_OVER` at `change/modules/shadow/change-shadow.module.code.ts:112` and what `gathered([])` answers at `change-answer.module.code.ts:256`. `nest-modules` answers `refusing` for `every module's folder sits under a modules folder already`, which means done, so at that one site the two meanings share one channel. Mending that site leaves the exit status the same, because `repeating` reads neither channel. The same fault sits at the other end in `a-lint-audit-falls-short-when-a-landing-moves-a-path-while-the-linter-walks`: there one reader drops a distinction the type carries, here one writer does. `unrun` sits on every verdict and `check/modules/audit-verdict/audit-verdict.module.code.ts:64` honours it, while `check/modules/audit-asking/audit-asking.module.code.ts:46` alone does not consult it. Each is a distinction the type carries and nearly every site honours, dropped at one site, unread there and unwritten here, and each is a one-line mend.

value.claim: A subagent's page is put up at SubagentStart and taken away at SubagentStop by the `state-subagent` hook. Both are detached landings it does not wait for, while it begins its turn at once, so a resumed subagent can run with no page: the stop has taken the page away and the put-up has not landed. With no page every change call is refused through `noPageSaid`. Three causes sit behind that one refusal and cannot be told apart: the put-up is still queued, the put-up refused, or no put-up was ever fired. The first two clear on a start event rather than on elapsed time, each SubagentStart firing a fresh put-up; whether waiting inside one turn clears them is unknown. `landingAgain` retries only where the reason names the lock or a put-back, so a landing refused for anything else is retried by nothing. A take-down also drops the reading record, so the agent owes its required reading again.
value.evidence:
One case, timed. Seat `nimue` resumed subagent `a62ddc0cb2ee9da93` at 16:11:11.533Z; its first turn lands 2.1 seconds later. Its page had gone at 16:10:31Z under the take-down for the previous return, `c0d2c598e27`, and the put-up for the resume landed only at 16:12:41Z, `414363d4fc9` — 89.5 seconds after the resume. In that interval the subagent made its only two change calls, drafting a `change-file` edit at 16:12:24.196Z and asking to list what it had kept at 16:12:31.777Z. Both were refused. It tried no more, and ended its turn at 16:13:29.432Z saying it was going to stop rather than work around it. The page it wanted had been there since 16:12:41Z: ten seconds after its last attempt, forty-eight seconds before it gave up.

What moves a page, and on what signal. `agent/hook/agent-hook/state-subagent/state-subagent.agent-hook.code.ts:113-115` calls `puttingUp` at a SubagentStart payload and `takingDown` at a SubagentStop, and the hook registers at those two events only. Each spawns a detached process running `agent/subagent/modules/presence/subagent-presence.module.code.ts` and is not waited on, the hook being given five seconds. The take-down is `took` at `:190-210`, landing `change-mechanical-file/remove-file-page` under `<slug> is done, so its page goes; what it was is in this repository's history` at `:208-209`. Nothing on that path reads how old a page is or looks for a live process.

What a resume restores, and how late. `wrote` at `:111-156` rebuilds a returning subagent's page out of `subagentPageInHistory`, minted id and all, and lands `<slug>: a subagent resuming takes up the page it had` at `:151-152`. A resume does restore the page. It restores it through `runMechanicalChange`, which takes `.git/akasha-landing.lock` and waits up to the 300 seconds `WAITED_AT_MOST` states, and `landingAgain` at `agent/subagent/modules/landing-again/subagent-landing-again.module.code.ts:33-43` retries five times at 30-second waits where the reason names that lock or a put-back. Nothing refused in the window above: the 89.5 seconds went on waiting for the lock behind other landings.

The census is a second reaper, it did not do this, and it cannot mend it. The subagent sweep judges each page WORKING, STALE or UNDETERMINED at `agent/subagent/modules/census/subagent-census.module.code.ts:143`; only STALE goes, and nothing schedules it. `pagesIn` enumerates pages from the index, so an agent with no page is not in the census at all.

What the agent reads. The first clause is `command/modules/change-acting/change-acting.module.code.ts:24` exactly: `this call names no agent whose page the edits would be kept beside`. `noPageSaid` at line 59 adds `PAGE_LANDING` from line 26. Draft, list, apply, show and drop all answer through it, so a page-less agent cannot even list what it kept. The page is found by `agentPathOf` at `domain/context/modules/warranting/warranting.module.code.ts:365-367`, out of the index and nowhere else.

The third cause, measured on this page's own writer. `nimue-a6f6ed863db6cd5fe` was taken down at 10:32:48 on a correct stop and resumed. Eight minutes later no put-up commit existed and the seat's log held zero occurrences of its id, while put-ups for other subagents landed that minute: the lock was free and the machinery working. No SubagentStart fired at all, and that variant never clears by waiting.

Cause two clears, and not on a clock. `state-subagent.agent-hook.code.ts:113-115` fires `puttingUp` at every SubagentStart, so each new turn asks for a fresh put-up whatever the last one did. A put-up refused is therefore not terminal — but what clears it is the next start event, not elapsed time. Whether an agent retrying inside one turn ever sees it clear is not established here.

A second case, and the scale behind it. `athena-ac3f05d42421ae25f` landed `8778562` at 09:58:19 -0600 on 2026-09-13 and was reaped 137 seconds later at 10:00:36, `4b58611a0da`. Its put-up that second refused rather than queuing: `subagent-presence.log:43`, 10:00:36.431, `holds a body already, so nothing is added` — the add-file answer at `change/modules/answer/change-answer.module.code.ts:161`, a reason `worthAnotherTry` does not retry. The page came back at 10:06:10, `88a2580e06b`, 334 seconds page-less, and was reaped again at 10:08:56. The agent reported four refusals over roughly seven minutes and a fifth call that worked. Across 2026-09-13, 82 reap commits landed and 19, 23.2%, were followed by a restore for the same id: mean gap 163 seconds, longest 679 (`ember-a9ba157c93365e2fa`, reaped and restored nine times that day). 23.2% is a floor rather than a rate — a subagent reaped mid-work that never resumed leaves no restore commit, so nothing here counts it.

What is not verified. Neither case was reproduced; both rest on an agent's report plus the commits, the presence log line and the code path. The interleaving behind `holds a body already` is undetermined: `wrote:122` must have found the path absent while the answer step moments later found it held, and what re-materialised it in that window is not established. What is established is the weaker claim this rests on — nothing orders the take-down against the put-up, and both decide against an unlocked read of the working tree before `applied` takes the lock.

What would close the gap rather than soften it: stop taking the page down at SubagentStop and let the census reap instead. At a resume the page would still be there and `wrote` returns early, so no landing runs. It needs a service to schedule it, which nothing does.

value.claim: Retiring a finding is itself a removal, and it orphans the prose of any page whose evidence names the slug going with it. `akasha edit --remove` judges the paths it takes away and never whether another page names them, so clearing dangling citations makes new ones. Repointing would not close it: a page retired for being false took a fact with it, so the sentence citing it wants rewriting rather than a new address.
value.evidence:
Measured 2026-09-02, and the experiment was one I ran on myself without meaning to.

Clearing 18 dangling citations, I retired `player-profile-is-web-code-that-shared-auth-bars-from-akasha` at `6ddd2941ed`, correctly: the hook it said could not land had landed at `5531ceda0a` as `akasha/temper/temper-player-profile/use-player`. That retirement orphaned a citation in `a-reversal-outlived-the-reason-it-was-taken-for`, which named it as an example of a hold already eroding. Repaired at `6d0636a5ed`.

The repair was no repoint. The hold had not eroded, it had fallen, so the sentence had to say something else. A mechanical sweep swapping the dead name for a live one would have carried a false sentence forward under a name that resolves, which is worse than one that does not: a reader can see a name reaching nothing.

The scale to size it by, over the findings after those repairs: 743 live findings carrying 105 cross-citations to 89 of them, and one dangling by deliberate annotation. That is a healthy reading and nothing keeps it there.

Two things an auditor of this wants. A slug is not recoverable once removed and a commit hash is, which is why every repair I landed named the removal commit rather than the removed name. And findings lived at `akasha/domain-system/finding/findings/` before they lived where they do, so a census globbing today's folder alone under-counts against history: my own first sweep missed `a-manifest-check-is-blind-to-tsx`, removed at `e1c441febe` from the old path, and reported 17 where there were 18.

What is unheld is that no page's prose names a slug being taken away. Whether that is worth holding is not decided here.

value.claim: Three rolling writers name the next part by incrementing, and none asks whether that name is free. Each finds its last part by walking contiguously from part 1 and stopping at the first gap, so a part past a gap is invisible to the writer that would name it next. Where the name is taken the file is opened for append rather than replaced, so live lines join the middle of what is already there. The log roller alone then zeroes its own byte count, so it would pour up to a full ceiling into a file it never measured, while the other two re-read the file's size before each append and would put at most one line in.
value.evidence:
Read 2026-09-12 at HEAD. Nothing was run: bun is refused inside the checkout, so this is read off the code rather than exercised.

THE ROLL. `agent/seat/log-day/modules/log-day-writing/log-day-writing.module.code.ts:261-271` reads `if (bytes > 0 && bytes + size > ENTRY_CEILING)`, then `const next = partAt(pagePath, part + 1)`, a guard on `next === null`, then `part += 1`, `path = join(root, next)`, `bytes = 0`. There is no `existsSync` on `next`. Line 278 writes with `appendFile`, so a name already taken is joined rather than replaced. `lastPartOf` at lines 136-151 walks up from `FIRST_PART` and breaks at line 146 on `!existsSync(join(root, next))`, so `part` counts the contiguous parts rather than the parts present. Those two together are what let `part + 1` be occupied and let the writer not know it.

THE SAME SHAPE TWICE MORE. `change/modules/edits-keeping/edits-keeping.module.code.ts:160-184`: `fillingAt` breaks on the same test at line 166, names `partAt(page, part + 1)` at line 173 with no existence test, and `appended` writes `appendFileSync` at line 182. `check/modules/cost/check-cost.module.code.ts:293-315`: `fillingAt` breaks at line 304, names the next part at line 313, and `appendedIn` appends at line 340. No sibling makes the check the log roller omits.

WHAT THE ROLLER ALONE DOES. Both siblings call `sizeOnDisk` on the part they found, at `edits-keeping.module.code.ts:170` and `check-cost.module.code.ts:308`, on every append, so an occupied part would be measured and rolled past after one line. The roller raises `bytes` in a closure at line 227 and sets it to 0 at line 269, so it would append up to ENTRY_CEILING, 8,388,608 bytes at `page/modules/entry-ceiling/entry-ceiling.module.code.ts:1`, on top of whatever the file already held.

WHO ELSE NAMES A PART. The roller's names carry the uncommitted mark: `uncommittedPartAt` composes `<page>.lines.partN.uncommitted.jsonl` through `page/modules/file-parts/page-file-parts.module.code.ts:20-27` and `page/modules/file-name/page-file-name.module.code.ts:180-186`. The only other caller composing that name is `change/mechanical/file/rename/rename-file-page/rename-file-page.change-mechanical.code.ts:130-136`, which renumbers a page's uncommitted parts from one by index as it carries them to the new name. `change/mechanical/file/divide/divide-file-page-property/divide-file-page-property.change-mechanical.code.ts:79-86` writes `partN` names for any page and any property, but through the committed `partsOf`, so it never names a `lines` part. So no second program contends for a log part today. What holds the roller up is an assumption it neither states nor tests.

WHAT THE DAMAGE WOULD LOOK LIKE. Nothing about the file's form would be wrong. The lines would still be JSONL, still one object to a line, out of order only against the timestamps they carry, and `partFiled` at line 279 would file the path as newly opened whether or not it was. Whether any reader of these lines judges their order was not established. The one consequence a check is written for is the overshoot: `check/code/pages/file-length/file-length.check-code.decision.code.ts:83` gives any `.jsonl` file ENTRY_CEILING, so a part carried past it would be named by size, long after the joining, and saying nothing of the order.

value.claim: A route file importing its generated types cannot be written at all until that app has been built in this checkout, because the guard reading its imports looks for typegen output that the commit does not carry. Three apps have never been built here, so every route file in them is unwritable.
value.evidence:
Measured on 2026-09-11 by an agent working under seat thea, while folding the web band of no-rule-in-two-files.

The guard is import-reaches-a-file, at change/guard/pages/import-reaches-a-file/import-reaches-a-file.change-guard.code.ts:89. It judges every import in a body the change writes, resolves a specifier through rootDirs from the nearest tsconfig, and refuses where it finds no file. A React Router route says `import ... from "./+types/root"`, and product/audhdalan/web/tsconfig.json:7 gives rootDirs as [".", "./.react-router/types"].

.react-router is a build folder: route-types-directory.build-folder-property.ts:10 names it, and build-folder-property.page-type.ts:14 says a build folder is outside the commit. So the file the guard needs is one a fresh checkout does not have and no landing writes.

value.claim: Starting a service again whenever the code it reaches changed starves any service whose work takes longer than the gap between landings. Nothing is violated while it happens: the unit text is what the page states, the reach is computed correctly, every invariant on every page holds, and the service still never finishes a unit of work. The system is consistent and starving at once, so no check placed on a page could catch it. What makes a service vulnerable is not being slow but being unable to resume: work deferred or retried from the start of a process is lost on every restart, and a service restarted more often than that work takes never lands any of it. The failure is in the interaction between two correct mechanisms rather than in either, which is why it survived review of both.
value.evidence:
On 2026-09-11 `command/modules/unit-landing/` began starting every workstation service again where a file that service reaches changed in the landing's commit. Ten long-running services import the akasha core, so any commit touching the core started all ten. At this repository's commit rate that was a start every three or four minutes.

`model-account-upkeep-service` renews each Claude account's OAuth token hourly. On starting it defers its work to a fixed moment inside the hour; the deferral measured as high as `startup delay 3566s`. Because the target is absolute rather than relative, a later start does not push the work further out — but a start before the target loses the wait entirely. Over 23:00-00:00 MDT the journal holds 16 starts, 16 `deferring` lines and 0 completed ticks, against 273 completed ticks earlier the same day. Across the ten services that hour there were 369 starts, 35 to 37 each.

One kill is recorded in full at 23:37:59: the service had reached 6 of 8 accounts, ignored SIGTERM mid-retry, took SIGABRT and dumped core.

The consequence ran outward. Upkeep renews tokens and nothing else does, so the `ctw` account's token expired. Two agents working in this repository then died mid-task with `401 OAuth access token has been revoked`. `model-account-upkeep-stall`, whose whole subject is ruling on whether upkeep has stalled, exited 1 and its unit read failed — correctly. The detector worked; the thing it watched was what broke. Nothing raised an alert, and the fault was found by reading `systemctl --user list-units --failed` for an unrelated reason.

The mend keeps 30 minutes between the starts a landing asks of one service, in `infrastructure/service/workstation/modules/service-restarting/`, with the start a service is owed written to `~/.local/state/workstation-services/service-restarts.json` naming the commit that service should be running, so a start held back is taken at the first landing past the interval rather than lost. After it landed: 167 landings, one start per service, 30 minutes 30 seconds of uninterrupted run, and `the tick is complete` at 00:39:44 with `ctw: its token re-authed`. The stall service cleared its own failed state by succeeding; no `reset-failed` was run.

The interval is a number read off one service's journal, which is the weakness of the mend rather than of the reading. A service crash-looping under `Restart=always` never accumulates the interval's uptime, so a start it is owed is never taken and it runs stale code indefinitely.

value.claim: A sign-out has to drop the reader's user id on the live component tree, and the url must not change until that render's effects have run, or the phone's keychain item is never cleared. `DeviceSecretSync` keys its effect on the user id, and the edge from an id to null is the only route to `clearAndRevoke`, which calls the native `DeviceSecret.clear()` — the one way a stale keychain item ever leaves the phone. Two ways of getting this wrong both leave the item on the phone forever. Returning from the sign-out branch without setting the id leaves the context holding the old id, so the effect never re-runs. Moving to `/sign-in` in the same commit unmounts `DeviceSecretSync`, because that route is outside the layout mounting the provider, so React runs the cleanup rather than the null-id effect. A whole-document reload is worse still: the remounted tree has no earlier id to compare against, so `signedOutFrom` is null and the clear is skipped on every sign-out.

WHAT THE CODE DOES. The sign-out branch of `onAuthStateChange` calls `setUserID(null)`, then awaits `afterEffectsRun()`, then `navigateRef.current(signInTo)` — a react-router navigate rather than a location assignment, so the tree is not torn down.

WHY THE YIELD WORKS. `afterEffectsRun` resolves a promise from a zero-delay `setTimeout`. React drains a queued commit's effects through a MessageChannel, and the event loop empties that queue ahead of any timer callback, so a zero-delay timer is a reliable marker that the last commit's effects have already run.

WHAT IS NOT CLAIMED. The comment said both rules had been broken here before; no commit was named for either break and none was looked up. Whether the other four web apps have the same coupling was not measured — `alan/web` is the only one mounting `DeviceSecretSync`.
