value.claim: A subagent's page is reaped by `took` at `agent/subagent/modules/presence/subagent-presence.module.code.ts:187-207` on one signal: liveness answering `returned`. `readOf` at `agent/subagent/modules/liveness/subagent-liveness.module.code.ts:53-55` answers `returned` whenever the agent id is among no running node folded out of the seat's transcript. Absence from a transcript cannot part not yet from no longer, and the reader resolves that ambiguity toward done. `seat-system/subagent/subagent.page-type.ts:68` already declares the opposite reading, and `:72` that a resumed subagent may be named nowhere while working, so the code contradicts its own page. What was not written down is how often it bites: 812 of 2055 reaps in history, 39.5%, were undone by the page coming back, and 120 of 183, 65.6%, since the liveness read was added for exactly this. The reader already answers which subagents ended, and `readOf` asks it nothing.
value.evidence:
What reaps. `took` spans `agent/subagent/modules/presence/subagent-presence.module.code.ts:187-207`; 194 is its `reading` parameter. 200 reads liveness, 201 leaves `working`, 202 leaves anything not `returned`, 205-206 land the removal under `<slug> is done, so its page goes; what it was is in this repository's history`. Only `returned` reaps, and the caller is the `state-subagent` hook at `agent/hook/agent-hook/state-subagent/state-subagent.agent-hook.code.ts:74` and `:111`: every SubagentStop asks, a turn-end rather than an agent-end.

Where `returned` comes from, in `agent/subagent/modules/liveness/`. `readOf:46-55` takes `transcriptOf(acting.seatId)`, builds a fresh reader at `:52`, then answers `namedAmong(running, own) ? working : returned`, with `HAS_RETURNED:24` reading `the transcript was read and names it nowhere`. `namedAmong:33-35` compares `one.agentId === own`. A running node's id is `agentByToolUseId.get(key) ?? null` at `code/editor/extension/modules/subagent-core/subagent-core.module.code.ts:201`, and `agentByTool` fills only at `:130-132` out of a tool result. So a subagent running but not yet named in its seat's transcript is a node with a null id, matches nothing, and answers `returned`: the not-yet reading as no-longer. A fold yielding no records answers the same way. `code/editor/extension/modules/tail-fold/tail-fold.module.code.ts:33-36` folds nothing where the file is gone, and `:47-55` returns before the fold loop where a banked offset meets a file truncated to nothing. Either way `forSeat` answers empty and every page under that seat goes at once, while `readOf:51` guards only a seat stating no transcript, never one stating a transcript with nothing in it.

The pages already say so, and the code does not. `seat-system/subagent/subagent.page-type.ts:68` is a departure: a subagent the transcript names nowhere is done for now rather than done for good. `:72`: a resumed subagent may be named nowhere while working. `:76` is a gap: a page goes once rather than going, coming back, and going again. The reader reads the other way. It parts could-not-look from looked already, three branches answering `unread` at `:49`, `:51` and `:57`, all three left alone by `took:202`; only looked-and-saw-nothing-yet is missing. `c0ff049f835`, 2026-09-12 07:15:59 -0600, added the liveness read for this: `a take-down leaves a page it cannot judge, so absence of a reading stops meaning the subagent is done`. Absence of a reading stopped meaning done. Absence within a reading did not.

One case, timed. `eec1a045cd9` at 09:18:23 -0600 removed the page of `athena-aabf299e2b4a09592` under `took:205`'s sentence. It was not done: `14118999788` at 09:19:29 put it back under `a subagent resuming takes up the page it had`, `wrote:149`. Sixty-six seconds page-less. Reaped again 09:25:20, restored 09:25:35, reaped last 09:25:55: three reaps over seven minutes.

How often. Every deletion of a `*.subagent.ts` page in history: 2292, with 2055 carrying `took`'s sentence, 193 a sweep's, 44 neither. Pairing each `took` reap with the next resume of the same slug: 812 of 2055, 39.5%, median gap 61s. Split at `c0ff049f835`: before it 692 of 1872, 37.0%; after it 120 of 183, 65.6%, median 66s, longest 1476s, over 36 slugs and 18810 page-less seconds in 2.2 hours. The windows are not matched populations, the later being heavy multi-turn work, so the rise is no proof the mend made things worse; what it shows is that the mend did not stop it. One slug, `athena-a1af23720bf9d1ac5`, was reaped 24 times. The gap at `:76` is the common case rather than an edge.

The repository disagreeing with itself, a second time. `agent/subagent/modules/census/subagent-census.module.code.ts` judges the same question on four routes and defaults to undetermined: `judgedOne:144-147` reads `/proc` for a live process under the agent id, the one signal the reaper never consults, then `:148-155`, `:156-162` and `:164-170`, falling to UNDETERMINED at `:172-178`. An ending is one route there and never load-bearing alone.

The mend, proposed, refused, not built. This pairs with `the-no-page-refusal-reads-two-index-entries-and-asserts-more-than-it-read`: there the refusal asserts more than it read, here the reaping does. The one-step mend — `readOf` answering `returned` only where the id is among the endings `endedForSeat` reports at `code/editor/extension/modules/subagent-reading/subagent-reading.module.code.ts:43` — was put up and refused. `forSeat:156-160` ends in `descend`, walking a child transcript per subagent to `MAX_SUBAGENT_DEPTH` 5 at `:33` and `:101-132`, and `namedAmong` recurses that tree; `endedForSeat:161-162` folds the seat transcript alone. Liveness covers the whole tree and endings one level of it, so the one step trades a race on every subagent for a leak on every grandchild. It would help on the empty-fold route, where absence reaps everything and an ending reaps nothing, but that does not carry it. A worry that a rotation loses recorded endings was raised and disproved: `restart` at `tail-fold.module.code.ts:39-51` re-folds from offset 0 over the whole file, and the one case skipping the fold is a file with nothing in it, where an empty state is the right answer. So the mend is two steps in order: `endedForSeat` descends the tree `forSeat` descends, and only then does reaping move onto endings. Until it descends, nothing should be reaped on them. The collector that would make a leak safe is not scheduled: `subagent-sweep` is named by no service or timer in the tree, so what is on offer is a leak with no collector. Scheduling it is a seat-system decision and no part of this finding. `notWorking` at `presence:215` is no part of it either: it collects everything not `working`, and `subagent-presence.module.test.ts:270-273` names that as chosen, a sweep leaving what a reading names as working and taking what it could not read.

value.claim: A subagent presence write takes the repository landing lock and holds it for tens of minutes under load, so every agent's landings queue behind the fleet's subagents starting and stopping.
value.evidence:
Measured on 2026-09-13 between 15:32 and 16:05 local, load average 43 to 72, memory 55 of 62 GB used with 0 free.

Four `akasha change apply` calls of mine in a row were refused with `another landing has held .git/akasha-landing.lock for longer than 300s, so this change was not judged and nothing was written`. The change was one edit to one page's text.

The lock file holds the holder's pid. Sampling it named a different process each time, and every one but the first was `agent/subagent/modules/presence/subagent-presence.module.code.ts <root> write <seat> <subagent-id> Explore <uuid> <millis>`: pid 3389566 at 25:56 elapsed, pid 39129 at 17:18, pid 4094195 at 28:28. One sample held the same pid across six reads eight seconds apart. Five such processes were alive at once, each about 600 MB resident.

They are doing work rather than hung. pid 39129 was in state R with 21 threads, and its `read_bytes` went from 1899200512 to 1937760256 over six seconds. pid 3030430, the one non-presence holder, was in state D reading about 55 MB a second and had read 4.5 GB.

The cost is not checks. `MECHANICAL_KIND` in `mechanical-change-running.change-runner.code.ts:29` states `runsChecks: false`, and `subagent-presence` lands through `landedMechanically` at line 107 of that file. What a mechanical change does before it writes is `foldedOver(ledgerAt(root, bodyIn(root), runAt), asked)` at line 76, which builds the whole change world.

That `ledgerAt` is what reads the gigabytes is inference from where the time can be rather than something measured. What is measured is the elapsed time, the read volume, the resident size and the lock.

A subagent starting and a subagent stopping each write a presence page, and there are many seats. At this load the lock is held more often than not, so a landing of any size is a coin toss.

value.claim: `check-reaches-a-path-through-the-index` cannot be widened to judge a page's test fixtures, because the check names a page wherever the index knows a page ending with the path spelled, and a fixtures file spells short paths into a tree it invents rather than into this one. Closing the hole the widening aimed at takes a narrower rule matching a whole path rather than a suffix, which is a redesign of the check rather than a widening of its reach.
value.evidence:
A fixture builds a small tree of its own and spells paths into that tree. Those paths are short, so the suffix rule the check states matches a real page almost every time. The fixtures beside `rooting.module.test.ts` spell `cli/cli.module.code.ts`, and the check names the page at `command/modules/cli/cli.module.code.ts`, which the fixture never meant.

The widening landed as `aad3381d614`, and an audit of the check over the whole tree then answered `1 check answered for aad3381d61443031ff27fc625bbe159e462b6efd, and 141 refusals in all`. Counting the literals that exactly equal a tracked path had predicted 17. The gap between 17 and 141 is the suffix rule firing on invented paths.

Every refusal becomes ratchet debt for whichever seat next touches that file, so the widening would have charged 141 files to every other seat for a hole nobody had hit. It was reverted at `8949f12afd9`.

The hole the widening aimed at is real: a captured fixture holding a path a move respelled goes stale with nothing judging it. Catching that wants the check to match a literal against a whole path rather than against any page ending with it, and to run that narrower rule on fixtures alone.

The sweep. `remove-unused-export-keywords.change-agent.code.ts:46` asks `surplusIn` which exports a file may lose, and `surplusIn:28` takes what to spare from `sparedIn` in `no-unused-exports.check-code.decision.code.ts`. So one rule decides both what the check refuses and what the sweep strips, and a hole in that rule is a hole in a change that writes files.

The hole. `a9b5bcd45de` ('stop publishing the values only their own files name', 2026-09-12T08:00:05-06:00) ran the sweep and took `export` off the root loader of `alan/web/root.tsx:104`. React Router finds a loader by its export alone, so the root loader stopped running. `root.tsx:109` reads the nonce from that loader's data, `:134`, `:146` and `:147` hand it to `<script src="/sidebar-boot.js">`, `<ScrollRestoration>` and `<Scripts>`, and `security-headers.module.code.ts:31` writes `script-src 'self' 'nonce-...' 'strict-dynamic'`. Under `strict-dynamic` the browser ignores `'self'`, so four un-nonced tags including the module entry were blocked and nothing hydrated. The console said so twice: the blocks, then `TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'streamController')`, because the nonced streaming script reached for a `window.__reactRouterContext` the blocked script never wrote.

The mend, and what it left. `bb19b4f647a` ('spare the names React Router reaches a route module by, rather than the whole file', 2026-09-13T08:21:11-06:00) added `ROOT_ROUTE`, `APP_LAYOUT` and `BY_FILE` at `no-unused-exports.check-code.decision.code.ts:58-85`, so the sweep can no longer strip these names. It restored none of the files the sweep had already stripped. Twenty-five hours separate the two commits, and for all of them alanwalton.com served a page whose client never booted.

The spread. On 2026-09-13, before this was restored, seven route modules across five apps held an unexported route convention: `alan/web/root.tsx:104`, `alan/atlas-web/root.tsx:37`, `alan/atlas-web/routes/atlas-page-detail/atlas-page-detail.route.code.tsx:15`, `temper/web/root.tsx:63`, `product/archive-of-worlds/web/root.tsx:40`, `product/smilingjenny/web/root.tsx:25` and `product/audhdalan/web/root.tsx:27`. The last two are `const loader = rootNonceLoader`, which a search for `function loader` does not find. Live pages confirmed the render: alanwalton.com and smilingjenny.me each served un-nonced script tags until `b218a5d9ab5` restored the exports and the two web apps were put up again.

Why nothing caught it. `no-unused-exports.check-code.ts:156` states `experimental: true`, and `:77` states that nothing is judged while it does, so the check refuses nothing while the change reading its rule writes files. No check anywhere refuses a route module that declares a route convention and does not export it, so neither the landing nor the twenty-five hours after it were judged by anything. The fault was found because Alan could not sign in.

What the directive says. `Blame The Mechanism` on `akasha.domain.ts:150-155` reads 'Treat a fault a mechanical change lands as a fault in the program that composed the change', with the aid 'Mend the program, never the one landing.' Read against a sweep that has already written to many files, that aid names the mend and excludes the restoration.
value.claim: A change that writes across the repository leaves damage that outlives the mend of the rule it wrote by. Mending the rule stops the next sweep and restores nothing the last one landed, so the damage keeps running until something outside the repository notices. Here one stripped `export` was mended in the rule twenty-five hours later while seven files and five live sites stayed broken, and the aid on `Blame The Mechanism` reads as instructing exactly that division. Nothing in akasha measures what a sweep already landed, so the size of a sweep's outstanding damage is not a quantity anyone can ask for.

A rebuild that ablates behaviour states its reason in the code, and that reason can stop being true without anything failing. `akasha/collections/great-courses/sync-run` records no sync run and says so, on the ground that the record lives outside akasha. The record now lives inside akasha. Two of the three syncs stopped recording runs and nothing reported it, because a sync that records nothing and a sync that records a clean run both exit zero.
value.evidence: Measured 2026-09-03. `akasha/collections/great-courses/sync-run/sync-run.module.code.ts` exports `trackSyncRun(source, syncFn)`, whose whole body is a `console.warn` naming `NO_ROW_ROAD` — "a `sync-run` row is inside a page's body rather than at a path of its own, the store answers for `akasha/` alone, and this record is `pages/sync/<source>.sync.runs.jsonl` outside it" — then the sync, then a throw if any item failed. Row counts and newest row at the time of measurement: wandering-inn 213, `2026-09-02T13:41:50Z`; the-great-courses 29, `2026-09-01T13:39:34Z`; royal-road 1,382, `2026-08-18T00:30:43Z`. `akasha/collections/royal-road/syncing/royal-road-syncing.module.code.ts` matches `sync-run|runStatus|recordingRun|trackSyncRun|rowLanding|running-run` zero times, against a control confirming the search sees `syncWanderingInn` where it is present. So the only live implementation of run recording in the repository was `tools/lib/wandering-inn/run-record.ts`, reached by the wandering inn sync alone. It was carried into akasha at `ba266f5e38` as `akasha/story/wandering-inn/modules/sync-run-recording`, kept generic in the `source` it records for so great-courses and royal-road can adopt it. value.claim: A Tailwind `@source` glob is path-keyed configuration no typecheck and no build failure can see. While a package is half-moved its classes are emitted only where a `globals.css` names both halves, and four apps named the shared half alone. The cost rises as the move finishes rather than falling. One class here is built at run time rather than written, so no glob reaches it and only a safelist can.
value.evidence:
Measured against built stylesheets rather than read. `alanwalton/web/app/globals.css:26` and `app-capacitor/globals.css:26` named `shared/pages-ui/src/**` alone while `akasha/pages-system/pages-ui` held 233 files reached by 44 subpath imports and was scanned by nothing. Five literal classes from `use-app-version-check.module.code.ts:21-24` stood at 0 occurrences in `root-BkDy5U6f.css` at 113,920 bytes. Naming the akasha half returns exactly those five and takes the sheet to 114,234 bytes, the control figure this initiative already recorded.

A glob adds paths to the scan set and Tailwind emits the union over scanned files, so the repair cannot regress an app.

The cost curve is why this is worth a page. The akasha half is 186 logic modules against 5 `.tsx`, so one toast was affected. 116 `.tsx` components still stand under the other glob. When they move, the shared glob matches nothing and the omission drops most of a site's styling rather than one toast.

value.claim: Every inventory chunk already filed is deleted on the next import, because the import matches a chunk's snapshot against a page id and a filed chunk names its snapshot by slug.
value.evidence: `temper/items-core/modules/plan-inventory-import/plan-inventory-import.module.code.ts` keeps a chunk only where `row.inventory === targetSnapshotId`, and pushes the chunk onto `chunksToDelete` otherwise. `targetSnapshotId` comes from `planSnapshotImport`, which reads the snapshot row's `id`, a uuid. value.claim: A test file already over its processor budget refuses every landing that touches it, so the file cannot be mended by the landing that would mend it. The budget is read only when a landing carries that file, so a file drifts over the budget with nothing saying so until someone is barred. The refusal names the file rather than the debt, so whoever arrives next reads the cost as their own and shortens what they wrote.
value.evidence: `rename-code-token.change-agent.test.ts` spends 5.3 processor seconds against a budget of 5, judged by `tests-pass` over the tree with nothing drafted. Three landings that shortened the file were each refused, one of them measuring 5.2. The cost is structural: eighteen of its tests build a whole TypeScript program, because the change under test builds one before any guard of its own is consulted. The audit does not read this budget, so nothing finds such a file until a landing touches it.

value.claim: A test file held under a memory ceiling pays the kernel's reclaim as its own processor time, so the processor ceiling refuses that file for being slow and the advice the refusal gives cannot work. The ceiling a test file states is written to `memory.high` of the cgroup the run is made in, and the processor seconds that same file is judged by are read from `cpu.stat` of that same cgroup. `memory.high` throttles rather than refuses, and reclaim is kernel time inside the cgroup, so a file wanting more than the ceiling is charged for being held under it. Nothing in the refusal names memory, because the comparison is against the processor ceiling alone.
value.evidence:
Measured on one workload, one machine, with only the cgroup's ceiling differing. 128 MB: 5.13 to 5.96 processor seconds, 3.76 of them system, peak resident held to 168 MB. 256 MB: 2.36. 512 MB: 2.06. 1024 MB: 1.99. No ceiling: 1.86 to 1.88, 0.22 system, peak resident 382 MB. The whole cliff sits between 128 and 256, and the system share is what moves.

Loading the import graph of a test file that imports the TypeScript parser peaks at 163 MB before one test runs, so every such file was over a 128 MB ceiling at import time rather than under test.

`code/module/properties/test.code-file-property.ts` stated `maxMemoryMb: 128`. `code/running/modules/code-tests/code-tests.module.code.ts` reads that value at line 70 and hands it to `ran` as `memoryCeiling` at line 279. `util/run/modules/running/running.module.code.ts` writes it to `memory.high` of the cgroup it makes, and reads `usage_usec` from `cpu.stat` of that same cgroup for the seconds the file is judged by.

The file this was found on went from 5.6 to 2.6 processor seconds on the ceiling alone, which landed at 3213afde36f. The refusal it had been drawing advised deleting a test nothing needs, which would not have helped, because the cost sat in no test.

value.claim: A test run under the deploy gate's merged tree is measuring a tree no commit ever had, so a failure it reports cannot be told apart from a real one by reading the failure.
value.evidence:
`mountedOver` at `code/running/modules/test-overlay/test-overlay.module.code.ts:78` mounts an overlay whose `lowerdir` is the live checkout and whose `upperdir` holds the bodies the caller hands it, which for the deploy gate are the bodies of the commit being deployed. Upper wins wherever both layers carry a path, and lower shows through everywhere upper is silent. Only paths named with a null body are taken away, by the `rm -rf` at line 37. So the merged tree is one commit's bodies for the files that commit touched, over the working tree as it was at the moment the run began, for everything else. No commit ever had that tree, and the lower half keeps moving while the swarm lands.

The confirmed instance is module resolution. A gate run on 2026-09-12 refused with `Cannot find module 'akasha/util/narrow/as-object-record/...'` reached from `merged/person/modules/enrolment/person-enrolment.module.test-fixtures.ts`. The importer's body came from the commit, where that specifier was right. The target's folder had been moved to `util/narrow/modules/as-object-record/` in the checkout by `4d1ad78bf19` at 09:10:17, and that move was not among the bodies the upper layer carried, so the lower layer showed only the new path. Both ends of the specifier existed; neither end was broken; the two ends were from different commits. A refusal naming a path that exists at both ends is this.

What makes it worth writing down is that the failure reads as a real one. A missing module reads as a bad import and invites mending the import. A measurement that comes back short reads as a miscalibrated threshold and invites loosening the threshold. Either mend would be landed against a tree that no commit had and would then be carried by every tree that follows.

The reading error is worth more than the mechanism. Three unrelated faults were cleared inside one window on 2026-09-12 and the first mend to land was credited with all three. The overlay mends landed at 08:46:31 and 08:53:44; a gate run at 08:57 carried both and still refused on everything. Astra's fixture mends landed at 09:03 and 09:04, Aine's `76c37d27c3c` at 09:18:09, and the deploy that came back clean began at 09:18:30. The peak-memory assertions in `util/run/modules/running/running.module.test.ts` were never overlay-caused at all: they were unsatisfiable under the 128 MiB ceiling `code/running/modules/code-tests/code-tests.module.code.ts:279` holds every test file to, and Aine's commit brought them under it and recorded why on `util/run/modules/running/running.module.ts` as a constraint. Sequence was read as consequence, twice, by two agents in turn. A correct mend landing first is how a wrong theory gets its evidence.

`a-hook-loads-against-the-checkout-a-landing-leaves-between-its-edits-and-its-moves` is the same fact from another direction. value.claim: A unit that fails and runs again within one timer period is well again before the watcher's next sample, so its failures are told to nobody and nothing keeps a count.
value.evidence:
`workstation-deploying.service` failed nine times between 07:15:07 and 07:46:49 on 2026-09-12, and `service-watching` told nobody. The outage ledger at `~/.local/state/workstation-services/service-outages.json` holds `{}`, so the watcher recorded no outage at all. The two tellings it has ever sent about this unit went to aranya at 06:31:16 and 06:45:11, both before that window opened.

The unit is a `oneshot` on `workstation-deploying.timer`, which fires every 60 seconds, and `service-watching.timer` samples every 60 seconds. `brokenIn` at `infrastructure/service/workstation/modules/service-health/service-health.module.code.ts:102` reads `ActiveState`: `failed` is broken, `active`, `activating` and `reloading` are well, and a unit with a timer reading `inactive` is well. A oneshot reads `failed` only between the run that failed and the next start, so the watcher sees a failure only by sampling inside that window. At 07:23:22 a run failed and the next run began at 07:23:23, leaving one second. While a deploy is in flight the unit reads `activating`, which is well, and a deploy runs for minutes.

The nine failures were four faults rather than one. Two were `akasha deploy` running past the 300 seconds its page allows, at 07:15:07 and 07:21:05. One was a scope name loaded with no deploy holding it, at 07:15:09, mended by `602c17195f4`. Six were `akasha deploy service-workstation` refusing because the tests it runs were red, at 07:23:22, 07:30:06, 07:33:55, 07:40:44, 07:43:46 and 07:46:49, over six different commits; the last reported 72 of 1009 tests failing across six test files. In those six the loop was right and the repository was red, and a unit marked failed for that reads exactly like a loop that is broken.

The failures ended without a mend. The tests are red now: the `tests-pass` verdict at `99172024da6`, recorded 2026-09-12T14:01:24.259Z, refuses with nine test files failing. `akasha deploy` runs only the tests beside what the change carries, so whether a tick refuses depends on which files the swarm landed since the deployed commit rather than on anything having been put right.

The loop's mends are running rather than written. `service-workstation` is deployed at `eec1a045cd9f52b02d7e9f77fc4e16a4c346ab93`, which `infrastructure/service/workstation/service-workstation.page-type.uncommitted.ts` records beside `deployEndedAt` 2026-09-12T15:23:34.340Z. That tree carries both `--measured` and `--property=RuntimeMaxSec=3600` on every deploy a tick starts, so a deploy is ended by systemd at an hour rather than by the 300 seconds the shared stop allows. The hour is what makes that ending an ending rather than a kill mid-work, and no scope kill has fired: this boot's journal holds no runtime-limit ending for any deploy scope.

A tick that refuses a red tree no longer fails the unit. At 09:10:42 a tick refused `dc68b09c3006ca6f5bfbd810b59122bf97233920` because four tests in `util/run/modules/running/running.module.test.ts` were red, said so in one sentence, and the unit finished well; the same page records that refusal as `deployRefusedAt` 2026-09-12T15:10:42.365Z, which is how the loop tells a refusal apart from an ending.

The hole that remains is a service the loop leaves unchosen for many ticks running, which nothing tells. A deploy that hangs keeps its hold, `heldNow` reads the holding process alive, and every tick after that weighs the service and says nothing of it was put up. Five ticks in a row between 09:19:04 and 09:23:08 each said one service was weighed and one of those had a deploy running, which is what a deploy in flight looks like and equally what a deploy hung for hours looks like. A service left unchosen silently reads exactly like a service with nothing to do, and no count is kept either way. A telling after some number of ticks is named here and not built.

A watcher that samples the current state of a unit sees a fault only while that fault is the unit's current state. A unit that fails and runs again on a short timer is well again before the next sample, so its outage is told to nobody and nothing keeps a count of how often it broke.

value.claim: A web pod's server loads `build/server/index.js` on its first line, so a pod with no build beside that server never becomes ready. A deploy makes its build inside a pod that is already running, so a pod that cannot become ready is a pod no deploy can build for: nothing builds until something is up, and nothing comes up until something has built. `alan/web` alone breaks that deadlock, with an init container that builds at pod start where no build is there and exits at once where one is, so a fresh commit's build is served rather than made a second time. The other four web apps emit no such container and the deadlock is open for them.
value.evidence:
Read 2026-09-08 while marking the client env keys for vite. This was a ten-line comment above `webBuildInitContainer` in `alan/web/alanwalton-web/alanwalton-web.manifest.code.ts`, which `no-code-comments` refuses at patch, so it is moved here rather than deleted.

WHAT THE CONTAINER DOES. `webBuildInitContainer` emits an init container whose script opens `if [ -f build/server/index.js ]; then ... exit 0; fi`, then reads `git rev-parse HEAD` out of the orchestrator cache checkout, exports it as the build sha, and runs `bun run build`. It takes `envFrom` the whole `alanwalton-secrets` secret and the same Supabase values the serving container is given.

WHY IT IS NEEDED. `buildInPod` in `infrastructure/cluster/services/web-app-building/web-app-building.module.code.ts` finds a pod with `livePod` and answers `no running pod carries <workload> in <namespace>, so nothing holds a build` where there is none. It then execs the build into that pod's `code-sync` container. So the deploy's only build path wants a pod already up, and the serving container cannot come up without a build.

WHAT PUTS A POD THERE. A node whose orchestrator cache is cold, and a manifest change moving the package path away from the build the old path held. `command/modules/deploy-web-putting-up/deploy-web-putting-up.module.ts` states both as constraints: `A pod starts on a build kept beside the package that pod runs from`, and `A manifest moving that package rolls out a pod holding no build to start on`.

WHAT IS NOT CLAIMED. Only `alan/web` emits a build init container. `alanwalton-atlas`, `archive-of-worlds-web-manifests`, `smilingjenny-web-manifests` and `temper-web-manifests` emit none, so the same deadlock is open for those four. Whether any of them has been left down by it was not measured and no incident was looked for.

value.claim: `landedMechanically` takes a whole file body, so two workers adding entries to one shared manifest silently revert each other. The second landing carries a body read before the first landed, and writing it whole takes the first worker's lines back out. Both calls answer code 0, both commits stand, and the loss shows in neither. The shared manifests of this migration are exactly where every worker in a lane must write: a package's `exports` block and a workspace package's `part-slugs`.
value.evidence:
Measured 2026-09-03. I landed a34a6cb54e, which added two lines to akasha/seat-system/package.json: `./seat-attached` and `./seat-modes`. `git show a34a6cb54e:akasha/seat-system/package.json` carries both at lines 13 and 15.

The next commit touching that file, 51db8ff642, has a34a6cb54e as its PARENT — `git log -1 --format=%h 51db8ff642^` prints a34a6cb54e — and its diff on that file is two deletions and no additions, both of them my lines. So the clobber is not a merge and not a base-commit collision: the worker composed its body from a snapshot of the file taken before my landing, and the landing wrote that stale body whole.

Nothing reported it. My call had already returned code 0 and its commit stands untouched; the other worker's call returned code 0 too. I found it only because I checked the file on disk afterwards rather than trusting the answer, and the two lines were not there. A worker that verified with `git show <its own commit>` instead of reading the working tree would have seen its lines and concluded the landing held.

What this bears on is every lane writing a shared manifest, which in this migration is all of them. The read-the-file-then-write-it-whole shape is what the brief's own landing recipe teaches, so the defect is in the recipe rather than in the worker. A landing that took a line to add rather than a body to write would not have this failure mode. Until then the workable practice is to re-read the manifest and re-apply immediately before landing, and to verify on the working tree rather than on one's own commit.

value.claim: A writer and a reader of one persisted shape, with no test between them, drifted apart in silence. `loadChapterForOffline` in `alan/library` wrote six keys; the zod shape in `alan/web` required ten, one of which no writer in this repository has ever produced. Every chapter body Alan's phone held failed on read-back, so his whole offline library read as empty, and it had never once worked. Nothing reported it: the reader drops a row it cannot parse, and the downloader asks the index which ids are held rather than asking the bodies, so ids read as held forever and nothing is fetched again. Each down-sync run logged completion. The general shape: a value written in one package and validated in another needs a test running both halves, because a test written against the reader alone is written to fit the reader and proves nothing.
value.evidence:
Read 2026-09-10 at HEAD before dd455a53e8, and repaired at dd455a53e8, 1a604d1344 and 96ea9c95e4.

THE TWO SIDES. `alan/web/modules/content-pages-cache-core/content-pages-cache-core.module.code.ts:24-37` declared `PersistedContentPageSchema` over ten keys: `id`, `seq`, `title`, `icon`, `slug`, `userId`, `pageTypeId`, `pageTypeSlug`, `uniqueKey`, `parentKey`. Nine were `.nullable()`, which in zod admits a null value and still requires the key. `.passthrough()` admits extra keys and relaxes nothing. `alan/library/reading/modules/offline-reading/offline-reading.module.code.ts:86-92` selected `["id","title","position","ownLength","body"]` and handed `savePages` an object of six keys: those five and `text`. Eight of the ten required keys were absent, so `safeParse` failed on the first of them, `seq`.

I ran both shapes against the writer's own object outside the repository, on the zod the workspace holds: the old one refuses with `expected number, received undefined` at `seq`; the new one admits it and keeps `text` and `body`, while still refusing a `title` that is a number and an object with no `id`.

`parentKey` is produced nowhere. A repository-wide grep finds four hits: a local parameter at `infrastructure/cluster/k8s-types/modules/k8s-manifest-walker/k8s-manifest-walker.module.code.ts:133`, a field at `temper/addon-generators/modules/addon-data-page/addon-data-page.module.code.ts:15`, and the declaration itself. It is not among the ten entries of `PROMOTED_COLUMN` at `page/access/modules/routing-core/routing-core.module.code.ts:6-17`, and it is not a key of `Page` at `page/core/modules/page-types/page-types.module.code.ts:4-14`. No write path could have satisfied that shape.

WHAT THE READ SIDE CONSUMES. `parsePersistedContentPage` hands its result to `asPage`, which is a cast rather than a check. `doSave` and `doLoad` at `alan/web/modules/content-pages-fs/content-pages-fs.module.code.ts:94-132` touch `page.id` alone, as the index key and the file name. `page/ui/supabase/modules/use-page/use-page.module.code.ts:124-127` and `page/ui/supabase/modules/related-pages-coalesce/related-pages-coalesce.module.code.ts:46` hand rows to `toPageWithProperties`, which reads `props.id` and spreads the rest under `properties`. The reader itself, `page/ui/components/modules/page-reader-content/page-reader-content.module.code.tsx:92-96`, reads the body under a key its page type names, so no fixed body key can be required of every held page. `id` is the whole of what the read side needs, and requiring a body key would refuse every held page that is not a chapter.

NOT MEASURED. I did not run the repaired code on a device, so that Alan's held library now reads is inferred from the round trip rather than observed. value.claim: `add-property-values` does not reach the agent change `add-property-value`. It reaches the mechanical change directly and works out for itself the four things that agent change works out: whether the key holds one value, what the key holds, whether the page's type declares the key at all, and where a new key falls in the body. All four were mended twice on 2026-09-10, once in each change, because the plural change cannot delegate to the one. It cannot delegate because `addPropertyValue` answers the answer alone, while the plural change needs the world each line leaves so the line after it is put in over that world. Until the two are joined, a fault mended in one is live in the other, and which of the two an agent picks settles what that agent gets.
value.evidence: The duplication is at `change/agent/file-content/add-property-values/add-property-values.change-agent.code.ts`. `putIn` calls `readFor`, `typeIn`, `declaresIn`, `targetsIn`, `reaches`, `singleIn`, `afterIn` and `holdsIn`; `addPropertyValues` then assembles `single`, `holds` and `after` onto the line and reaches `change-mechanical-file-content/add-property-value`. `change/agent/file-content/add-property-value/add-property-value.change-agent.code.ts` calls the same eight readers and assembles the same three keys onto its own argument. The two bodies are the same work written twice. Four mendings on 2026-09-10 show the cost. `57c8ad6ae8` refused an undeclared key in the singular change; `19f62f57b3` spelled a value as its property is spelled in the singular change; `753bea1afe` placed a new key in the singular change. Each left the plural change as it was. `7c6613e317` placed a new key in the plural change and `56a96ef17d` did the other two there, three weeks of drift compressed into one day only because one agent happened to read both. What delegation would need: `addPropertyValues` threads `seen = reached.world` after every line, so each line is worked out over the edits the lines before it left, and that is an invariant on its page. `reach` answers `{ said, world }`. `addPropertyValue` throws the world away and answers `.said`. So delegation needs `addPropertyValue` to answer both, with its own `runChange` taking `.said` off. What that costs is smaller than it looks and was not fully read. `addPropertyValue` is imported by its own test alone. The runner reaches `runChange`, and `change/runner/pages/agent-change-running/agent-change-running.change-runner.addressed.ts` binds only that function's `Parameters`, not what it answers. So the signature to change is the inner one, not the one the runner holds. What was not read is whether any guard or any other agent change reads what an agent change answers in a way that a wider answer would disturb, and whether the same shape is wanted for the other agent changes a plural change might one day reach. One thing found on the way, worth knowing before touching these tests. The fixture world at `page/index/modules/fixture-world/fixture-world.module.code.ts:139` declares `module` as carrying `code`, `test`, `note` and `part-slugs` and nothing else, while every module page that fixture writes carries a `definition`. So a change that refuses an undeclared key refuses `definition` in the fixture though it would never refuse it in the repository. Two tests in `add-property-values.change-agent.test.ts` had to move off `definition` onto `test` for that reason. The fixture is a poor model of the repository on this point, and mending it means adding a `text-property` page type and a `definition` property to `REPO_VOCABULARY`, which many tests read.

value.claim: Two `file-property` pages, `addon-git-ignore` and `git-ignore`, carry the same `propertySlug`, the same `definition` and the same `fileName`. Nothing tells the pages apart but their own slugs and their folders. `eso-addon` reaches for the first and `ios-app` for the second, and both resolve to a `.gitignore` beside the page. The duplicate wants deleting, and the surviving property wants a home outside `ios-app`, where any page type can reach it.

`akasha/code-system/eso-addon/properties/addon-git-ignore.named-file-property.ts` is 12 lines: `slug: "addon-git-ignore"`, `propertySlug: "git-ignore"`, `definition: "what a build leaves behind that git does not keep"`, `fileName: ".gitignore"`, id `01a06036-9b79-7b11-972f-655af36acfd5`.

`akasha/code-system/ios-app/properties/git-ignore.named-file-property.ts` is the same 12 lines with `slug: "git-ignore"` and id `01a0591d-e23c-76ca-8764-552fd305e707`. Every other field matches character for character, exported type included, both being `"gitignore"`.

`akasha/code-system/eso-addon/eso-addon.page-type.ts` names `named-file-property/addon-git-ignore` in `partSlugs` and `{ pagePropertySlug: "named-file-property/addon-git-ignore", required: false, many: false }` in `properties`. Nothing else in akasha imports either page.

Nothing breaks today. `filePropertiesAt` in `akasha/pages-system/index/index-entries/index-entries.module.code.ts` line 140 keys the file-property map by `propertySlug`, so both pages write `git-ignore` to `.gitignore` and the second write is the same as the first. The mend is two moves. Delete `addon-git-ignore` and point `eso-addon` at `named-file-property/git-ignore`. value.claim: akasha says a day's span twice and the two do not agree. `getEsoDayWindow` answers `{ start: Date; end: Date }`, the stretch from one six-in-the-morning reset to the next; `DayWindow` in `health-samples-day` answers `{ from: string; to: string }` in ISO text, the stretch from when a day was recorded as opening to when the next day opened. One day string draws two different pairs of instants, and neither name says which stretch it hands back. Nothing derives either shape from the other, and reconciling the two onto one is unclaimed.
value.evidence:
Measured 2026-09-14.

`alan/harness/day/modules/eso-day/eso-day.module.code.ts:57` declares `getEsoDayWindow(dayStr): { start: Date; end: Date }`: the six-in-the-morning New York reset on that day to the same reset on the day after. A day string that is no day answers `{ start: new Date(0), end: new Date(0) }` rather than refusing.

`alan/harness/health-samples-day/modules/opening-window/opening-window.module.code.ts:13-16` declares `DayWindow` as `{ from: string; to: string }`, ISO text. `openingWindowIn` at `:151-161` fills it from the first sleep block recorded on the day's page to the first on the next day's, and refuses where either is unrecorded. `spannedWindowIn` at `:170-185` fills the same shape but falls back to six in the evening Mountain time the day before and to now or that evening, so two callers asking the same module about one day are handed two different stretches under one type.

Where the two meet: `alan/track/daily/modules/day-opening/day-opening.module.code.ts:20-25` (`openedDayWindow`) answers `spannedWindowIn` where that answers, and otherwise builds a `DayWindow` by hand out of `getEsoDayWindow` with `.toISOString()` on each end. That is the one place one shape is turned into the other, and it converts the type without converting the meaning: the reset-to-reset stretch is handed back under the name of the opening-to-opening one.

Who reads each: `agent/model/account/modules/pacing/model-account-pacing.module.code.ts:53` and `alan/harness/alan-readouts/modules/day-readout-watching/day-readout-watching.module.code.ts:298` take `getEsoDayWindow(day).end.getTime()`. `alan/harness/attributes/modules/totalling/attributes-totalling.module.code.ts:111-112`, `alan/harness/attributes/modules/reading/attributes-reading.module.code.ts:93`, `alan/harness/plants/modules/reading/plants-reading.module.code.ts:30` and `alan/track/daily/modules/nutrition-grams/nutrition-grams.module.code.ts:27` take `openedDayWindow`; `alan/harness/health-samples-day/modules/active-calories/active-calories.module.code.ts:30` takes `spannedWindow`. Nothing reads both, so no one caller has to reconcile them.

What lets it drift unseen: `new Date` and `Date.parse` take an ISO string and a millisecond count alike, and `.getTime()` on one side meets `.toISOString()` on the other, so a stretch handed across the seam typechecks whichever it is. No test judges that `openedDayWindow`'s fallback and `spannedWindowIn`'s fallback name the same instants, and they do not: one starts at six in the morning New York, the other at six in the evening Mountain.

Searching every `*.code.ts` for a type spanning a day answers these two and no third. Reconciling them touches `health-samples-day`, `day-opening` and every caller above, which is design work rather than a mend.

value.claim: `akasha service install --all` plans to remove every unit it owns when the service index reads empty, because an empty read is not a refusal and `planFor` treats 'nothing should stand' and 'nothing was read' as the same state. The guard that told them apart stood in `tools/lib/service-project.ts` and did not come across.
value.evidence:
Measured 2026-09-03 by reading the predicates rather than the refusal texts, while ablating the `tools/lib` service island.

THE CHAIN, END TO END. `akasha/service-system/workstation-services/service-reading/service-reading.module.code.ts:78-89` — `everyService` collects pages and returns `{ services }`; where the index lists none it returns `{ services: [] }`, which is not the `{ refused }` shape. `akasha/command-system/command/service/service.command.code.ts:56-57` — `if ("refused" in read) return refused(...)`, so an empty list passes. Line 64 then takes `owned = ourInstalled(home)`, every unit symlinked out of our staging directory. `akasha/service-system/workstation-services/service-installing/service-installing.module.code.ts:100-113` — `planFor` builds `ours` from `standing`, so for an empty `standing` it is empty and `remove = owned.filter((one) => !ours.has(one))` is every owned unit.

The single-slug path is not exposed: line 64 narrows through `ownedByService`, so a bad slug is refused at `readFor` and reaches no plan.

WHAT WAS LOST. `tools/lib/service-project.ts:124-125` raised `NothingRead` — 'no service document was read, so nothing here can say which units should stand' — precisely to keep an empty read from being read as an empty intent. That file is deleted in this same change as unreachable dead code, its command layer `tools/command/service/` having already gone, so this page is where the guard now stands recorded. The blob is recoverable at `git rev-parse <commit>:tools/lib/service-project.ts`.

WHY IT MATTERS HERE. This is the failure the migration has already paid for once: a service plan that removes 37 units, 20 of them live, among them the seat system and the tracking handler. `--dry-run` shows the plan before it acts, so the hazard is reached only by a writing run over an index that reads empty.

THE FIX IS ONE BRANCH: refuse in the command where `slug === undefined && read.services.length === 0`, rather than planning from it. Not taken here because the service surface is another lane's live territory and this lane was ablating, not editing it.

value.claim: No agent change adds a field to a record a list already carries. `change-property-record-field` refuses where the record carries nothing under that field, and `add-property-value` takes `where`, `is` and `field` without reading one of them, so the value is appended as a new element of the list and a record property gets a bare string where a record belongs. value.evidence:
Met on 2026-09-10 adding `workingMemory` to an intent of `domain/initiative/pages/aranya-one-package.initiative.ts` that carried a statement alone.

`change-property-record-field` with `key: intents`, `where: statement`, `is: <the statement>`, `field: workingMemory` answers `that record states no text under workingMemory`. So the act that changes a field will not add one.

`add-property-value` with those same arguments plus `value` was taken without a word and drafted. The apply refused with `domain/initiative/pages/aranya-one-package.initiative.ts — line 42: TS2322: Type 'string' is not assignable to type 'Intent'`, so the value had been appended to `intents` as an element.

The reason is at `change/agent/file-content/add-property-value/add-property-value.change-agent.code.ts`: `AddPropertyValueAsked` declares `at`, `key`, `value` and `after`, and nothing else. That change does carry a guard for this shape — `A field inside a record is reached through the record rather than as a key of its own` — but the guard fires on `declaresIn(world, read.value, given.key) === false`, and `intents` is a property `initiative` declares, so the guard passed. The guard catches a field named as the key; it does not catch a key named rightly with a field beside it.

What was not read: whether the argument reader every agent change shares could refuse an argument the change does not declare, and what that would refuse across the changes that already take arguments loosely.

value.claim: An apply whose every edit names a path git ignores makes no commit and takes the file off the disk all the same. The answer says nothing was committed, which reads as nothing having happened, and the repository's history records the write nowhere. An agent reading that answer, or anyone reading the log after, has no way to learn from either that a file went.
value.evidence:
I ran `akasha change draft remove-file` with `at: change/mechanical/file-content/remove/remove-page-property/remove-page-property.change-mechanical-file-content.entries.uncommitted.jsonl`, a 73409-byte file git does not track, and then `akasha change apply`. The whole answer was two lines:

`folded change/mechanical/file-content/remove/remove-page-property/remove-page-property.change-mechanical-file-content.entries.uncommitted.jsonl in`
`nothing was committed, because git ignores the path(s) this apply took away: change/mechanical/file-content/remove/remove-page-property/remove-page-property.change-mechanical-file-content.entries.uncommitted.jsonl`

Listing the folder after that apply showed three files where there had been four. The file was gone. `git log` names no commit for it, because there is none, and the kept edits were cleared, so nothing beside the agent's page records it either.

The two readings this sits between: an apply that writes the disk and commits, which the log records; and an apply that is refused, which writes nothing. This is a third, and its answer's first word is the word a landing uses — `folded … in` — while its second sentence says nothing was committed. Reading the second sentence as "nothing happened" is the mistake available here, and I made it far enough to have to go and look at the folder to find out.

What it is worth is for whoever picks it up. The write may be right and only the saying wrong, in which case the answer could name what went off the disk rather than only why no commit was made. Or an apply over only ignored paths could be refused, on the ground that a change the repository cannot record is not a change this system should make. I did not mend it.

value.claim: Seven readout code files compose a query keyed `page-type`, and `asking`'s `Query` has no such field — it takes `pageTypeSlug`. Four assertions across three test files certify that spelling by reading the same key back off the query the readout itself composed, so the test restates the code rather than judging it. Run against the live index, such a query refuses with "`undefined` names no page type the index holds", and two further faults sit behind it: the page-type name is not a page type, and the keys are kebab where pages carry camel. Nothing typed the seam — `Asking` takes `Readonly<Record<string, unknown>>`, so any object satisfies it. The suite passed 300 of 300 over the `upkeep-surplus` case before it was repaired and passes 255 of 255 at HEAD with the same defect left in `upkeep-capacity`, `upkeep-safety` and `attribute-charisma`.
value.evidence:
Measured 2026-09-05 between 13:20 and 13:50 MDT, read-only. The tree moved under me: HEAD went through four commits while I worked, two of them repairs to this very code.

THE STATE I FOUND THE NAMED FILE IN. The brief named `readout-system/readouts/pages/upkeep-surplus/upkeep-surplus.readout.test.ts:20`. It had already been repaired. `841c0e961b` of 13:28:58 MDT took the query out and `9b3bbc8bb8` of 13:36:05 took seven more. At HEAD the file is 48 lines and holds no query. I measured the original claim in a throwaway worktree at `d4db1f5107`, which is `841c0e961b^`, then removed the worktree.

WHAT WAS THERE AT `d4db1f5107`. Lines 18-23 of that test read `const query = trackingOn(DAY) as Record<string, unknown>` and then `expect(query["page-type"]).toBe("daily-tracking")`, with `DAY` being `"2026-09-01"` at line 10. One correction to the brief: the assertion does not run over a kebab fixture. It runs over `trackingOn(DAY)`, the query the readout composes at `upkeep-surplus.readout.code.ts:17-24`, which returns `{ "page-type": DAY, where: ..., keys: [...], limit: 1 }`. Fixtures are imported at line 2 but used only by four other tests, and `readout-asking.module.test-fixtures.ts` is nine lines whose `answering` and `refusing` hand back what the caller supplies without looking at the query, so they could not have failed on the spelling either. The shape is narrower and worse than a wrong fixture: the assertion reads a value straight back out of the object under test, so it holds for whatever spelling that object uses.

THE SUITE COUNT. `bun test readout-system` from the checkout root: at `d4db1f5107`, `300 pass, 0 fail, 604 expect() calls, Ran 300 tests across 24 files`. At `841c0e961b`, 295 pass. At `9b3bbc8bb8`, 255 pass. At HEAD `832fa11720` I ran it myself: `255 pass, 0 fail, 543 expect() calls, Ran 255 tests across 24 files`. The 300 is exact rather than rounded.

THE QUERY REFUSES, RUN FOUR WAYS. `asking` has no CLI subcommand, so it was called directly against the live index for 2026-07-20. Spelled as the readout wrote it, `page-type` plus kebab keys: `{"refused":"`undefined` names no page type the index holds"}`. With `pageTypeSlug: "daily-tracking"` and kebab keys: `{"refused":"`daily-tracking` names no page type the index holds"}`. With `pageTypeSlug: "wake-day"` and kebab keys: refused for `keys` naming `surplus-hours`, which `wake-day` declares under no spelling. With that slug and camel keys: `{"rows":[{"surplusHours":-5.5,"sleepHours":7.5,"spendHours":13}]}`. Three faults each masking the next, and only the fourth spelling answers.

WHY EACH FAULT IS REAL. `page/service/modules/page-asking/page-asking.module.code.ts:45-53` declares `Query` with `pageTypeSlug` and no `page-type`; lines 229-231 interpolate `query.pageTypeSlug` into the refusal, which is why an absent field prints as `undefined`. No `*.page-type.ts` carries `slug: "daily-tracking"` — it is a text-property, at `alan/tracking/daily/wake-days/properties/daily-tracking.text-property.ts:8`. Key matching is exact both ways: `unkeyed` at 179-188 rejects any `where`, `sortBy` or `keys` name outside the declared set, and `meets` at 59-66 does a bare lookup with no normalisation.

WHY NOTHING TYPED CAUGHT IT. `readout-system/readout-asking/readout-asking.module.code.ts:7` declares `Asking` as `(query: Readonly<Record<string, unknown>>) => Promise<Answered>`, so every object satisfies it. The reader that does work, `alan/tracking/daily/day-reading/day-reading.module.code.ts:45-58`, names `pageTypeSlug` and camelises keys inbound at line 49 — and still ends its query literal with `as never` at line 50, the same seam untyped from the other side.

WHAT IS STILL THERE AT HEAD. Seven readout code files compose a query keyed `page-type`: `attribute-charisma`, `five-hour-back`, `upkeep-capacity`, `upkeep-safety`, `weekly-back`, `weekly-ends`, `weekly-usage`. Three of the seven name `session-tracking`, and no `*.page-type.ts` carries that slug; the only other file in the tree spelling it is a finding page's prose. The other four name `model-account`, which is a real page type at `agent/model/account/model-account.page-type.ts:56`, so those four are wrong only in the key. Four assertions certify the wrong key: `upkeep-capacity.readout.test.ts:11`, `attribute-charisma.readout.test.ts:27`, `upkeep-safety.readout.test.ts:55` and `:96`, each expecting `"session-tracking"`. Meanwhile four `.module.code.ts` files in the same package spell `pageTypeSlug` correctly — `readout-scale-reading:22`, `readout-none-left:27`, `readout-serving:76`, `readout-group-serving:58` and `:113` — so both dialects sit side by side in one workspace package.

WHAT I DID NOT ESTABLISH. I did not run the seven surviving queries against the index, so I have not shown those refuse — only that they carry the same `page-type` key that made `upkeep-surplus` refuse. I did not judge whether the repairs in flight intend to reach them. I did not measure how many other test files in the repository assert a value straight back off the object under test.

value.claim: An audit verdict names the commit HEAD was at when the round opened and holds what the live checkout said minutes later, so a verdict can refuse a commit whose tree it never read.
value.evidence:
`typecheck` refused once in the round recorded at 2026-09-12T12:42:34.199Z. The refusal named `infrastructure/service/modules/deploy-looping/deploy-looping.module.code.ts` at line 2, TS2305, module `akasha/command/pages/deploy/modules/holding/deploy-holding.module.code.ts` having no exported member `heldNow`. The verdict holding that refusal in `/var/home/walton/.local/state/workstation-services/audit-verdicts.json` named `commit: b54caedd669a4022801280b031cd2c0fabe2345c`, and `audit-running` messaged that commit and that line to thea.

Neither half of the diagnostic is in that commit. `b54caedd669` landed at 12:26:52Z. At its tree, line 2 of `deploy-looping.module.code.ts` opens an import from `deploy-kind-reading` and names no `heldNow`, and `deploy-holding.module.code.ts` exports `holdAt`, `sinceAt`, `saidOfHeld` and `saidOfNoHold` and nothing else. There is no importer and there is no missing export. The commit the verdict names could not have produced the refusal the verdict holds.

What the round read was the live checkout, sixteen minutes after the commit it named. `a6d0a1cd7fd` landed at 12:41:29Z, 65 seconds before the verdict was written, and it is whole in one commit: `heldNow` is added at `deploy-holding.module.code.ts:26`, the import is added at `deploy-looping.module.code.ts:2`, `slugIn`, `deployingIn` and the `listing` parameter defaulting to `systemctl` go, and both test files and both pages are carried beside the code. The round read `deploy-looping.module.code.ts` after the importer line had reached disk and before `heldNow` had reached `deploy-holding.module.code.ts`, catching one file of a two-file save mid-write.

The next round agreed. `typecheck` at `f0ea3cf8490`, recorded 2026-09-12T13:00:17.304Z, holds no refusals, and `f0ea3cf8490` carries `a6d0a1cd7fd`.

The cost was a whole subagent run. A seat read the verdict as a broken build at HEAD and sent an agent to mend it. That agent read four files, followed the history of both, and checked `deployingIn`, `slugIn`, `systemctl` and both service runners for stranded importers before landing nothing, because there was nothing anywhere to mend. The verdict remained the answer for `b54caedd669` from 12:42:34Z until the next round replaced it.

It happened again the same morning, with a different check and a different symptom. `typecheck` at `99172024da6`, recorded 2026-09-12T14:02:41.397Z, refused three times with TS2307: `seat-control.module.code.ts`, `seat-record.module.code.ts` and `seat-turn-pending.module.code.ts` each naming `akasha/seat-system/seat-beside/seat-beside.module.code.ts`, which could not be found. At `99172024da6`, landed 13:46:33Z, that module is there and all three importers name it, so the tree the verdict names is whole. At HEAD all three name `akasha/agent/seat/page/modules/seat-beside/seat-beside.module.code.ts`, that file is there and the old folder is gone, so the tree now is whole as well. The move landed as `8a718a861b0` at 14:01:53Z, 48 seconds before the verdict was written, and it carried the moved module and the three rewritten importers together. The diagnostic is in neither the commit the verdict names nor the commit HEAD is at. It is in the 48 seconds between them.

A half-written pair is the ordinary state of a tree fifteen agents are landing into, and a round is long enough to meet one. The repository already keeps a worktree per deploy kind under `.git/trees`. An audit judges the commit it names when it reads a worktree checked out at that commit rather than the live checkout.

A checkout copied with `cp -a` inherits `origin`, and three commands carry the branch to whatever remote that copy names without asking whether the root is the resolved akasha checkout: `push`, and the two deploys, which push for themselves before they build. The automatic half is gone: no landing hands a push off any more and `handOffPush` has no caller left, so a copy no longer pushes unasked. What remains is that asking works — a push from a copy reaches the shared remote exactly as it would from the real checkout, and a test commit lands on the shared branch. Isolating the working tree still does not isolate the remote, and nothing in the copy says so.
value.evidence:
Measured 2026-09-02, narrowed and then widened 2026-09-08.

I copied the checkout to a scratch path to test a repair to `sidecarsOf`, ran a real `mv` of a made-up page there, and read `push: handed off to origin — this write is durable at its commit` in the output. `git ls-remote origin refs/heads/main` then answered my test commit. My copy's base was newer than what origin held, so it went as a fast-forward with nothing to refuse it.

WHAT HAS GONE. The automatic handoff. `rg 'handOffPush'` at HEAD finds the definition and its own test file and no production caller, so no landing carries a branch off any more. A copied checkout that only lands is now quiet.

WHAT IS WIDER THAN I FIRST WROTE. `rg 'pushBranch\('` outside tests answers four production sites. Three are commands an agent can name: `command/pages/push/push.command.code.ts:52` on `given.root`, `command/modules/deploy-web-putting-up/deploy-web-putting-up.module.code.ts:75` on `given.root`, and `command/modules/deploy-ios-shipping/deploy-ios-shipping.module.code.ts:110` on its own `root`. The fourth is `git/modules/push-repo/push-repo.module.code.ts:86`, the detached pusher `handOffPush` no longer calls. Neither deploy refuses first any more — where origin does not carry the commit, the deploy pushes for itself before it builds.

WHAT NONE OF THEM ASKS. Not one compares the root it is handed against the resolved akasha checkout. The question `AKASHA_ROOT` already answers for reads is never put here, so any of the three run inside a `cp -a` copy reaches whatever remote the copy inherited, which is the shared one.

NOTHING WAS LOST from the first firing: everything origin held is in the shared checkout, and my two test commits are the only things on origin that are not. I could not put them back — `block-destructive-git` refuses `git push --force`, correctly, and no non-forcing sequence restores a branch moved onto a side chain.

WHAT WOULD CLOSE IT: a copied checkout dropping its remote, or `pushBranch` refusing a root that is not the resolved akasha checkout, which closes all three at once rather than one command at a time.

value.claim: `block-akasha-shell-writes` judges an `ln` that replaces an existing symlink through that link rather than at it. `landedAt` reads a landing at the link itself only for `TAKING_AWAY`, `rm` and `rmdir`; `ln` sits in `ONTO_THE_LAST` and falls through to `settled()`, which follows the symlink. The hook's own page already carries the right idea for removals: a removal naming a symlink itself is judged where the link is rather than where the link points. `ln -sfn` says as much of itself, `-n` being `--no-dereference`, which means replace the link rather than write through it. Because the landing is resolved, the gitignore escape at the foot of `refusalFor` is asked about the target instead of about the link, so a refusal names one file while judging another. The narrow mend is to read an `ln` carrying `-n` at the link, as `rm` already is. Narrowing what a hook refuses needs Alan's approval, which has not been given.
value.evidence:
WHERE IT IS. In `block-akasha-shell-writes.agent-hook.code.ts`, line 29 puts `cp`, `mv`, `install` and `ln` in `ONTO_THE_LAST`, and line 33 puts `rm` and `rmdir` in `TAKING_AWAY`. `landedAt`, lines 330 to 337, answers the path at the link only where `TAKING_AWAY.has(landing.how)` and `namesTheLink(landing.at)` and a link really is there; every other landing answers `settled(spelled)`, which follows the symlink. `refusalFor`, lines 350 to 382, judges each landing at `landedAt`, and at lines 373 to 380 lets through any judged landing the repository ignores. For an `ln` those ignore rules are therefore read over the file the link points at.

WHAT I RAN, 2026-09-11 09:13. `ln -sfn .. /var/home/walton/repos/akasha/node_modules/akasha` was refused, the message reading that `ln` lands on `/var/home/walton/repos/akasha/node_modules/akasha`, inside the akasha folder. That link pointed at the repository root, so `settled()` answered the root. `git check-ignore -v` answers `.gitignore:13:node_modules/` for `node_modules/akasha`, and answers nothing for the root at exit 1. Judged at the link the write would have been let through by the ignore rules; judged through the link it was refused. The message named the link while the judgement was about the root.

THE SHARPEST CASE. I made a symlink under my scratch folder pointing at `/var/home/walton/repos/akasha`, a link with nothing about it inside the checkout. An `ln -sfn /etc` onto it was refused as being inside the akasha folder, naming a path under `/tmp`. An `rm` of the same link was allowed, exit 0, and took the link away. One link, two commands, two different files judged.

WHY THE FLAG IS THE LINE. Measured in scratch: `ln -sf /etc L`, where `L` is a symlink to a directory, leaves `L` alone and writes `etc` inside that directory. It writes through the link, and resolving the landing is right for it. `ln -sfn /etc L` replaces `L` and leaves the directory alone. So the fault is not `ln`; it is `ln` told not to dereference, and the hook reads no such flag.

THE TESTS DO NOT REACH IT. Line 171 of the test beside the hook refuses `ln -s /var/tmp/x akasha/held.domain.ts` and line 200 lets `ln -s /var/tmp/x /var/tmp/y` through. Neither names an existing symlink as its target, so nothing here is failing: the case is unreached rather than broken.

WHAT IT COST. The repository's `node_modules/akasha` was absolute this morning and wanted putting back to `..`. The putting back is an `ln -sfn` and was refused, so the route out was to take the link away and install again. `a-scratch-folders-node-modules-is-the-repositorys-own-node-modules` holds that.

THE NARROW MEND. Read an `ln` at the link where the call carries `-n` or `--no-dereference`, the way `editsInPlace` already reads `-i` for the tools that edit in place, and hand that to the same `namesTheLink` and `aLink` test `landedAt` already runs for `rm`. `cp`, `mv` and `install` keep resolving, which is right for them. That narrows what this hook refuses, and the page type's rule Alan Approves Hooks reserves narrowing to Alan: its aid says how an approved hook reads needs no approval, and what it refuses does. The hook is unchanged, and this is the record for that decision.

NOT MEASURED. Whether `cp -P`, or `mv` onto an existing link, have the same shape. How often this has refused a write nobody filed; I found it by meeting it once.

value.claim: `besideAt` composes a beside-file name without applying `HELD_PART`, the character class its own module applies when reading such a name apart. Its module page declares that what the builders put together and what `heldIn` takes apart are one rule. A value that could never be an extension therefore becomes one, and the git reader downstream throws where it would otherwise have judged.
value.evidence:
Read 2026-09-03 on the akasha checkout.

`page-file-name.module.code.ts:7` declares `HELD_PART = /^[a-z0-9]+$/`. `partedIn` applies it at line 63 and `besideNamed` at line 111, both when reading a name apart. `besideAt` at line 146 guards only that the page's own path ends `.ts`, then interpolates the value verbatim. `page-file-name.module.ts:68` states the rule the builder is missing: what `heldIn` takes apart and what the builders here put together stay one rule. `page-file-parts.module.ts:29` asserts the same of `partAt`.

Every file property in the repository holds one of 19 values, all matching `HELD_PART`: css, diff, entitlements, html, json, jsonl, lua, md, pgn, plist, py, rs, sh, svg, swift, ts, tsx, txt, xml. Every other caller of `besideAt` hands it a short literal. So the rule costs nothing to apply and only the untrusted path through `partsOf` is affected.

What the omission buys is a fault dressed as a verdict. `git cat-file --batch -z` takes its request NUL-terminated, so a value carrying a newline goes in whole, but git echoes the name back on a newline-terminated response line. The reader at `commit-reading.module.code.ts:163` reads one line, finds neither a record nor a missing marker, and throws. A single-line value instead yields a plain refusal naming a file nobody meant. Either way the message names the agent's own prose, so an agent reads it as its own text being malformed.

I wrote the three-line guard and could not land it: the write gate refuses every code change over four TypeScript errors in `akasha/alan/web-capacitor/root.tsx`, `akasha/alan/web/.server/page-detail-loading/page-detail-loading.module.code.ts` and `akasha/alan/web/modules/alan-auth-provider/alan-auth-provider.module.code.tsx`, none of which my change reaches.

value.claim: `Bun.spawn` given `stdin` as a pipe hands the child a socket rather than a pipe, and a socket cannot be reopened through `/proc/self/fd/0`, so `inputIn` gets ENXIO from `/dev/stdin` and every akasha command driven that way is refused for arguments that would not open rather than reading the body it was written.
value.evidence:
Measured 2026-09-08 on bun 1.3.14, Linux.

WHAT WAS OBSERVED. A child started by `Bun.spawn` with stdin asked for as a pipe sees `/proc/self/fd/0` as `socket:[1182313136]`, and `fstatSync(0).isSocket()` is true. The same program run behind a shell pipe sees `pipe:[1182313140]`, and `isFIFO()` is true. In the spawned child, `openSync` of `/dev/stdin` with `O_RDONLY | O_NONBLOCK` throws `ENXIO: no such device or address`, on all 60 rounds of a run that varied how much was written and how slowly. Behind a shell pipe the same open succeeds. Linux answers ENXIO for an open of a socket through `/proc/self/fd`.

WHAT IT MEANS HERE. `inputIn` in `command-system/piping/piping.module.code.ts` opens `/dev/stdin` rather than reading descriptor 0, so it answers unreadable there, and `argumentsIn` in `command-system/change-running/change-running.module.code.ts` turns that into a refusal saying the arguments would not open. So a caller driving an akasha command from `Bun.spawn` with a piped stdin is refused rather than read, however well formed the body is. `Bun.spawnSync` handed a stdin buffer, which `bytes` in `utils-run/running` uses, gives the child a regular file instead, and reads whole at every size from 1 KB to 1 MB.

WHAT IS NOT CLAIMED. No caller in the tree was found driving an akasha command this way, so this is the mechanism rather than a failure anyone has hit. The piping module already carries the gap that an input no second descriptor can be opened on is answered as an input that would not open; what is new is which spawn shape lands in it. Whether reading descriptor 0 directly would be a safe mend was not worked out, and the second descriptor is opened on purpose.

value.claim: The reaper is the only thing bounding what an agent takes on this workstation, and every leg of it sits above what a runaway agent process reaches. The per-process ceiling is 32 GiB VmRSS on a 62 GiB host. The headroom leg wants MemAvailable at or under 4 GiB and SwapFree at or under 4 GiB together, and with 80 GiB of swap the host thrashes a long while before the second can hold. The per-tree ceiling reaches nothing at all. Lowering the per-process number alone is no answer: the tick weighs every process uid 1000 owns, so one ceiling answers an agent's script and a browser and a game alike. Telling a fleet process from a desktop one wants the supervisor predicate mended first. What ceiling an agent's own processes want is not measured anywhere.
value.evidence:
THE INSTANCE. 2026-09-11, Alan killed a python process holding 16 GiB by hand to keep the workstation usable. Nothing killed it for him, and nothing was going to.

WHY NO LEG TRIPPED. The reaper's banner at its last start, read from the journal: `ceilings per-process=32 GiB VmRSS per-tree=32 GiB PSS headroom-leg=MemAvail<=4 GiB when SwapFree<=4 GiB global-recovery-window=60s tick=10s (rootless-podman containers excluded)`. 16 GiB is half the per-process ceiling. assessGlobalKill takes `swapDrained && availableKb <= minAvailKb`, and /proc/meminfo the same day answered MemAvailable 29.7 GiB, SwapTotal 80 GiB, SwapFree 54.3 GiB. Neither side of the conjunction held.

THE REAPER IS RUNNING. memory-reaper.service read active (running) since 2026-09-10 21:51 MDT, main pid 80733. It did what it is written to do.

THE PER-TREE LEG REACHES NOTHING. readSupervisorPids calls isSupervisorCmdline, whose pattern wants the literal `supervisor.ts`, and every live supervisor is spelled run-supervisor.module.code.ts. Walked /proc 2026-09-11: 447 live command lines, 28 holding run-supervisor, zero matching the pattern, and no file named supervisor.ts in the checkout. So the per-tree ceiling has no roots to weigh, and the headroom leg's tree branch always falls through to taking the largest single process. `no-live-supervisor-matches-the-supervisor-predicate` holds this and is still true; it is not re-filed here.

ONE CEILING FOR THE FLEET AND THE DESKTOP BOTH. runReaperTick calls readUserPidSnapshots(uid) and drops only rootless-podman cgroups, so the per-process leg weighs every process uid 1000 owns. `ps aux --sort=-rss` the same day put a game at 2.1 GiB RSS and a browser process at 0.9 GiB at the top. A per-process ceiling lowered to catch a 16 GiB agent script would reach them by the same rule.

NOTHING ELSE BOUNDS ANYTHING. memory.max, memory.high and memory.swap.max all read `max` on -.slice, user.slice, user-1000.slice, user@1000.service, app.slice, on the tmux-spawn scope the seats share, and on all nine akasha-* scopes under app.slice. An agent shell reads `ulimit -v` and `ulimit -m` unlimited and RLIMIT_AS unlimited in /proc/self/limits. earlyoom and nohang are not installed. seat-launching states CPUQuota, CPUWeight and TasksMax on the scope it opens and no Memory property at all, and the workstation-service systemd record models no memory property for any service to state.

SYSTEMD-OOMD IS ARMED ON ONE LEG AND INERT ON THE OTHER. /etc/systemd/oomd.conf.d/99-swap-used-limit.conf states SwapUsedLimit=25%, but ManagedOOMSwap reads `auto` on every slice in the chain, so swap killing was never enabled; swap sat at 25 of 80 GiB, above that limit, with nothing killed. /usr/lib/systemd/user/slice.d/10-oomd-per-slice-defaults.conf sets ManagedOOMMemoryPressure=kill at 80% on user slices, and every seat shares one cgroup, tmux-spawn-e1ae61b7-4e90-4102-bf68-5f74890f5cf4.scope, so the one armed leg would take the whole fleet in a single kill. Zero kernel OOM kills and zero oomd kills in the journal for this boot, which began 2026-09-08.

THE SETTINGS PULL THE OTHER WAY. ~/.claude/settings.json states NODE_OPTIONS=--max-old-space-size=61440, which is 60 GiB of heap on a 62 GiB host, beside CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_CONCURRENT_SUBAGENTS=65.

WHAT DOES WORK IS ADMISSION. memory-guard states MIN_FREE_MEMORY_GB=8; enforceMemoryGuard refuses to start a dev-server or spawn a supervisor child under it, and enforceSpawnAdmission refuses a seat start. Both refuse new work under pressure and bound nothing already running. readHostMemoryPressure reads /proc/pressure/memory and has no caller.

THE CEILINGS ARE ALREADY MOVABLE. memory-reaper-config resolves AGENT_MEM_MAX_RSS_GB, AGENT_MEM_MAX_TREE_PSS_GB, AGENT_MEM_GLOBAL_MIN_AVAIL_GB, AGENT_MEM_GLOBAL_MIN_FREE_SWAP_GB and AGENT_MEM_GLOBAL_RECOVERY_WINDOW_SEC over the defaults, read once at load, and nothing sets any of them.

NOT MEASURED. The largest a seat tree legitimately reaches under a build or a test run is recorded nowhere, so no lower ceiling is yet defensible.
