value.claim: Folding a package into the root takes away the Tailwind `@source` glob that covered its tree, so a utility only that tree used is purged from every web app's built CSS. `source-globbing` writes one glob for each package the stylesheet's own package reaches through the manifests. A folded package is no longer a package, no manifest names it any more, and the root package is not among the packages `reachedIn` reads, so nothing is written in its place. The `design-badges` fold has already cost `group-hover:bg-primary/8` and `placeholder:text-current/40`, which no tree still globbed uses. Nothing refuses the landing and nothing says a glob went. The mend is Alan's call, because the root package's tree is the whole repository and scanning it is a build-time cost.
value.evidence:
Where the globs come from. `code/stylesheet/modules/source-globbing/source-globbing.module.code.ts:68` reads manifests with the pathspec `*/package.json`, which matches no manifest at the repository root, so the root package `akasha` is never one of the `Reached`. `reachedFrom` at :100-112 walks a package's own `dependencies` and what those reach. `blockFor` at :123-144 writes one `@source` per reached package whose tree has a `.tsx`, and drops any package under another it already names. So a glob follows a manifest entry and nothing else.

What a fold does to that. `remove-package-manifest` takes the folded package's entry out of each manifest that named it and puts nothing in its place: `alan/web/package.json` names no `akasha` after the folds landed today. The reach still works, because the workspace has `akasha: link:.` at the root and the specifier is `akasha/{file-path}`, and `manifest-names-what-is-reached` waives it because some manifest states that name. The glob does not follow, because `akasha` is not a package `reachedIn` read.

What it has already cost. `design/badges` was folded by `e47c750ed8d` and its thirteen `.tsx` draw with Tailwind utilities. No `.stylesheet.styles.css` in the tree names `design/badges` now. Of the 34 class tokens those files spell in a `className` literal, 32 are used by a tree still globbed for `alan/web` — `design/{forms,layout,patterns,primitives,system}`, `page/ui`, `persons`, `alan/harness/supabase-rr`, and `alan/web` itself. The two left are `group-hover:bg-primary/8` and `placeholder:text-current/40`, and Tailwind emits a utility only where a scanned file spells it.

Why `alan/web` itself is not enough. `alan/web/vite.config.ts` runs `@tailwindcss/vite` with the Vite root at `alan/web`, so Tailwind's own detection reaches that folder and no further. Everything outside it is covered by the written globs alone.

What is not hurt. `alan/chess` was folded today and draws only through its own `chess-board-look.stylesheet.styles.css`: every `className` in its three `.tsx` is one of that sheet's own classes, so it needs no Tailwind scan. The other folds landed today — talos, mobile-cli, idle-system, git, testing-system, location-traces-access, health-samples-access, errors-client — carry no `.tsx` that draws, so none of them moved a glob that mattered.

What the mend needs. Making the glob follow the reach means treating the root as a package, and the root package's tree is the repository, so its one glob replaces every other glob and Tailwind scans everything not ignored. That trades a correct stylesheet for build time, which is Alan's to spend. Reading only what an app imports, rather than what its manifest names, is the other shape, and it is a larger change to a module whose page says a glob names a package.

Not established. I read only `className` string literals, so a class composed at runtime or handed through `cn` is not counted, and the two missing utilities are a lower bound rather than the whole cost. I did not build any web app, so I have not seen the purge in an output file.

value.claim: The solar planning case does not fit the interconnection it is designed against. Provo City Code 12.03.080(5) puts standard residential net metering under 25 kW on inverter AC nameplate; the planning case is 40–41 kW AC on 49 kWp DC. `scope.md` sets the revised target at or below 25 kW AC, and every sizing file under it plans 49 kWp regardless. `customer-generation.md` names the two ways out — derate the AC side, or take the commercial licence at a worse export credit — and picks neither.
value.evidence:
Read 2026-08-16 across the 41 files of `alan/book/all-about-alan/projects/solar-power`.

`customer-generation.md`: "12.03.080(5) classifies licenses under 25 kW as standard net-metering … the Standards document and License Application use **inverter AC nameplate (kW)** as the size field." Then: "**Practical implication for ~50 kWp DC array:** at typical 1.1–1.3 DC/AC ratios this is ~38–45 kW AC, well above the 25 kW residential threshold. **It does not fit standard residential net metering.**" Its two paths: "Reduce inverter AC capacity below 25 kW (oversized DC / clipped AC)" or "the **Commercial Net Metering rate (`NTCR`) at −$0.0453 / kWh**". It closes: "This is a real constraint to bring back to scope."

`scope.md` took it back: "**System at or below the 25 kW AC residential cap**, unless the commercial path is explicitly chosen. With 1.20 ILR this is ~30 kWp DC", and lists it among three constraints that "shape every downstream sizing decision".

Downstream it vanishes. `sizing/pv.md`: "49 ÷ 1.20 = **41 kW AC**. Round to 40 kW." `sizing/topology.md` sizes the back-fed breaker on it: "At 40 kW AC / 240 V = 167 A". `sizing/recommendation.md`'s bid anchor: "49 kWp … ILR 1.20 → 40 kW AC". None of `sizing.md`, `sizing/pv.md`, `sizing/topology.md`, `sizing/cost.md` or `sizing/recommendation.md` names the cap; the third of `recommendation.md`'s four open items is the softer "Provo City Power Schedule 1.1 net-metering details … may impose a cap that re-sizes the project", written as though it were not already found.

Not measured: I did not open the code, the Standards or the rate sheet, so the cap and both rates are as `customer-generation.md` reports them. Whether a 25 kW-derated build serves the modelled demand is arithmetic nobody in the thread ran, and I did not run it either.

value.claim: utils-narrow carries isObjectRecord and isRecord whose bodies differ only by excluding arrays. A private isRecord in web-app-building was the same rule as isObjectRecord rather than as the module sharing its name, so merging by name would have quietly made build-env parsing stricter. Anyone collapsing the two modules as duplicates changes that caller without seeing it.
value.evidence: is-object-record.module.code.ts:1-3 returns `typeof value === "object" && value !== null`. is-record.module.code.ts:1-3 adds `&& !Array.isArray(value)`. web-app-building.module.code.ts:225-227 held a private isRecord byte-identical to isObjectRecord, and the audit paired it with isObjectRecord rather than with the like-named isRecord, which is the check reading bodies rather than names. A differential over 28 values spanning primitives, plain objects, arrays, typed arrays, functions and classes diverged on exactly the four arrays. Carried through that caller own isEntry the divergence survived on one value: `Object.assign([], { name: "A", value: "v" })` is an entry to isObjectRecord and is not one to isRecord. So the two names are two rules, and the shorter name is the stricter one, which reads backwards. Landed at fb3be57cb3 importing isObjectRecord, which leaves the caller behaviour identical. Whoever tidies utils-narrow should either keep both or rename so the stricter one says what it excludes.

value.claim: Landing a new `package.json` under `akasha/` was seen once to leave the repository's root `package.json` holding the body of the new file. The root manifest lost its workspaces array and every dependency, in the working tree only — the commit was correct. Nobody has reproduced it, so this records an observation and not a mechanism.
value.evidence:
Seen 2026-09-02 while landing `akasha/editor-extension/package.json`, a six-line manifest, at `2abf58d75d`. Afterwards the root `package.json` held those six lines verbatim: 143 lines gone, the whole `workspaces` array and every dependency with them. The commit did not carry it — it names four paths and `git show HEAD:package.json` is right — so the working tree alone was hit, most likely while the lockfile was regenerated in the same call. It was put back from `git show HEAD:package.json` and the tree agrees with HEAD again: 147 lines, 47 workspace entries, 67 dependencies.

Why this is filed without a mechanism. Two attempts to reproduce it both answered `unchanged`, and both were blind: the first handed an identical body so no regeneration ran, and the second was refused by a manifest check before regeneration was reached. Neither could have shown the fault, so their agreement says nothing. What can be said is narrow — it happened during that write sequence, and the body left behind was exactly the `--content-file` handed in.

Why it is worth a page anyway. The damage is silent and total. A root manifest with no workspaces array breaks resolution for every package and every agent in the checkout, the commit looks clean, and `git status` is the only place it shows. In a worktree where a hook reverts `akasha/` constantly, everyone is trained to read a dirty root file as somebody else's business.

Until somebody catches it in the act: after landing a new `package.json` under `akasha/`, read the root manifest.

value.claim: Two akasha landings can only judge at the same time and both land where what each check read is recorded, absences included. Every cheaper rule either serializes the gate, as the lock does, or refuses one of two unrelated landings.
value.evidence: Read in the repository rather than reasoned. `reachedSince` asks git for every path under `akasha/` changed between a base and now, so a compare-and-swap on HEAD refuses any landing whose sibling committed while it was judged — with the gate outside the hold, that is every concurrent pair. Refuse-and-retry spends the wall time of the lock and one wasted gate besides, so it is worse than what it would replace. Two earlier claims for a narrower rule were both disproved: an index entry file is keyed by what is referred to rather than by what changed, so two landings on disjoint paths importing one module contend on one entry file and lose an update; and git serializes commits by failing rather than by waiting, six concurrent path-limited commits leaving five dead on `index.lock`. What survives is recording what each check read. It is narrower than feared — `typecheck` walks the importer closure of the changed files rather than the whole tree, and 25 of the 27 checks reach the filesystem only through `Leaving` and `Reading` — but comparing paths does not close it. Two landings each introducing one identifier read no file of the other's, because neither file was there. What each depended on is an index entry it probed and found absent, so what a check read has to include what it looked for and did not find. `typecheck`, `page-named-as-stated` and `importersOf` reach past both surfaces today and would come into line first, and a check reading through anything unrecorded would answer that nothing it read had changed.

value.claim: Every row landed beside the generation log rewrites its whole `.jsonl` part, so a run costs about 2.4 MiB of git objects and a persisted run about 3.1 MiB, against 2.3 KiB of appended text. At the present 74 runs a day that is roughly 175 MiB a day, and the rate now rises, because from today nine `inference` commands land a row where nothing landed one automatically. Append-only files delta almost perfectly, so a repack collapses this to near the appended bytes: the cost is transient rather than cumulative, but large between repacks, and I found nothing scheduling one. Separately, `MOST_PARTS` is 16, and that is a counter at whose end all nine commands go dead at once. The mend that suggests itself is a smaller entry ceiling rather than a larger part count, and it wants its own measurement.
value.evidence:
Measured on the landings themselves rather than estimated, on the night `landRow` was filled.

The cost of one landing. `git cat-file --batch-check` over three consecutive run-row blobs, asking object size and size on disk: `2287b9ebcd4c` 8,087,829 bytes to 1,191,957 on disk, `ba5f62b1742a` 8,087,936 to 1,191,998, `790c6ed550b0` 8,089,529 to 1,192,760. `landRow` reads the last part and writes it whole, so one row of about 2.3 KiB costs a fresh object holding the whole part.

Landings per run. Two for every run, a land and a patch, as `121611354bc` and `01b9840ff0d`. Two more where the run persists, as `1e3313514b6` and `d124fbbb3dc` on the images part, which is smaller at about 2.3 MB. So about 2.4 MiB a run and about 3.1 MiB a persisted run.

The rate. `alan.generation-log.runs.jsonl` and its `part2` hold 7,142 rows over the 96 days from 2026-06-08T15:38:42Z to 2026-09-12T14:27:09Z: 74.4 rows a day at a mean 2,308 bytes. That is 0.16 MiB a day of appended text against about 175 MiB a day of rewritten objects. It is the rate of a log nothing landed rows into automatically, so read it as a floor rather than as a forecast.

What a repack does, which is the whole decision. Consecutive versions of an append-only file delta to near the bytes appended, so a `git gc` erases almost all of this. The figures above are loose-object cost, not repository growth, and the two are different claims. At the time of measuring the loose store held 4,128 objects at 37.49 MiB against 1.83 GiB in eight packs, so the large blobs were already being packed by something. What I did not find is anything that schedules a repack. Where one runs often enough this cost is noise; where it does not, the loose store grows by the figures above.

The ceiling, which matters more than its date. `lastPartOf` throws that the runs beside the log are in 16 parts and this reads 16. That throw is raised inside `landRow`, which is the first statement of `recordInferenceRun`, before `run()` is called and before any model is reached. So at the ceiling all nine `inference` commands exit 3 on every call, landing no row and writing nothing — total, silent until called, and the same failure this log was mended for, waiting at the end of a counter. The headroom is 112 MiB, about 51,000 rows, about 685 days, near 2028-07-28 at the present rate and sooner as it rises.

The mend, recorded and not taken. Raising `MOST_PARTS` moves the counter and leaves the per-landing cost where it is. Lowering `ENTRY_CEILING`, at `page/modules/entry-ceiling/entry-ceiling.module.code.ts:1` and presently `8 * 1024 * 1024`, does both: at an eighth of the size each landing writes an eighth of the blob, and the sixteen-part ceiling moves out with the smaller parts. The read barely notices, because the search for the last part pays only for the parts that are there — measured at about 300 ms for a present 8 MiB part against 6 ms for an absent one, so three further probes cost nothing. It is not taken here because that ceiling is shared well beyond this log, and changing it wants measuring against the other files sitting under it.

value.claim: The harness landing lock and the akasha landing lock sit in one `.git` folder under different names, so a rename is all that parts them. A rename alone would not be safe. The harness reads a lock's mark with `Number` over the whole line, and the akasha mark carries two fields, so the harness would read a live akasha hold as unheld and delete it.
value.evidence:
Measured 2026-09-02 at commit 923a2f4fde.

`repo/git/git.ts` line 90 names the harness lock `harness-landing.lock`, and line 103 places it in `git rev-parse --git-common-dir`, which answers `.git` in this checkout. `akasha/command-system/holding/holding.module.code.ts` line 5 names the akasha lock `.git/akasha-landing.lock`. One folder, two names, so neither hold excludes the other while both commit paths run.

The two marks differ. `holding` line 40 writes `${pid} ${startedAt(pid)}`; `whileHoldingLanding` at git.ts line 121 writes `${pid}` and a newline. `repo/holder/holder.ts` line 6 reads a mark with `Number(readFileSync(path).trim())`. `Number("12345 998877")` is NaN, checked here at the shell, so line 10 answers that no holder runs, and git.ts lines 133 to 137 then remove the lock and take it. A rename therefore turns a lock the harness ignores into a lock the harness takes from a running akasha landing, under twenty concurrent writers.

Two more things gate the merge. git.ts line 155 releases only where the mark equals its own pid as a whole string, so writing the two-field mark without changing that line leaves every harness landing holding the lock for ever. And `tools/lib/page-commit-queue.ts` line 16 allows a landing 2000ms of patience, where an akasha landing waits 120s; sharing one lock with judged landings would drive the queue into the stall path at lines 28 and 151 and turn `landingsHealthy` at line 83 false.

The merge is three coordinated edits across `repo/git/git.ts` and `repo/holder/holder.ts`, not one rename. None of the three was made here.

value.claim: `services/monarch-poll.ts` throws away the `PollTally` `pollTransactions` hands back and returns 0 unconditionally, so a minute that fetched rows, dropped every one and wrote no file exits like a minute that landed them all. Two drops hide behind that 0: a row naming an account no account file carries is warned about and skipped, and the `skipped` count `linesFrom` returns is never read in `monarch/poll.ts`. The exit code answers whether the process threw, never whether a row arrived.
value.evidence:
Read rather than run, because running it means calling Monarch.

`services/monarch-poll.ts` `main()` is three lines: it handles `--help`, awaits `pollTransactions(...)` discarding the result, and returns 0. The `PollTally` type carries `seen`, `changed`, `landed` and `retired`, and no caller looks at any of them.

Two ways `landed` reaches 0 with no throw. First, `monarch/poll.ts` filters the fetched rows to `ready` — those whose account the mirror already carries — and `console.warn`s the remainder as "left for the daily full sync rather than failing every run after this one". That is a deliberate trade, but the daily full sync is `monarch-sync`, whose own last success was 2026-08-26 00:02:56, so through this outage the fallback was itself broken and the drop was permanent rather than deferred. Second, `linesFrom` returns `{ lines, skipped, unknownTags }` and `monarch/poll.ts` reads `lines` and `unknownTags` and never `skipped`; `monarch/sync.ts:70` does report the same count, so the omission is in the poll alone. A row `lineOf` rejects leaves no line of output at all.

Downstream of both, `landTransactionFiles` returns `[]` as soon as its `touched` map is empty, so `through()` is never reached and no write is attempted. Nothing distinguishes that from a quiet minute.

The inverse also holds and matters on the first run after a backlog: `pollTransactions` runs `categorizeRecent` after the rows have landed and throws when any row is contested, so a run can write every file correctly and still exit 1.

value.claim: `pageTypeSlug` spells four different things, and only one of them is the key a page states. Whoever takes the last step of the two-key window will grep the name and get thousands of hits, most of which must not change. The three that are not the page key are an index record field, a query key on the wire into the pages service, and a value worked out from a file's name rather than read from a body. Telling them apart is the difference between a day and a week, and nothing in the tree says which is which.
value.evidence: The page key is the one written into a page body and read as `textAt(value, "type") ?? textAt(value, "pageTypeSlug")`, at `page/index/identity/index-identity.index.code.ts:66`, `path/index-path.index.code.ts:49`, `relation/index-edge.index.code.ts:28`, `value/index-value.index.code.ts:41` and `reaching/reaching.module.code.ts:185`. The index record field is a different thing wearing the same name: the `Carried`, `Held`, `InPageType` and `Renaming` shapes all carry a `pageTypeSlug`, and `page/service/modules/page-asking/page-asking.module.code.ts:124` builds an output row as `type: one.pageTypeSlug` off it. The wire key is an argument to a query rather than anything a page states, as in `ask({ pageTypeSlug, where })` at `page/access/modules/file-write/file-write.module.code.ts:79`, across `page/access/*`, and in every route named `api.pages.$pageTypeSlug.ts` under `alan/web`, `temper/temper-web` and `smilingjenny`. The fourth is worked out from a path by `@akasha/pages/page-file-name`, which is how all of `folder-matches-a-shape` and its folder shapes come by it. Around 326 files name it outside page values, and 148 test files hold a `pageTypeSlug: "` fixture in a scratch world; those fixtures are correct today and all go red at once when the window closes, rather than batch by batch.

value.claim: A subpath pattern cannot land in akasha, so patterns cannot relieve `@akasha/pages-ui-components`. `package-manifest` reads a pattern target as an ordinary one and `manifest-lands-on-a-file` then asks that target to be a file, so `./view-engine/*` is refused for landing on a literal `*`. The weight sits elsewhere: 127 of the manifest's 144 ways in are reached only from inside the package, and those lines are 12,170 of its 14,570 bytes.
value.evidence:
Measured 2026-09-02 by asking the gate rather than by reading it.

`akasha edit --dry-run` on `akasha/pages-system/pages-ui/components/package.json`, adding `"./probe-group/*": "./probe-group/*/*.module.code.ts"`, answered: names `@akasha/pages-ui-components/probe-group/*`, which lands on `.../probe-group/*/*.module.code.ts`, where no file is. The same refusal came for `"./view-engine/*"` put in place of the six real `view-engine` lines, whose six files are all there. The control, a second exact key naming a file that is there, answered every check clean over the one path. So what is refused is the pattern rather than the edit.

The cause is `akasha/code-system/package-manifest/package-manifest.module.code.ts:37-42`, where every string target becomes a way in, `*` and all, and `manifest-lands-on-a-file.check-code.check.code.ts:8-13`, which then asks `change.after` of that literal target. Patterns do resolve at runtime: node 22.20.0 and bun both take `@t/pkg/media/x` through `"./media/*": "./media/*/*.module.code.js"` on a scratch package naming no akasha path. A runtime is not what judges a write.

The census, `.git` and `dist` left out: 144 export lines, 144 distinct specifiers reached anywhere in the repository. 17 are reached from outside the package folder by something other than `shared/pages-ui/src`. The other 127 are reached only from inside it, or only by the 21 files yet to move in, and are worth 12,170 bytes. value.claim: Every `akasha inference` command and every `akasha temper inventory` command reaches the page-store before it reaches its own script, and nothing measures whether that store is serving. The readiness probe on the socat forwarder gave the pages service two seconds to answer a whole query while the kubelet allowed five, and the workstation takes six to seven seconds to answer that same query while it is loaded, so a service that was listening and answering correctly read as unready and the cluster service lost its only endpoint. Probe failures ran for 22.6 hours and reached nobody. Two agents found it the same night from opposite directions, each because a real command stopped, and neither was looking for it. Nothing between the two of them was a check. A check would have had to measure the readiness of the service over time rather than the health of any one part, because socat, the tailnet and the pages service each read as healthy on their own throughout.
value.evidence:
The pod `page-store-7595586bd5-lpvmg` carried 530 occurrences of `Readiness probe failed: wget: download timed out`, first at 2026-09-11T16:10:38Z and last at 2026-09-12T14:43:35Z, a span of 22.6 hours, against a replica set that had rolled out twelve seconds before the first of them. Whether the pod was unready for that whole span is not recoverable from what Kubernetes keeps: the `Ready` condition holds only its last transition, which was to `True` at 2026-09-12T14:46:27Z, and the deployment's `Available` condition transitioned at 2026-09-12T14:48:48Z. What is proven is 22.6 hours of intermittent failure rather than 22.6 hours of continuous outage.

The probe was not asking wrong. Its exact payload posted to `/ask`, naming page type `service-workstation` with a limit of one and the key `slug`, answered 200 with one row and a count of 47, both against `127.0.0.1:8787` on the workstation and from inside the pod through the tunnel. The tunnel was dropping nothing either: socat logged a successful connection to `workstation.alanwalton.ts.net:8787` through the proxy at `tailnet-egress.tailnet-egress.svc.cluster.local:1055` on every attempt, and the `Connection reset by peer` about two seconds later was wget hanging up at its own `--timeout=2` rather than the far end closing.

What the probe measured was latency it had not budgeted for. Ten calls to the local server ran 3, 3, 4, 5, 7, 7, 8, 343 and 443 milliseconds and then 6.24 seconds. Ten through the tunnel from inside the pod came back under a second seven times and at 5, 6 and 7 seconds three times. A 90-second scan at one call a second, with no service restart inside it, put 2 of 67 calls over a second and the worst at 4.41 seconds. The workstation has 24 cores and carried a load average of 37.11, 61.13 and 57.83 while those were taken, with concurrent `bun` processes at 90 to 176 percent of a core each. `page-service.service` had also been stopped and started 949 times since 2026-09-11 08:00 local, under `Restart=always` with `NRestarts=0`, so every one of those was a deliberate restart rather than a crash, and each is a window in which the store cannot answer.

The dependency that makes one service cost more than itself: `page/access/modules/file-backed-roster/file-backed-roster.module.code.ts:40` asks the live service which page types are file-backed and throws `RosterUnreachable` when it cannot, so the roster of what is a file arrives over HTTP even though the page bodies are files on the same disk.

The two surfacings were reported by other agents and were not witnessed here. `akasha inference` died before reaching any script until it was worked around with a page store origin of `http://127.0.0.1:8787`, and `akasha temper inventory rule list --json` exited 3 after six attempts on `http://page-store.page-store.svc.cluster.local:8787/ask`. The mechanism behind both was verified here, and once the probe was mended that same temper call exits 0.

`page/service/page-service.domain.ts` already states the rule the probe broke: the store the cluster reaches reads as ready only while the pages system service is listening. The service was listening throughout.

Left as a question rather than a design: the workstation reaches its own page-store by going out to the cluster and back, which is why pointing the origin at `127.0.0.1:8787` was a workaround that worked.

value.claim: No change guard judges the folder a page moves into. `move-file-page` names one guard, `claimed-file-not-left-behind`. Of the twelve guards `change-guard` declares, the nearest is `folder-not-left-named`, and it reads the folder a page leaves rather than the folder a page lands in. What a folder is to be named — a page gives its folder its slug, with the opening it shares with the page above taken off — is stated on `folder-shape` and read by the check `check-code/folder-matches-a-shape` alone. So an act may put a page in a folder of any name and nothing that act runs through refuses it. A conversion taking each folder name from the page's file stem misnames every folder whose page is slugged for its page type in front of a digit.
value.evidence:
Measured 2026-09-09 over commit 2ce0eb53e6b.

`change/mechanical/file/move/move-file-page/move-file-page.change-mechanical-file.ts` line 14 names one guard, `change-guard/claimed-file-not-left-behind`, which is about a file the move leaves behind. `change/guard/change-guard.page-type.ts` lines 17 to 30 declare twelve guards in all, and reading each one's definition, none reads the name of the folder a page lands in. `folder-not-left-named` comes nearest and reads a body spelling a folder the answer empties, which is the folder a page leaves. An agent change names no guard, per `change/agent/change-agent.page-type.ts` lines 32 to 34, so `move-page` and `move-pages` carry what `move-file-page` names and nothing more.

The rule such a guard would read sits on `check/code/pages/folder-matches-a-shape/folder-shape/folder-shape.page-type.ts` lines 166 to 189: a folder with one page answers with the name that page gives its folder, a page stating no plural slug gives its folder its slug, and that name has the opening it shares with the page above taken off, taken off again while what is left still opens with a name the page above has.

What it cost. The eight commits `df0c7b8fa89` through `43afcfb2c42` gave each of 1597 scripture passages a folder of its own and took every folder name from that page's file stem. For 1282 the stem and the wanted name agree. For 315 they do not, because those pages are slugged for their page type in front of a digit and the wanted name has that opening taken off. Counted on disk, `alan/library/reading/scripture-passage/pages` held 1597 folders and 315 opened with `scripture-passage-`, and those 315 were exactly the pages whose bare slug would open with a digit, with no exception either way. Nothing refused the conversion. The 315 folders are renamed in the session this finding is filed, which repairs the folders and leaves the guard missing.

The wanted shape is settled rather than proposed. Three page types carry the prefix and already strip it: `alan/track/days/pages` 252 folders, 0 opening with `day-`; `alan/track/food-entry/pages` 97 and 0; `alan/book/pages/learn-everything/topic/pages` 271 folders holding 270 pages slugged `learn-everything-topic-...`, 0 folders opening with it. Those three are written a page at a time rather than converted in bulk.

No composer is at fault for the slugs. Both slug groups were written by one commit, `00c80c6d985`, and no code in the repo writes a scripture passage. The prefix is required: `page/properties/slug.text-property.ts` lines 15 to 19 hold the constraint that a slug which cannot become a page's export name is no slug, and `page/modules/export-name/page-export-name.module.test.ts` lines 65 to 68 name the remedy, that the page type slug in front of the digit is what makes such a slug name an export. Running `exportedAs` and the `BARE` test from `page-export-name.module.code.ts` over the two forms answers `1Samuel26` refused and `scripturePassage1Samuel26` admitted.

Why it recurs. `domain/finding/pages/thirteen-flat-pages-folders-need-per-page-folders-and-three-more-only-look-as-though-they-do.finding.ts` queues twelve more `pages` folders for the same conversion.

What is unmeasured. Which of those twelve hold pages slugged for their type in front of a digit was not counted, so how many folders would be misnamed again is unknown. `akasha audit` was not run for this finding and the counts are read off the disk rather than off the index. Whether a guard is the right answer here, and whether it belongs on `move-file-page` or on the conversion reaching it, is undecided.

value.claim: Every hook akasha registers runs before the work that hook watches, so nothing sees what a bash call spent. Fourteen agent-hook pages state runs-at. Eleven of them run at PreToolUse, one at SubagentStart and SubagentStop, one at PreCompact and PostCompact, one at SessionStart. PostToolUse is admitted by the runs-at property and is named by no page. A hook at a tool call is handed the command and answers whether the call may run, and it is gone before the call starts, so it sees no elapsed time, no exit, no processor time and no memory. A bash call that is no command, change, check, audit, test, deploy or guard is the one kind of work an agent starts with no page of its own, and it is also the only kind nothing watches to the end.
value.evidence:
agent/hook/agent-hook/properties/runs-at.select-property.ts lists thirteen harness events at lines 11 to 23. PostToolUse is the second of them.

A search over the whole repository for PostToolUse finds that one line and two lines in agent/hooks/modules/answer/hook-answer.module.test.ts. No page states it.

The fourteen pages and what each states: block-akasha-edits, block-akasha-reads, block-akasha-shell-writes, block-biome, block-bun-test, block-combined-akasha-calls, block-destructive-git, block-git-writes, block-subagent-audit, block-typecheck and name-subagent all state PreToolUse alone; state-subagent states SubagentStart and SubagentStop; state-compacting states PreCompact and PostCompact; clear-reads-on-context-replaced states SessionStart.

agents/hooks/agent-hooks/agent-hook.page-type.ts states at line 41 that a hook at a tool call answers whether the call may run or hands back the input the call runs with. That is the whole of what the harness asks a hook at that event, and the call has not run yet.

That page type also carries the rule Alan Approves Hooks at line 101, so closing this is his call rather than an author's.

check-cost already writes cpuSeconds, childCpuSeconds, wallMs, peakBytes and peakAddedBytes for a check, an audit, a command and a change, and each of those is measured inside the process that does the work. A bash call runs in no process akasha starts, so there is nothing for that pattern to wrap.

value.claim: `isSupervisorCmdline` requires the literal `supervisor.ts` in a command line, and no file of that name is in the repository. It matches none of the live supervisors. The memory reaper draws the roots of its per-tree leg from that predicate, so the per-tree ceiling has no tree to measure and cannot fire. The unit test asserts the predicate against a command line shape the repository no longer produces, so a passing test reports on a predicate that can never match.
value.evidence:
Measured on the akasha checkout on 2026-09-05, by ryn, on a quiet tree.

The predicate is `SUPERVISOR_CMDLINE_RE = /^(?:\S*\/)?bun\b.*supervisor\.ts/` at `seat-system/seat-proc-liveness/seat-proc-liveness.module.code.ts:5`, read by `isSupervisorCmdline` at `:10`.

Ran that exact expression over `/proc`: 312 processes owned by uid 1000, 84 of them running bun, 0 matching. A live supervisor was among them and was not matched — pid 34855, `bun /var/home/walton/repos/akasha/agent/seat/supervisor/supervisor-process/modules/run-supervisor/run-supervisor.module.code.ts -a aawalton --agent-id 01a06c7b-...`.

A zero and a blind instrument answer alike, so the expression was given a control in the same run: it still matches `bun tools/run-supervisor.ts` and `/usr/bin/bun /repo/seat-system/supervising/supervisor.ts`. The expression works. What it is looking for is gone. `git ls-files` names no file ending `supervisor.ts` anywhere in the tree; the entry point is `agent/seat/supervisor/supervisor-process/modules/run-supervisor/run-supervisor.module.code.ts`.

The sibling expression three lines below settles that this is staleness rather than intent. `SEAT_INFRA_CMDLINE_RE` at `:7` still names `packages/agent/oauth-proxy/src/main.ts`, and `git ls-files` tracks nothing at all under `packages/`; but that same expression carries an alternative spelled `messages-mcp(?:\.module\.code)?\.ts`, which is the layout in use now. One expression was carried through the move and the one beside it was not.

The test is the part worth keeping. `seat-proc-liveness.module.test.ts:35` and `:40` assert `isSupervisorCmdline` holds of `bun supervisor.ts`, a command line nothing in this repository produces. The test passes. It proves the predicate can recognise a supervisor that no longer exists, which is a different claim from the one anybody reading a green run would take from it.

value.claim: The false refusals left in lone-quantifier and lone-determiner are parser mistakes rather than shape design, and no predicate over the parse separates them. Every discriminator that would separate them is the very thing the parser gets wrong: whether the word after the quantifier is a noun or a verb. Four candidate rules were measured over the whole population before landing and all four were rejected, two for cutting true refusals at the same rate as the artifacts and two for cutting almost nothing. So a shape narrowed as far as a predicate can narrow it still refuses about a fifth to a quarter of what it names, and turning the check on at patch enforces that share.
value.evidence:
Read by hand: 40 of lone-quantifier's 909 statements, drawn evenly across the population, and all 29 of lone-determiner's. 11 of the 40 and 6 of the 29 are false refusals. Both samples are readings rather than measurements and are not multiplied up here.

The families in lone-quantifier's 11: 3 a determiner the parser filed under a noun slot ("lands as one commit", "names one listen", "the files one write puts"), 3 a numeral used as a value or a measure ("is numbered one", "one above the highest"), 2 a conjunct of a numeral ("two or more refunds"), 2 an idiom with no plainer form ("said more than once", "wants any more"), 1 a floating quantifier ("A missing value and a null value both become `nil`.").

The four rules, each run over every match before any edit was drafted:

`determinesTheNextWord` — the token after the quantifier is the quantifier's own head, the same word-order test `fillsNounSlotAsFreeRelative` already uses. Cuts 140 of 943, and most are the shape working: "the one reported", "the one held", "each carries", "none stands". The parser files a reduced relative's verb as the quantifier's head as readily as it files a determined noun there.

`determinesTheNextNoun` — the token after it is tagged NOUN or PROPN. Perfect on lone-determiner's 29 and 45% wrong on lone-quantifier's 943: it cuts "one ESO day", "two or more orders", "the one mac", "both debug switches" rightly, and cuts "one Jenny chose", "one Alan wrote", "an interactive one answers", "every reader below this one uses" wrongly. The wrong cuts are a verb tagged NOUN and a possessive `'s` tagged NOUN.

`joinsAModifier` — a `conj` of a `nummod` or a `det`. Sound, and cuts 2.

Widening `marksADegree` past its every-child test — cuts 3, all `nothing ... at all` where an `acl:relcl` was hung on `all`.

The two rules that did land the same day landed because they turn on a word rather than on a tag: `isReciprocal` reads `each other`, `headsAComparative` reads a `fixed` child spelled `than`, `marksAProportion` reads `much`, `countsItsParts` reads a `nummod` inside a partitive. None of them asks the parser what part of speech anything is.

Astra's `bebdf802fa` at 06:20:46 moved the page and its folder under `page/service/`, leaving that constant naming a slug no page carried. Her `13c3bd15c3` at 06:27:51 repointed what still named the old slug, with her tests green at 10/10 and 14/14.

I did not touch the constant, because the rename was Astra's and in flight. I read those four commits with `git log`, and the times here are from that log.

She cannot produce the landing run's own report: her retry loop overwrote the scratch file it was written to, so no artifact of that run survives.

The wording is worth keeping as a property of the tool. `read each and judge it` hands the judgment back at the moment a rename is widest and a seat's attention is thinnest, and it reports how many rather than which ones carry load. A constant a service uses to find its own page reads exactly like a string in a test fixture when both sit in a list of 24.

One of the 24 was outside the code: this initiative's own constraint named `pages-system-service`. I repointed it at `f75099f20b`, 06:40:07.

value.claim: The moved-on-disk refusal at landing.module.code.ts:280 has two causes and its wording names only the first, so the remedy it implies is wrong half the time. `sameBody` at reading.module.code.ts:118-121 returns false on either of two grounds: the recorded body differs from the disk, or `partly(held)` is true, which holds whenever the reading carries a `readThrough` and is therefore true for any file delivered in runs rather than whole. The first is cleared by reading the file again. The second is not, because reading again in runs records another partial reading; it is cleared only by taking the body whole. The refusal says the disk disagrees with what was read, which describes the first cause and misdescribes the second as disagreement when the real defect is incompleteness.
value.evidence:
Traced end to end while writing up a related hazard, and every line was opened rather than taken on report.

The predicate, at akasha/command-system/reading/reading.module.code.ts:118-121, is `if (held === null || partly(held)) return false` followed by `return held.oid === oid || held.carriedOid === oid`. The first line is an unconditional refusal for a partial reading: no comparison against the disk happens at all, so no state of the file can satisfy it. `partly` at :73 is `held !== null && reachOf(held.readThrough) !== null`, and `reachOf` at :67 admits any positive integer.

That the partial road is reachable rather than theoretical: akasha/command-system/command/read/read.command.code.ts:333 writes `readThrough: reachedTo(long.run)` when a long file comes back in runs, and :208 and :210 both branch on `partly` when deciding what a later read answers. The read command truncates at 28,000 bytes per answer without breaking a file partway, so any file over that ceiling is read in runs and every one of them records a partial reading.

The caller: `movedOnDisk` at akasha/command-system/change-freshness/change-freshness.module.code.ts:8 blob-ids what is on disk and asks `sameBody` for each recorded reading, collecting the failures; landing.module.code.ts:280 turns each into a refusal saying the disk holds something other than the body that was read, and adds a tail telling the writer to read them again.

Why the wording matters rather than being a quibble. For the stale-record cause the advice is right and one read clears it. For the partial cause the advice is wrong in a way that wastes a lane: reading again the same way records another partial reading, the refusal returns unchanged, and the writer has every reason to think the file is being changed underneath by another agent, because that is what the message describes and a swarm is running. The remedy is to take the body whole with `--full`, which the refusal never mentions.

The two causes are also told apart cheaply, which is worth writing down: a stale record is cleared by one read, so a refusal that survives a clean re-read of an unchanged file is the partial cause rather than the stale one.

A third case already on file is neither, and is worth naming so it is not merged into these two: `a-stale-lockfile-record-locks-one-agent-out-of-the-root-manifest` records a path outside `akasha/`, where the read the refusal asks for cannot be run at all, the read command answering only for what is inside the folder.

value.claim: akasha holds two orders for the keys in a page body. One is bound by `page-composing`: `orderedIn` groups the properties a page type declares by the type declaring them, reverses the groups so the furthest ancestor comes first, and `bodyOf` writes the keys in that order. The pages service uses it whenever it composes a page. Hand-written pages keep a different order, near-unanimous within each page type, that no document states. Of 70,121 page files, 26,235 agree with the bound order and 43,894 do not. No check compares a page's key order against its type, which is why the two orders drifted apart unnoticed. A mechanical act placing a new key by the bound order would put that key where the page's siblings do not put it.
value.evidence: Measured over every `*.<page-type>.ts` file git tracks, taking the top-level keys of the exported object and comparing them against the order derived from the page type's `properties` array walked up its `extends` chain: 70,121 pages read, 26,235 agree, 43,894 do not. The disagreements are systematic rather than scattered. `text-property`: 628 of 628 disagree, every one putting `propertySlug` before `definition` where the derivation puts it after. `module`: 3,431 of 6,838 disagree, writing `code` and `test` before `invariants` where the derivation writes `invariants`, `directives`, `expands` and `parts` first. `domain`: 254 of 465 disagree, writing `parts` before `invariants` where the derivation has the reverse. Restricting the comparison to single-line keys, so that multi-line lists floating to the end are forgiven, still leaves 39,170 pages disagreeing, so the deviation is not only about where the long lists sit. Practice itself is near-unanimous. Counting pairs of keys that two pages of one page type order differently: 0 for `text-property` over 628 pages, `relation-property` over 142, `boolean-property` over 130, `view` over 51, `subagent` over 48, `record-property` over 45 and `nav` over 26; 8 pairs across 6,838 `module` pages; 2 across 465 `domain` pages. Each page type has an order its pages keep. It is simply not the order its page type declares. The bound order: `page/service/modules/page-composing/page-composing.module.ts:43` says the keys are written in the order the keys are declared, and :47 says the type deepest in the descent declares first. `orderedIn` at `page/service/modules/page-composing/page-composing.module.code.ts:88-96` buckets by `declaredBy`, reverses the buckets and flattens. `propertiesFrom` at `page/type/modules/declared-properties/declared-properties.module.code.ts:247` feeds it, and `bodyOf` at `page/modules/body/page-body.module.code.ts:44` obeys the array handed to it. A byte-for-byte round trip is asserted at `page-composing.module.test.ts:361-365`, so the bound order is real and load-bearing for pages the service composes. Nothing enforces it anywhere else. Every check page under `check/code/pages/` was read for order and none compares a page's key order against its type; `page-matches-its-type.check-code.ts:152` says a value's own sort is not judged there, and its test sorts keys before comparing. Noticed while mending `add-property-value`, which puts a new key after the last one already there, at `change/modules/literal-splicing/literal-splicing.module.code.ts:36-47`. Two keys landed at the end that way and were moved by hand afterwards: `webEntry` on `code/ios-app/pages/alanwalton/alanwalton.ios-app.ts`, corrected by 8a43307616b, and `test` on `alan/web/routes/alan-web-page-detail/alan-web-page-detail.route.ts`, landed by 82e56b5355b. In both, the slot a human chose is the slot the bound order gives once the keys already there are read in that order, so the bound order is right about these two. It is wrong about `invariants` on a module page, which it would place before `code`.

value.claim: `page-listening`'s test for concurrent reads asserts that a narrow question finishes inside the first ten of 21 real HTTP round-trips. That measures completion order under load rather than concurrency. It failed 3 of 4 whole-tree runs on 2026-09-01 and passed 7 of 7 every time it was run alone. The invariant it reaches for is real and is written on the package: a read is answered while another read is being answered.
value.evidence:
The test binds `Bun.serve` on loopback, fires 20 questions at page type `module` plus one narrow question at `invariant-kind` keyed to `slug`, awaits all 21, and asserts `order.indexOf("narrow") < 10`.

Four whole-tree `akasha test` runs on 2026-09-01, the tree unchanged between the first two: run 1 failed, `Expected: < 10, Received: 12`, at 3871 pass and 1 fail; run 2 passed at 3872 pass and 0 fail; runs 3 and 4 failed at 3923 pass and 1 fail. Run alone by `--file-path`, the file passed 7 of 7 on every attempt.

`page-listening` starts no process. It reaches `index`, `page-value`, `page-serving` and `page-writing`, and none of those runs anything while a read is answered. The verdict moved with what else the machine was doing rather than with any change to those modules, and the assertion carries no ceiling of its own.

What it costs is not the red run. An agent meeting a red whole-tree test spends the next run working out whether its own change caused it. This session did exactly that, and withdrew a causal claim about a neighbouring agent before checking the timestamps that showed it false.

value.claim: `parts` targets `page-type/domain`, so a page type whose pages are not domains cannot name one of its own pages among its parts. Every folder shape that reads `parts` therefore refuses a folder holding such a page, and the only shape left to that page is `pages-of-the-type-above`, which asks for a folder named `pages` between the page type and the page.
value.evidence:
`domain/properties/parts.relation-property.ts` states `targetPageType: "page-type/domain"`. `domain/plain-language/parser-model/parser-model.page-type.ts` states `extends: ["page-type/page"]`, so a `parser-model` page is not a domain. `domain/plain-language/parser-model/compact-parser/` held one such page beside the page type's own folder, and `folder-matches-a-shape` refused the folder above it as `2 subfolders are no part `parser-model` declares: compact-parser, properties`.

Declaring the part is refused rather than merely wrong. `akasha change draft change-file` adding `"parser-model/compact-parser"` to that page type's `parts` answered: `parser-model/compact-parser` names a `parser-model`, and this property admits only `domain` and what extends it.

Both shapes that read `parts` reach the same end. `a-domain-with-its-parts.folder-shape.code.ts` and `a-page-type-with-its-parts.folder-shape.code.ts` each keep a subfolder only where `standing.declared(folder)` holds what `standing.holds(subfolder)` answers, and `standing.declared` is built in `folder-matches-a-shape.check-code.decision.code.ts` from `parts` alone. `a-page-type-with-its-parts` skips a subfolder named `modules`, `pages`, `properties`, `scripts` or `workstation-services`, so `pages` is the one name that clears without a declaration.

The mend for `compact-parser` was `move-folder` to `domain/plain-language/parser-model/pages/compact-parser`, landed as `dcfcf9509595fafaedf9dacc1b7d89771eaddb78`. That move is the only mend available to any page of a page type beneath `page-type/page` rather than beneath `page-type/domain`, and the class is wider than one page: every such page sitting in a folder beside its page type is refused today and can be cleared only by moving, never by declaring.

value.claim: Reading a file property without naming it under `files` answers the ending rather than the body, and a caller that parses the answer reads it as unset. `getPage`, and a query naming the key only under `keys`, both hand back the four characters `json` for `settings`. value.evidence:

value.claim: Reading one page's value loads every page's value in the repository. shadow.pageOf is the single-page value reader every check calls, and its first call builds a map over the whole tree. The identity index answers one slug in one small read, but the value index keeps one file for each page type rather than one for each page, so no single-page value read exists to call instead. The design is declared rather than accidental, so mending it changes a stated invariant.
value.evidence: shadow.module.code.ts:33 is `if (filed === null) filed = everyValue(reading)` then `return filed.get(path) ?? valueAt(path, root)`. Five single-page callers reach it: phone-number-is-e164:90, key-names-one-property:102, introduced-property-is-a-part:86, folder-matches-a-shape:93, relation-resolves:89. The cost is memoized for each shadow, so it is amortized rather than paid twice. index-reading.module.ts:14 states `The value every page carries is answered as one map from path to value`, so the map is the declared design. Beside it, index-reading.module.ts:18 states `An answer about one page is one file read or one directory listed`, and the identity index keeps that promise: 31370 files, near 100 bytes each, one for each page. The value index holds 191 files, one for each page type, 9.3 MB, of which module.jsonl alone is 2.3 MB. So one module's value costs 2.3 MB read. page-type-properties.module.code.ts:47-56 resolves a path in one index read with listedAt and hands that path to a pageOf it takes as a parameter, so the cheap path lookup is there while the value read is whatever a caller passes, which is this map. Three narrower cases have the same shape and no such excuse. filePropertiesAt at index-entries.module.code.ts:352 builds on schemaAt:171, which walks every page-property type folder, and two of its callers immediately narrow it to one key: client-reaches-a-server-module-through-a-route.check-code.check.code.ts:21 and page-composing.module.code.ts:238. schemaOf(reading, name) answers each in one read and already carries fileName. carriedFor at page-asking.module.code.ts:83 calls valuesOfType over every page-type page to answer what one page type carries, three lines after asking:153 resolved that page type with listedAt. checkout-roots.module.code.ts:110 memoizes a readdirSync of pages/repo and answers a single-string question from it at :121, going around the index entirely.

value.claim: Rewriting the workstation units from their pages is not inert. Thirteen units whose installed `ExecStart` sources `~/.secrets.env` lose that sourcing, their pages omitting `needsSecrets`, and `surplus-fall-notifier` also loses `RestartPreventExitStatus=1`, which no page property writes. A regeneration repairs the paths and quietly takes credentials away from services that read them. Anyone rewriting a unit owes a census of what its import closure reads out of the environment.
value.evidence:
Measured 2026-09-03 by taking `serviceUnitText` and `timerUnitText` over every workstation-service page and comparing the bytes against the installed file in `~/.local/state/workstation-services`. Of 83 units: 23 identical, 2 absent, 58 different.

Thirteen lose the `set -a; [ -f ~/.secrets.env ] && . ~/.secrets.env;` prefix from their ExecStart: model-account-upkeep-service, model-account-upkeep-stall, maintain-seat-pending, memory-reaper, recipient-resolver, repos-empty-dir-purge, rule-population-sweep, send-due-reminders, surplus-fall-notifier, sweep-editor-pages, sweep-log-days, sweep-page-answers, sweep-supervisor-logs. Two of those, maintain-seat-pending and recipient-resolver, are the seat system's own. `unit-writing.module.code.ts:60-62` writes the prefix only where the page says `needsSecrets: true`, so the loss is a page omission rather than a generator defect, and the shape is already recorded at `a-service-page-omitting-needs-secrets-regenerates-a-unit-that-starts-and-fails`. The number is what is new.

One loses more. `surplus-fall-notifier` also loses `RestartPreventExitStatus=1`, and no property of the page type writes that line, which the page itself records as a stopgap: `The exit status that must prevent a restart stands nowhere the unit is written from`. Its notifier ends on exit 1 after three thrown ticks in a row, so without that line a hard failure is restarted every 30 seconds forever rather than left alone.

Whether a service truly needs the secrets is answerable per service, by reading the names in `~/.secrets.env` and asking which are named anywhere in the service's import closure, the closure taken with `localClosure` from `service-reaching` so it is the same set the wrapper follows.

My first instrument for that was blind and answered zero on all three arms it was given. It matched `process.env.NAME` and `process.env["NAME"]` and so could not see `process.env[APNS_AUTH_KEY_ENV]` at `tools/lib/push-notification/apns.ts:197`, where the name reaches the index through a constant. Three agreeing zeros over a service that plainly signs Apple push tokens is what gave it away. Matching each declared secret name as a bare token against every closure body instead, the control fires: apns-push-notifier names `APNS_AUTH_KEY_P8`, inbox-tracking-poll names `GOOGLE_GMAIL_OAUTH_CLIENT_SECRET` and `GOOGLE_GMAIL_OAUTH_REFRESH_TOKEN`, and surplus-fall-notifier over 267 files names none. Two arms answering yes and one no is a live instrument; three zeros were a dead one.

So of the thirteen only surplus-fall-notifier is measured, and it reaches no secret. The other twelve are unmeasured and must not be assumed safe.

value.claim: A workstation service whose `runs` carries `podman run --replace --name` cannot be run by hand beside its own installed unit. Podman honours `--replace`: the by-hand run removes the installed unit's container and takes the name and the port. The unit's own `podman` then leaves on 0, and `Restart=on-failure` answers no clean exit, so the unit goes `inactive (dead)` and stays there until someone starts it by hand. Running `akasha infrastructure service run dcgm-exporter` at 12:25 on 2026-09-11 took the GPU metrics down for twenty-three seconds this way, and nothing in the unit would have brought them back. A service running a plain binary has no such shape: a second `node-exporter` loses the race for 9100 and dies, and the installed one keeps running.
value.evidence:
`akasha infrastructure service run dcgm-exporter` was run by hand on the workstation on 2026-09-11, while `dcgm-exporter.service` was up, to watch the `running.code.ts` landed in `1f5c52d2b20` run. `infrastructure/service/workstation/pages/dcgm-exporter.service-workstation.ts:10` carries `runs: ["/usr/bin/podman run --rm --replace --name dcgm-exporter --device nvidia.com/gpu=all -p 9400:9400 nvcr.io/nvidia/k8s/dcgm-exporter:3.3.8-3.6.0-ubuntu22.04"]`. The installed unit at `~/.local/state/workstation-services/dcgm-exporter.service` runs that same line under `/usr/bin/env bash -c 'exec ...'`, with `ExecStop=/usr/bin/podman stop dcgm-exporter`, `Restart=on-failure`, `RestartSec=10` and `SuccessExitStatus=143`.

`podman events` over 12:25:20 to 12:26:10 MDT reads, under the one name `dcgm-exporter` throughout: at 12:25:34 `container died 0` and `container remove 0`, then `create`, `init`, `start` and `attach` in that same second; at 12:25:44 `container died 137` and `container remove 137`; at 12:25:57 `create`, `init`, `start` and `attach` again. The first death is the installed unit's container, removed by the by-hand run's `--replace`. The 137 is the by-hand container, stopped by the unit's own `ExecStop`.

The journal, `journalctl --user -u dcgm-exporter`, agrees. `container died e866cc82a1e5...` at 12:25:34.045, the container the unit had held for 2d 21h. `podman[1068637]: dcgm-exporter` at 12:25:44.363, `podman stop` printing the name of what it stopped, and `dcgm-exporter.service: Consumed 4min 21.731s CPU time over 2d 21h 35min 39.250s wall clock time` at 12:25:44.367, the line systemd writes for a unit going down. Then nothing at all until `Started dcgm-exporter.service` at 12:25:57.556, from a `systemctl --user restart` run by hand; the new container was listening on `[::]:9400` in that same second. No restart job was scheduled in the gap and none is in the journal. The unit read `inactive (dead)` across it, and 9400 answered nothing from 12:25:34 to 12:25:57.

The mechanism. The unit's main process was the `podman run` started with the unit days before, attached to the container `--replace` removed, and it left on that container's code, 0; the run recorded at the time has it as PID 2079 leaving on 0. `Restart=on-failure` answers no clean exit, so systemd started nothing again. Ten seconds after the main process left, the unit's `ExecStop` ran `podman stop dcgm-exporter` and stopped the container then holding that name, which was the by-hand one, so the by-hand run died too and the name was free with nothing on it. The `--rm` in the run means the evicted container is gone rather than stopped, so there is nothing to start again by hand either.

The sweep. Of the pages under `infrastructure/service/workstation/pages/`, `dcgm-exporter` is the only one whose `runs` names `podman run` at all, so today it is the only workstation service of this shape; a later service stating `--replace`, a fixed `--name`, a listen port, a lock file or a device takes the shape with it. The contrast is `node-exporter`, converted the same hour in `cada117`: its `runs` is `/home/linuxbrew/.linuxbrew/bin/node_exporter --web.listen-address=:9100`, and a second copy of that binary cannot evict the first. It loses the race for the port and dies on its own, and the installed unit neither notices nor stops.

It breaks the alarm and all of them at once, so the alarm's own failure is perfectly correlated with the largest outage it exists to report. value.claim: Three reading services are in systemd `failed` state and the reason is not the same for all three. Measured over all 135 wake-day pages: `activityIn` answers a number on 77 of them, so activity is honestly dark today and its silence is right. `sleepIn` and `surplusIn` answer on 0 of 135. The keys each reads, `sleep-hours` and `spend-hours`, are present on 0 of 135 days, while the reducers themselves are sighted — seeded rows answer 7.25 and 6. So those two tiles cannot light for any day, past or present, and their exit 2 reports an absent reading where the truth is a reader no data can satisfy. It is not a key-spelling fault: today's row carries 28 keys, 28 kebab and 0 camel, so `kebabisedRow` is doing its work on the day arm. Separately and independently, exit 2 meaning `nothing to report` reaching systemd as `failed` is a signalling mismatch on all eight readings.
value.evidence:
Measured 2026-09-03 18:10-18:20 MDT, read-only, over every wake-day page on disk.

THE POPULATION, NOT A SPOT CHECK. 135 wake-day pages, and `asking` answered a row for 135 of 135, so no day was lost to the query. Over those rows: `sleep-hours` present on 0, `spend-hours` present on 0, `active-calories` present on 34, `strength-calories` present on 77. Readings that came back with a number: `sleepIn` 0 of 135, `surplusIn` 0 of 135, `activityIn` 77 of 135, with real values such as 2026-06-19 at 462.857, 2026-06-22 at 530 and 2026-06-23 at 725.714.

THE CONTROL, WHICH IS WHAT MAKES THE ZERO A MEASUREMENT. A zero from a reducer nobody exercised is a dead instrument. Seeded rows in the store's own kebab spelling: `sleepIn({'sleep-hours': 7.25})` answered 7.25; `surplusIn` over sleep 8, spend 2, surplus 6 answered 6; `activityIn` over active 400 and strength 100 answered 400. All three reducers are alive, so the two zeros are about the data reaching them and not about the code.

THE KEY-SPELLING CLASS IS REFUTED HERE, AT ITS OWN SCOPE. The session-points fault is real and is on a different arm. `askDayByDate` applies `kebabisedRow` at `day-place.ts:215`, so the DAY arm answers kebab, which is the spelling every readout reducer is written against. Today's row carries 28 keys and every one is kebab: `activity-calories`, `inbox-tasks`, `faith-stoplight` and the rest, with 0 camel keys. `allSessions` at `day-place.ts:631` hands its rows back untouched, which is where 821 of 821 rows spell `startTime` and a reader spelling `start-time` keeps none. Two arms, two spellings; the day arm is not the broken one.

WHY THE TIMESTAMPS LOOKED LIKE HONEST BEHAVIOUR. All three ran clean 48 times and then failed from 04:00. `getEsoDayStr` puts 03:55 local in eso day 2026-09-02 and 04:05 in 2026-09-03, so 04:00 is the eso day rolling, and a new day with nothing logged is a true absent reading. Sleep and surplus then answered 8 more times, last at 06:45:10 and 06:45:06, and have answered none since. That pair of successes is what makes this worth writing down: it shows the reader COULD answer earlier today, so the present 0 of 135 is a change rather than a standing condition. `adabb4f33a` at 16:15:48 flipped the day arm off the markdown engine, and the markdown deriver was what computed `sleep-hours` as a relation reduction. The 06:45 successes predate that flip. Activity never recovered after 04:00 at all, which fits its own data: today's row carries neither `active-calories` nor `strength-calories`, so no rollup has landed for the new day.

WHAT I AM NOT CLAIMING. I did not establish why the 06:45 answers stopped hours before the flip, and I did not weigh whether the repair belongs at the reducer, at the wake-day page type or at whatever should roll a night's stretches onto the day. `asking-declares-a-formula-property-and-fills-it-with-nothing` already holds that `sleep-hours` and `spend-hours` are formula properties `asking` declares and never fills; this adds the population count, the firing control, and the fact that the two answered as recently as 06:45.

THE SIGNALLING MISMATCH, WHICH IS TRUE WHATEVER THE ABOVE. Every one of the eight readings exits 2 to mean an absent reading, and systemd has no way to read that as anything but `failed`. `workstation-service` carries a `success-exit-status` option that none of the eight sets. A tile deliberately showing no signal is the design `inbox.domain` and `sleep.domain` both hold, so a unit reporting failure for it teaches every reader of the unit list to ignore these three, which is the worst outcome for the day one of them fails for a real reason.

NOT TOUCHED. I changed nothing here. My lane carries the eight readings into akasha, and the carriage is faithful either way: both roads answer identically over real data, which for sleep and surplus means both answer nothing.

value.claim: Twelve page types say which module loads their pages, and the graph works that edge out from the saying. Three mechanisms put a load beyond the saying. One is handed a body rather than a path, so what it loads was never among the pages at all. One can load a page of any type, so saying it would give one module an edge to every page there is. Two load by slug or by a key the page states rather than by type, and the saying names a whole page type, so any edge written for them would be false for almost every page of that type. What is left is per-site judgement: a load is declarable where every page of the type really is loaded.
value.evidence: The two mechanisms with nowhere to be said are now absences on the pages that own them. `page-value.module.code.ts` loads through `declaredIn`, which is handed a body as a string and never a path: it transpiles that body with `Bun.Transpiler` and runs the result through `new Function`, so no file and no page is there for an edge to point at. `file-property.context-warrant.code.ts` takes `path` as an argument of `statedIn(root, path, slug)` and hands it to the `loadFrom` that `createRequire` made, so what it may load is every page there is, and `Never Depend On Everything` refuses that edge. The third mechanism is the property's own shape. `graph-asking.module.code.ts` routes `loaded-by` into `loadedFrom`, which answers one edge from every page of the type, so a saying speaks for the whole type. `gate-building.module.code.ts` loads two module pages named by the constants `CHECKING_IN` and `INDEXING_IN`, out of 6890 module pages; `type-generating.module.code.ts` loads the generator beside a page type only where that page type states `typeGenerator`, which two of 472 do. Neither can be said without asserting thousands of false edges, and gate-building now carries that absence. Cost is not what refuses them: nothing outside a test reads a relation edge, since `reachingInto` has one caller, the typecheck decision, and it asks only for import edges. Six page types were declared once each load was weighed this way: seat and subagent for `agent-stated`, container-recipe for `recipe-composing`, check-model for `model-running`, and both email rule types for `email-rule-reading`.

value.claim: Three times in one day an agent gave up on a structured page-editing act and reached for `change-file` with an old and new fence, because the act was wrong or missing. The acts exist so that a page edit is judged before it lands. `change-file` replaces a passage of text and is judged by nothing that knows the edit touches a page. Each time an act is routed around, the safety that act was built for is not had, and nothing anywhere records that it was skipped, so the rate is invisible. Two of the three causes are now mended. The third is a gap: no act edits a list field inside a record.
value.evidence: The three, all on 2026-09-10. First, `add-property-value` was asked for `figureOffScale: true` on a readout group and wrote `figureOffScale: "true"`, since it spelled every value with `JSON.stringify` whatever the property held. That fails at typecheck, so the agent dropped the drafts and used `change-file`. Mended at 19f62f57b3, which reads what the property holds from the page type and hands the spelling down to the mechanical act. Second, the same act was handed `key: aids` while an agent was trying to edit the `aids` list inside a directive record on a person page. It accepted the key and drafted a stray top-level `aids` property that the `person` page type declares nothing for. Nothing refused it; it was caught by reading `akasha change show` before applying, and cleared with a drop. Mended at 57c8ad6ae8, which refuses a key the page's type declares no property for. Third, and still open: `change-property-record-field` refused that same edit correctly, saying the record states no text under `aids`, because it states one field anew and a list field is not text. There is no act that puts a value into a list field inside a record, so the only way through was `change-file`. The pattern matters more than any of the three. An act that refuses is a good outcome, because the agent learns what is wrong; an act that is missing and an act that writes the wrong thing both end at `change-file`, and `change-file` lands whatever the fences say. value.claim: `remove-property-value` edits a page's body and nothing else. Where the property named is a file property, the file that value named is left in the folder, claimed by no page. Taking the `test` value off the media page module left `media-page.module.test.ts` beside the page, and a second landing with `remove-file` was needed to take it away. No check refused the first landing: `file-has-its-page` judges only what a change has, and the change had the page rather than the file left behind.
value.evidence:
MEASURED on 2026-09-09 while dropping the media page module's test.

`akasha change draft remove-property-value` with `at: alan/web/modules/media-page/media-page.module.ts`, `key: test`, `value: ts` landed as 2dfaed30d5. `ls alan/web/modules/media-page/` after that landing still answered media-page.module.test.ts. A second landing, da79815e28, ran `remove-file` at that path.

WHY. change/agent/file-content/remove-property-value/remove-property-value.change-agent.code.ts reaches one rung, `change-mechanical-file-content/remove-property-value`, and nothing in it reads whether the property named is held in a file. Its own page says as much: `Taking the value out is left to the mechanical change of the same name`, and that mechanical change acts on file content. The word `file` occurs nowhere else in the change's code.

WHAT THE PAGES SAY TODAY. page/file-property/file-property.page-type.ts says `A file property's value is beside its page rather than in the page's own file` and `A file property's value goes when its page goes`. Neither says what becomes of the file when the value goes and the page remains, which is the case here.

WHERE IT COULD BE ANSWERED. The change could read the property page and, where that property is a file property, compose the file removal beside the body edit. Or a landing check could refuse a change taking a file property's value while leaving its file. value.claim: The 458 inventory chunk pages are not 458 things. value.evidence:

The pages landed keeping the division, because akasha's own 15,000-byte file ceiling refuses a whole capture as firmly as a piece of one and the bytes are out either way, so rejoining now would move the loss without lessening it. Each page keeps `byte-count`, what its piece held, so the division is undone by arithmetic rather than by reading the pieces.

Rejoin them into 157 pages once a whole capture can land.
