value.claim: The akasha gateway takes its transport log destination as `logAt`, a page path or a call answering one, and `SURFACE` carries none. `optionsFor` in `proxy-process` hands the boot settings' log directory on as `getLogDir` and nothing turns that into a `logAt`, so `buildStreamObserver` returns early and no transport row is written. The tools entry does write them: `transport-log.ts` keys a `logWriter` on the agent id taken from the log directory's own name and lands rows on a seat-log-day page under the property `lines`. The akasha module lands them through `queueAt` under the property `transport`, which is a different destination rather than the same one spelt differently, so this is a design decision nobody has taken rather than a wire nobody has joined. Any cutover of the entry point stops transport rows until it is taken.
value.evidence:
Measured 2026-09-03 while building `akasha/agent/model/gateway/modules/proxy-entry`, the file that answers every seam `runGatewayProcess` asks for.

WHERE THE PATH DIES. `proxy-serving.module.code.ts:230` and `:245` read `doors.logAt`. `SURFACE` at `:130-153` declares `listened`, `socketCleared`, `socketRemoved`, `now`, `slept`, `said`, `warned` and `threw`, and no `logAt`. `forward.module.code.ts:78` reads `logAt !== undefined || observerSlot.endInFlight !== undefined` to decide whether an observer is built at all, and `transport-log.module.code.ts:180` returns early where `logAt === undefined`. `committed-keepalive.module.code.ts:70` does the same. So the rows are not lost late; they are never made.

THE TWO DESTINATIONS ARE NOT THE SAME. `tools/lib/model-gateway/transport-log.ts:17` builds `logWriter("supervisor-transport", seatName)`, where `seatName` comes from `seatNameForAgent(basename(dir))` — the log directory is named for the agent, so the directory is how the seat is found. `log-append.ts` lands that under `LINES_KEY = "lines"` on a `seat-log-day` page whose slug is `${source}-${seatName}-${date}`, rotating daily and by `ENTRY_CEILING`. The akasha module instead calls `queueAt(NO_ROOT, at, "transport", "jsonl", 8 * 1024 * 1024)` at `transport-log.module.code.ts:118`, where `at` is a page path — its own tests hand it `pageAt(root)` and `forward.module.test.ts:196` hands it `/var/tmp/fwd-build-9002/nowhere/nowhere.module.ts`. Property `transport` against property `lines`, a page path against a source-and-seat-and-date slug, an 8 MiB ceiling against `ENTRY_CEILING`.

WHY THIS ENTRY LEAVES IT ALONE. Guessing the page path would have written rows somewhere nobody asked for, on a live oauth write road, under a property whose rotation this lane has not read. The module page for `proxy-entry` declares the two gaps in its own words — `No transport log path reaches the gateway this entry starts` and `No transport row is written by the gateway this entry starts` — so the absence is recorded rather than silent. `proxy-process.module.ts:201` already declared the same gap before this entry was written.

WHAT IT COSTS AND WHEN. Nothing today: the live gateways are the tools entry and they write their rows. It costs the moment `ENTRYPOINT_REL` names the akasha entry, and it costs quietly, because a gateway with no transport rows serves every request correctly.

WHAT WOULD CLOSE IT. Someone who owns the transport destination decides which page a row lands on, and the entry hands `logAt` in as a call rather than a path so that a daily rotation is re-read per row. `recordTransportEvent` caches its queues by path, so a call answering a fresh path each day works without a restart.

value.claim: The `weigh-bash-call` hook answers `LET_THROUGH` and does nothing else, and the harness spawns it on every bash call every agent makes. Taking its page away would take that spawn away too, and two conditions block that. A registration naming the hook's code file is settled at a spawn, so an agent spawned before the page went would meet a registration naming a file nothing is at, which refuses the call rather than passing it. And the hook's own entries files beside the page hold about sixteen megabytes that taking the page away would take with them.
value.evidence:
THE SPAWN. `hook-dispatch.module.code.ts:135-146` spawns a process per hook per call, and `:168` runs that over every hook matching the event and the tool. `weigh-bash-call` matches `PreToolUse` over `Bash`, so every bash call any agent makes pays one Bun spawn for an answer of `LET_THROUGH`. The body it runs is `weigh-bash-call.agent-hook.code.ts` as of `1a6f6cd4597e44a4545af388bcf1cfc1afc17a98`.

CONDITION ONE, THE REGISTRATION. `agent-hook.page-type.ts:84` says a registration names the path of a hook's code file, and `:88` says the path a registration names is settled at the spawn rather than at the call. `:96-99` says a registration naming a file nothing is at refuses the call rather than passing that call. So taking the page away refuses every bash call from every agent spawned before it went, at once, and a bash call is how an agent would report it. The condition is met when no agent spawned before `1a6f6cd4597e` is running.

CONDITION TWO, THE SIXTEEN MEGABYTES. `weigh-bash-call.agent-hook.entries.part2.uncommitted.jsonl` and the `part3` beside it hold what each dispatch of this hook cost, written by `recordCost` from `hook-dispatch.module.code.ts:176` rather than by the trap that went at `952a5640db0b09ded010e82cff055ad760718df7`. Those rows carry the harness event as their phase rather than `bash`, so the census finding no reader for the bash rows says nothing about these. Whether they go with the page is its own decision.

WHY IT IS WORTH DOING. The spawn is a real cost on the hottest path in the tree. It is smaller than the outage condition one describes, and it is paid on every call for as long as the page is kept.

NOT ESTABLISHED. How long an agent in this swarm lives was not measured, so when condition one is met is unknown. No reader was looked for over the hook's own entries files.

value.claim: The 15,000-byte `file-length` ceiling now decides which refusals may be improved. The text an agent reads while it is already blocked is composed in the repository's busiest modules, and those are the modules at the ceiling, so a mend to that text is weighed against bytes rather than against whether it is right. On 2026-09-12 two such mends were written in one hour: one landed because 300 bytes of slack happened to be recoverable in the same file, and one did not because its file had 35 bytes free and the smallest honest version of it needed 117. Neither outcome turned on the mend.
value.evidence:
Measured on 2026-09-12 against `CEILING = 15000` at `check/code/pages/file-length/file-length.check-code.decision.code.ts:20`.

Three files reached the ceiling in one stretch of work on the subagent presence and warranting modules. `agent/subagent/modules/presence/subagent-presence.module.code.ts` was taken to 14,958 bytes by `9476180c61d`, 42 free, and was relieved only when `2175d551108` moved the body composer into a module of its own and left it at 13,586. `agent/subagent/modules/presence/subagent-presence.module.test.ts` is 14,948, 52 free. `domain/context/modules/warranting/warranting.module.code.ts` is 14,965, 35 free.

The first mend landed. `b21b0c492d1` narrowed `pathsUnder` so that a seat whose name opens another seat's name sweeps no page of that other seat, and it needed a new test in a file with 52 bytes free. The test was paid for by taking up an existing `pageWritten` fixture at four call sites in the same file, each of which had been spelling out `wrote(...)` and `pathOf(slugOf(...))` by hand. Four two-line setups became four one-line calls, and the file grew by 3 bytes, from 14,945 to 14,948. The mend landed because that slack was there to find, not because the mend was small.

The second mend did not land. `Warrant` at `domain/context/modules/warranting/warranting.module.code.ts:63` carries `{ path, oid, owed }` and no field for the page the warrant ran over, so a reading-owed refusal names a file and a rule and never says which page made that file owed. A live refusal taken on 2026-09-12 reads `agent/seat/properties/on-call.boolean-property.ts — the record does not show you read this.` and then `A page states each property as the page defining it shapes it, and that page is read first.` Nothing in it says that `agent/role/pages/operator.role.ts` is the page carrying `onCall`. Over one subagent page that same sentence arrives six times with six different property pages and no subject on any of them.

Three versions of that mend were costed against the 35 bytes free. Carrying the page as a field, attaching it in `warrantsIn` so that no warrant producer changes, and suppressing the clause where the warrant's own path equals the page it ran over: +313 bytes. The same inlined into `notReadOf` and wrapped as biome wraps: +155. The smallest version, with no helper and no suppression, which degrades the common case every agent reads in order to improve the deep case: +117. The first attempt was refused by `file-length` at 15,273 bytes.

The refusals an agent reads while blocked are composed in `warranting.module.code.ts`, `landing.module.code.ts` and `change-acting.module.code.ts`. `domain/context/modules/` holds two modules, one of 1,488 bytes and one of 14,965, which is the shape of a module that should have been two. Making room for a one-field mend means first landing a split of about 4,500 bytes across the refusal-composing half, a second landing with its own checks, or moving `bytesAt`, `blobAt` and `bodyAt` out, which buys 750 bytes and touches the twelve warrant files that import `blobAt`.

What this is not: no file named here is over the ceiling, and no mend named here was refused for being wrong. The cost is that the price of improving a refusal is set by how full its module happens to be, and the modules that compose refusals fill fastest because every improvement to a refusal lands in them.

value.claim: Akasha's byte ceiling forces a generated data table to be divided, and whether division corrupts the table rests on one thing: whether the emitter imposes a total order. Where it sorts, the wire index is a function of the keys and no division can move it. Where the gathering module spreads its groups in turn, division moves the index and nothing fails. Akasha reads no table for which of the two it is.
value.evidence:
Recorded 2026-09-01 and corrected 2026-09-02, and the correction matters more than the first reading.

The first reading held that division is dangerous as such, and three findings rested on it. The code says otherwise. `akasha/temper/temper-addon-generators/temper-set/temper-set.module.code.ts:115-117` sorts before emitting, `no-set` first and then by key. `akasha/utils-narrow/create-data-file/create-data-file.module.code.ts:24-25` takes `list` from `Object.values(data)` and `ids` from `list.map(item => item.id)`. So for the 707 sets the index is a total function of the set of keys, and the order of no file reaches it. Applying the emitter's sort to the 707 sets read back gives an ordered id list identical index for index, index 0 `no-set` and index 706 `zoal-the-ever-wakeful`.

The crafted potions table, which is the one real corruption, failed the other way. Its gathering module spread four groups in turn, so the order came from the concatenation rather than from a sort, and the index moved first at position 14. That is recorded in `splitting-a-data-table-for-the-byte-ceiling-moved-a-codec-index`. The fault was the missing re-imposed order, not the division.

So the rule is: a table whose emitter sorts may be divided freely, and a table whose gathering module concatenates may not. `akasha/pages-system/pages-core/generated/entries-00` through `entries-37` is 38 modules of divided generated data and is the precedent for the safe case.

The entry route was measured and does not answer this. Entries keep file order exactly, and 707 pages round-tripped with no mismatch. But an entry file is read at run time and `besideAt` binds one to a single page and property, so it cannot serve a table a compiler must read as a literal, which is what every consumer here needs.

What is open: no check reads whether a table's order comes from a sort or from a concatenation, and that is the thing worth building. A seat notices it by reading the emitter.

value.claim: Running each test file in a runner of its own would cost almost nothing at a change and a great deal at an audit. Over the last three hundred commits, two hundred and thirty-six named no test file at all, and thirty-eight of the sixty-four that did named exactly one, so the median change that runs tests already runs one file in one runner. Six commits in three hundred named more than seven. An audit is the other case, and it was run both ways over the same tree: the one thousand four hundred and twelve test files took 153 seconds and 123 processor seconds in about fifteen runners, and 263 seconds and 269 processor seconds one file to a runner. That is 1.7 times the waiting and 2.2 times the processor.
value.evidence:
The count for each commit is the files that commit touched, folded onto the page each one sits beside, kept where a test file sits beside that page and is there at that commit.

The spread over three hundred commits, as files named against commits: 0 named by 236, 1 by 38, 2 by 10, 3 by 5, 4 by 1, 5 by 1, 6 by 2, 7 by 1, 10 by 1, 16 by 1, 26 by 1, 31 by 1, 34 by 1, 52 by 1. They add to two hundred and seventy test files over three hundred commits.

So a run per file would add about two hundred spawns over three hundred commits, and almost all of them fall on the dozen largest changes rather than on the ordinary one.

What a spawn costs is read off the 2183 runs of the tests-pass check that ran tests: the median run took 701 milliseconds, the mean 2994, the worst 365054, and the mean processor time was 1.97 seconds.

A find over the checkout outside node_modules and the git folder answers 1412 files named .test.ts or .test.tsx. code-tests batches up to a hundred files of one group into one runner, so an audit's runners are counted in tens.

code-tests already holds the per-file road: spentIn runs one file per spawn, and slowIn calls it, but only where a batch has already gone past five seconds times the files in it or has died on a signal.

The audit comparison was made by calling ranOver and then spentOver over the same 1412 files, one after the other, on a workstation carrying its usual load. ranOver answered 152750 milliseconds and 123.496 processor seconds over 15547 tests in 1412 files. spentOver answered 263167 milliseconds and 269.217 processor seconds added over the files. The recorded audit runs of the tests-pass check average 155610 milliseconds and 114 processor seconds over 32 runs, so the batched number here is an ordinary one rather than a lucky one.

Three of the 1412 files went past the five processor seconds one file is allowed: service-watching at 6.11, rename-file-page at 5.04 and supervisor-iteration-outcome-db at 5.02. Nothing today holds them to it, because the whole batch came in under five seconds times the files in it.

value.claim: A round tells by refusal now rather than by check, and `refusalsNew` reads two refusals as the same refusal where they name the same path. `tests-pass` answers one refusal whose path is the first failing test file, so a test file that newly fails leaves that path where it was and the round reads as unchanged. The verdict and the cost row rest on that path too. Three readers key on a path naming one of many broken files, so mending this belongs in what the check answers rather than in how a round reports.
value.evidence:
Read at HEAD `bebfeccfe6b` on 2026-09-14. Every line cited here I opened with `akasha read` rather than took on report.

The filter. `291d27f78f5` put `refusalsNew` in `check/modules/audit-serving/audit-serving.module.code.ts` where `turnedRed` had been. It answers nothing where the verdict is clean, every refusal where there was no verdict before, and otherwise the refusals whose path is not among the paths the verdict before held. `refusalPath` beside it cuts a refusal at its first ` — `, which is the separator `verdictOf` joins a judgement's path and reason with. So the path alone decides whether a refusal is new.

The answer. `refusalsOver` at `check/code/pages/tests-pass/tests-pass.check-code.decision.code.ts:248-269` returns a one-element array on every road, and `refusedOf` sets that element's path to `ran.slow[0]?.path ?? failing[0] ?? first` — the first failing file alone. `failedIn` has gathered every failing file by then and `failinglyOf` writes them all into the reason. The roster is computed and then filed where nothing keys on it.

What it costs, measured. In `~/.local/state/workstation-services/audit-verdicts.json`, read 2026-09-14 at 21:10Z, `tests-pass` held one refusal whose reason opens `Measured between 2026-09-14T20:01:05.182Z and 2026-09-14T20:08:09.889Z. 13 test files failed:`. Thirteen files, one path. A fourteenth leaves that path alone wherever the first failing file is unchanged, and the round tells nobody. Five of the sixty-two checks in that file were refusing, and `no-unused-exports` held 5,141 refusals against a run from 2026-09-12.

What else rests on it. `costKept` at `audit-serving.module.code.ts` records how many refusals a run answered and no path at all, so the cost row reads one. The verdict keeps path and reason joined, one entry per check, replaced whole each round.

Why this was not visible before. Until `291d27f78f5` a round told only where a check turned from clean to refusing, and `tests-pass` has been red continuously, so nothing it newly found was told and the path decided nothing. The filter is what gave that path a second reader.

Read beside `one-refusal-covers-every-red-test-file-and-only-its-body-names-them`, which is about the unit a reader is handed. This is about the readers that now rest on it.

value.claim: The landing lock's wait is a race with no queue, so a caller that has waited long has no priority over one that just arrived. Forty processes each holding 250ms wait 0.75s at the median and 54.6s at the worst, which is 5.5 times what a fair queue would cost and 45 percent of the 120s ceiling. The lock is 7 percent busy in this checkout today, so the tail is latent rather than felt, and it grows with how long a busy period lasts rather than with how many callers there are.
value.evidence:
Holds were timed by polling the lock file from a separate process every 1ms and pairing each window with the caller's own clock, so no production code was changed to measure it.

Forty processes landing once each: hold 153ms mean, 176ms worst; worst wait 5,979ms against a packed drain of 5,967ms. Fair to within 12ms, because a closed field only shrinks. Four runs agreed within 25ms.

Forty processes landing ten times each with no think time, 400 landings in 16.9s at full utilisation: hold 42ms mean; wait p50 782ms, p90 3,592ms, p99 8,137ms, worst 12,951ms — 7.7 times the packed drain.

Forty processes taking the hold for a fixed 250ms ten times each, which is the length a landing takes in this checkout: wall 100s; wait p50 752ms, p90 25,788ms, p99 44,811ms, worst 54,565ms — 5.5 times the 10,000ms packed drain.

Watching `.git/akasha-landing.lock` in this checkout while the swarm ran: 64 holds over 223s, 258ms median, 297ms worst, 7.3 percent utilisation, 10 of the 64 handed straight to a waiter. Arrival runs 14 times below saturation, so the measured tail is what a busy period would cost rather than what today costs.

The median wait being under a second while the worst is a minute is the shape of barging: `holding.module.code.ts:52` waits 5ms and races again, and a fresh arrival is as likely to win as one that has lost forty rounds.

Measured 2026-09-09 while naming thirty-two temper folders what their pages call their folders.

WHAT HAPPENED. With a `move-folder` from `temper/character/mines` to `temper/character/temper-mine` already kept, a `change-file` against `temper/temper-addon-data/mined-motif-coverage/mined-motif-coverage.module.code.ts` was refused for reading. The refusal named the moved files rather than the file being changed, and closed with `58 more pages are owed than one answer holds`. Among the paths owed were `eso.temper-mine.items.part*.jsonl` sweep files of several megabytes each, which no reader wants and no read can hold.

WHAT MENDED IT. `akasha change drop` with `all: true`, then the same two edits drafted in the other order: the `change-file` first, the `move-folder` second. The `change-file` asked for the one file it changes. The `move-folder` asked for nothing further. The fold landed.

THE MECHANISM. Reading is charged against the fold rather than against the edit in front of the writer. A kept `move-folder` puts every carried path into the fold, so the next draft of any kind inherits the reading for all of them. This is the same gate `the-reading-gate-charges-a-draft-for-the-whole-kept-patch` describes from the other side: there the demand arrived at an arbitrary later draft; here it arrives at a predictable one, and reordering the two drafts removes it entirely.

WHY NOBODY WOULD PREDICT IT. The two edits are independent. They touch disjoint paths, they land as one commit either way, and the acts' own pages say nothing about order. The order that costs nothing is also the order that reads oddly aloud: mend the constant that names the new path, then move the folder to that path. An author working forwards will pick the expensive order every time.

NOT DETERMINED. I did not establish whether the reading owed is the moved paths themselves or the pages the index pulls in transitively behind them, nor whether a `move-folder` of a small folder charges the same way, nor whether the charge is per-draft or only at the draft that first exceeds what one read can answer.

value.claim: The read record says a body was sent, never that a body reached the agent. Four boundaries between the read command and the agent can eat a body. The record counts the first three as read. Two of those three say nothing an agent would read as a failure, and the third names an amount of output rather than a lost body. The fourth is the only one silent on both sides: the body reached the agent and no record was written at all.
value.evidence:
Measured 2026-09-02 across three agents on one checkout. `reading.module.ts:119` already names the gap: nothing is in the record that did not reach the agent.

First boundary: the read command's own 28000-byte answer. The command names the files left undelivered and hands back the exact next call, so recovery is possible. This boundary is the honest one.

Second boundary: an `akasha read` and an `akasha edit` chained into one shell call. About 20000 characters went missing from the middle of the read with no marker at all, while the record counted every file. The write then landed on bodies nobody held.

Third boundary: the harness answered `Output too large (44.8KB). Full output saved to <path>` with a 2KB preview. Four module pages were counted as read and no body reached the agent. Commit `a2118713a3` landed that way, and the debt was paid afterward with the change already in.

Both agents who met the third boundary read the marker as a note about output size rather than as the gate going blind. The rule an agent can act on: any message about output size near an `akasha read` is a read failure whatever the message calls the failure.

Fourth boundary, measured 2026-09-13 and since mended. A subagent's record file is found by looking its agent id up in the subagent page index, and that page is landed by a detached run the subagent does not wait for, so every read a subagent made before its page landed printed a whole body and recorded nothing. Landing latency measured over six subagents on one busy checkout: 9.1s, 11.6s, 12.8s, 14.7s, 15.2s, 15.8s. That is several agent turns, so an agent lost two or three calls to byte-identical output before one stuck, and read the repetition as the gate working. This is the only boundary silent on both sides: the first three lose the body and count it read, this one delivers the body and counts nothing. It failed safe for writes, an empty record refusing the write. `akasha read` now waits up to 60 seconds for the agent's own page, going the moment it lands and refusing with no body where it never does.

Two lists look alike and are not. The read's trailing `N files were left unread here` is the read's own output cap and never settles. The refused write's own list is the debt. Chasing the read's list went 19, 53, 31, 17. Taking the write's list went 19, 3, 1.

value.claim: `tsconfig.json` at the repository root is two lines, `{ "files": [] }` — no `include`, no `references`, no `compilerOptions` — so it names nothing to compile. Of nine tsconfigs the root alone carries the empty list. `akasha typecheck` judges the files named and every file importing them, and its `--seeded` control puts a fault into each named file in memory and refuses where that file draws no diagnostic. Nothing in the tree tells a reader to run `tsc`.
value.evidence:
Measured 2026-09-05 at HEAD `832fa11720`, read-only, from the checkout root.

THE CONFIG AND WHAT IT DOES. `git show HEAD:tsconfig.json` is the whole of `{\n  "files": []\n}`. `bunx tsc --noEmit -p tsconfig.json` answers `tsconfig.json(2,12): error TS18002: The 'files' list in config file '/var/home/walton/repos/akasha/tsconfig.json' is empty.` and exits 2. `bunx @typescript/native-preview -b`, which is verbatim what `package.json:85` binds the root `typecheck` script to, answers the same line and exits 2. So both obvious instruments fail loudly rather than passing quietly. That is the correction I owe the brief I was given, which held that the run reports clean and an agent gets a clean-looking answer; it does not, at either instrument.

WHERE THE CLEAN-EXIT CLAIM ACTUALLY LIVES. It is stated inside the tree, as a `constraint` invariant on the hook that refuses `tsc`: `hook-system/agent-hooks/block-typecheck/block-typecheck.agent-hook.ts:48` reads "A `tsc` run at the repository root compiles no file and exits 0." Line 44 beside it, "The repository's own `tsconfig.json` names no file", still holds. Line 48 does not. `0c8dc795c8` of 2026-09-04 13:55:47 -0600 removed a `references` array naming four web projects, leaving `files: []` alone. A build-mode run over references compiles those projects; the same run over nothing is the TS18002 error. So the hook's warrant expired about a day before this was written, and the hook still refuses on it.

THE CENSUS. `find . -name 'tsconfig*.json'` outside `node_modules` returns nine. Exactly one, the root, carries an empty `files`. Seven carry a non-empty `include` — four web apps and `language-design/lua-compiler/lualib` twice. The ninth, `tsconfig.base.json`, carries neither and is what the web apps extend. None of the nine now carries `references`.

WHAT `AKASHA TYPECHECK` DOES INSTEAD. Its help says it judges "the files named and the files importing them", and `--seeded` is "a fault put into each file named, in memory alone, to show the run sees the file". Run over one readout file it answered `typecheck judged 7 files, the 1 file named and 6 files importing them, and none refused`, exit 0. Run over the same file with `--seeded` it answered `readout-system/readouts/pages/upkeep-sleep/upkeep-sleep.readout.code.ts — seen: 1 diagnostic with a fault seeded into it` and `nothing was written — the fault was in memory alone`, exit 0. The control asserts one thing: each file named is inside the program the run built. Where a named file draws no diagnostic with a fault in it, the command refuses with `drew no diagnostic with a fault seeded into it, so a clean answer over it means nothing`. It says of itself that it says nothing about the rest of the folder, and points at `akasha audit --check typecheck` for that. The seeded control does not cover the importer reach, only the named files.

WHETHER ANYTHING SENDS A READER TO `TSC`. Nothing does. Across 723 markdown files outside `node_modules`, a grep for `tsc` as a whole word returns zero lines; the only substring hits are inside `Deutsch` and `wirtschaft`. No `CLAUDE.md`, `AGENTS.md` or `README` exists in the tree, and there is no `.github/workflows`. All eight `typecheck` scripts in package manifests reach `@typescript/native-preview`, none reaches `tsc`. The word `tsc` appears on 93 lines across 16 files, and every one is either the hook refusing it, a test of that refusal, a finding page recording its blindness, a vendored `.d.ts` or `--help` text, the lockfile, or a `.gitignore` comment. So the path by which this trap would be walked into is not written down anywhere, and a hook refuses the call besides — which makes this finding smaller than it would otherwise be.

A CLAIM IN THE BRIEF THAT DID NOT REPRODUCE. I was told an agent used `tsc` while landing `841c0e961b` and `9b3bbc8bb8`, reported "no readout typecheck errors", and that two files carried dangling imports at that moment. Neither commit body contains the words typecheck, compile or compiler; `841c0e961b` claims only the test suite, and `9b3bbc8bb8` says "What is left of each test file proves the reducer." Every import specifier in all sixteen touched files resolves against the git tree at both commits — fourteen relative specifiers plus eight `bun:test` externals — and the named bindings are exported too. A resolver seeded with two false specifiers reported both as dangling, so the sweep was not blind. What I could not do was run a compiler at those commits: `git worktree add` failed with `No space left on device`, so the negative rests on specifier and export resolution from git objects rather than on a compile.

WHAT ELSE I DID NOT ESTABLISH. I did not run the pre-`0c8dc795c8` config, so I have not shown by measurement that the exit was ever 0; I have shown only that the references it named are gone and that the exit is 2 now. I did not judge whether the root config should name anything.

value.claim: One refusal, the one saying these pages declare no property carrying a `unique`, is reached two ways, and a reader who knows only one of them looks for that one, does not find it, and judges the fault a different fault. Either way the sentence names the pages the change carries, so it reads as a fault in the change, and either way it is not. The root is not there: the reading holds nothing, so nothing declares a `unique`. Or the root is there and what the unique properties are read from is not filed yet, which is any world writing its own index for the first time. The guard runs behind `indexThere`, which asks only whether the root is there, so it turns the first off and leaves the second unmended: at HEAD an absent root settles a real page while a present root holding nothing refuses it. Telling them apart is cheap: ask whether the index root is there, and if it is, this is the second.
value.evidence:
Read and run 2026-09-11 on the akasha checkout, and again 2026-09-12.

The guard weighs two halves of different worlds. `index-settling.module.code.ts:222` calls `refusingEmpty(unique, held.filter((one) => one.now !== null).length)`. The count is the change's pages. The map is `uniquePropertiesAt(overValued)`, read off the reading. Whenever the reading answers an empty map while the change carries pages, the two halves disagree and the refusal fires. Two different things make the reading answer empty, and they are peers rather than one behind the other. The other call site, `indexing.module.code.ts:113`, weighs `uniquePropertiesIn(values)` against `held.length` over the whole tree, so its two halves match and it is sound.

First mechanism, the root is not there. `asBuilt` at `:149-151` turns a reading whose root is absent into `readingNone()`, so everything reads as empty while the count is not. Reproduced 2026-09-11 by driving `indexingAt(root, repo).settle()` over one real page, `nimue-a5a9445fddf156fcc.subagent.ts`, with its body off disk: against `.git/index` it settles; against a scratch path that is not there it throws `these pages declare no property carrying a `unique`, so no `identity` would be filed`. One page, one body, two roots, opposite answers.

Second mechanism, the root is there and what the map is read from is not filed. `refusingEmpty` runs behind `if (indexThere(given))`, and `indexThere` at `index-reading.module.code.ts:64` is `readingIn(given).holds("")` — it asks whether the root is there and nothing else. `uniquePropertiesAt` at `index-entries.module.code.ts:399-406` walks `shapesAt`, which is `shapesEvery` at `index-reading.module.code.ts:306-322`, listing `shapes/page-property/*.jsonl` off the reading. A root that is there holding no shapes answers an empty map, the guard runs, and it throws. Run at HEAD on 2026-09-12 through `settlingOver` over one real page body: against a scratch root whose `.git/index` is there and holds nothing, `indexThere` is true, `uniquePropertiesAt` is 0 and the settle throws that sentence; against a scratch root with no `.git/index`, `indexThere` is false and the settle is clean; against this checkout's own index, `indexThere` is true, `uniquePropertiesAt` is 9 and the settle is clean. The absent root is the one that settles and the present unbuilt root is the one that refuses, the reverse of the pairing above.

Where the second was met. `854b492cc52`, 2026-09-12 07:23, read which page types sit under a page type from the relation index: `kindsUnder` walked `idsNaming(given, listed.id, "extends-type")`, and at that commit `shapesAt` built its map by `for (const kind of kindsUnder(PAGE_PROPERTY, reading))`. A world whose root was there and whose `extends-type` relation was not yet filed reached no property kind at all, so the map came back empty and the refusal fired against the change's own page count. The `tests-pass` verdict `08e14756b09`, measured 13:38:09Z to 13:45:46Z, carries that sentence 171 times as the direct error for 89 of its 326 failing tests, a count recorded on `a-dozen-red-test-files-is-the-ordinary-state-rather-than-a-regression`. `c2b88405467` at 07:45 reads descent from each page type's own `extends` again, and `page-type-descent.module.ts` now carries the departure `A world writing its own index is answered before that index has any relation`. That closes the road through descent and does not close the mechanism.

What happened on 2026-09-11. `5de9009723a` at 10:22:56 added `.git/index` as a second root and nothing built it. `keepingIn` settles every root, so every landing carrying a page was refused at the second root while the real index was fine. In `/run/user/1000/akasha/01a08cd2-f750-7000-a7d8-5b558d039e25/subagent-presence.log` every crash frame is `indexing.module.code.ts:205:35` or `:207:35`, which in both versions of that file are the `settle` in `for (const one of also) one.settle()`; on `leading.settle()` the callee starts at column 28. Not one crash was the leading root. `git log` over 10:15 to 10:45 shows commits every five to twenty seconds up to 10:22:56, then five commits in the seven minutes to 10:30:27, then the normal rate again.

The mixed-kind bisection does not hold. `61c23aaa0c9`, `db98280eb8b`, `0590631b120` and `4811d66cb7e` are 10:33:26, 10:34:52, 10:35:12 and 10:39:29, all after the root was built, so every split that landed landed on the safe side of the boundary. The refusals it was splitting away from were inside the window. Which kind an edit is, is confounded with when it ran, and the timeline explains the whole set without kind.

Mended in part. `a9aec561d11` at 10:55 on 2026-09-11 put the guard behind `indexThere(given)`, so a settle into a root that is not there no longer reaches `refusingEmpty` at all. In a worktree `.git` is a file, so `join(root, '.git/index')` cannot exist, `indexThere` answers false, and a landing rooted there is refused nothing. That mends the first mechanism and is the very thing that leaves the second unmended, `indexThere` being true for every root that is there and unbuilt.

Telling the two apart. Ask whether the index root is there. Absent, it is the first, and the guard already turns it off. Present, it is the second, and the guard does not.

What is not verified. Which root a landing rooted in a worktree resolves to. The two commits that first wrote the guard. Whether anything other than the shapes listing sits on the road from a young index to an empty map.

value.claim: `block-akasha-shell-writes` refuses four shapes of call that write nothing into the checkout. Three of the four are one defect: it reads text that the shell would never run as a command as though it were one. The fourth resolves a relative path against the wrong directory. Each cost real time on 2026-09-04 and each pushed the agent that met it toward a workaround rather than the call it meant to make.
value.evidence:
Four reproductions, met on 2026-09-04 while repairing the flatten, numbered as they were first filed. None of them writes anything inside the checkout.

1 and 2 were a heredoc body read as a redirect, one carrying `>>>>>>> new` and one carrying `2>&1`. Both are fixed: `pastHeredocs` takes a body out from the line opening it to the line ending it, keeps the opening line so a redirect there is still read, and takes nothing out where the text never ends the body.

3. A variable in a redirect target is refused unexpanded. `... > "$SP/owed3.txt"` was refused as landing on `$SP/owed3.txt` "inside the akasha folder", where `SP` held a path under `/tmp`. Spelling the same path in full was admitted, so the refusal rests on the text of the target rather than on where it lands.

4. A relative path is resolved against the process directory rather than the one the command runs in. `cd /tmp/.../scratchpad && sed -i '...' scan2.mjs` was refused as landing on `scan2.mjs` "inside the akasha folder". The file is under `/tmp`; only the process directory made it look otherwise.

5. `bun` naming a path in the checkout as an argument is refused, whether or not it writes. `bun -e 'import("<a path in the checkout>")...'` was refused with "a program's own text is not read here, so a write through it is not parted from a read, and naming the path at all is what is refused". This blocks a read-only probe, which is what it blocked: the call was a control proving an import fails, and it had to be dropped.

6. `sed -i` is refused by naming the script rather than the file. `sed -i 's/x/y/' file` is refused on the substitution rather than on `file`, so the refusal names something the call does not write.

What 3, 5 and 6 share is that the hook decides from the command's text without the shell's own reading of it: a variable it does not expand and an argument that is a path but not a target read alike to it. Reproduction 4 is apart from those three and is about which directory a relative path is resolved against.

What to do about any one of the four left is a ruling nobody has taken. Each is a judgement about what the hook should refuse rather than about how the hook reads, which is why the heredoc defect was fixed and these were not.

value.claim: `Stoplight` in `readouts/group-serving/readout-group-serving.module.code.ts` declares `habit?: string`, but the key a stoplight carries is a parameter each caller hands in. value.claim: A taboo term reaches a word quoted out of akasha's own source, where the word is an identifier rather than prose. value.claim: Alan's web container goes unresponsive every so often, fails its liveness probe, and is killed and restarted — five times in three hours. Because a relayed reading is held only in that process's memory, every kill throws the reading away and the tile draws nothing until the next relay tick, up to five and a half minutes later. The restarts and the memory-only hold are each defensible alone; together they are a tile that goes dark on a schedule nobody chose.
value.evidence:
Measured on 2026-09-01 between 18:49Z and 18:56Z against pod `web-6f48c47fbc-kg2rc`, age 3h10m, `RESTARTS 4 (80m ago)` climbing to 5 while I watched. Events on that pod: `Liveness probe failed ... /api/health: context deadline exceeded` counted 29, `Readiness probe failed` counted 59, `Container web failed liveness probe, will be restarted` counted 5. The probe allows 5s and liveness has `failureThreshold: 6` at `periodSeconds: 10`, so the container is unresponsive for about a minute before each kill, and the tile route fails for that minute too. `lastState.terminated` reads `reason: Error, exitCode: 139` finished 18:55:26Z, while the container's last log line is `error: script "start" was terminated by signal SIGTERM (Polite quit request)` — so: probe times out, kubelet sends SIGTERM, bun's shutdown path faults, 139 is recorded rather than 143. Reading 139 as a spontaneous segfault, as I did earlier today, gets the order backwards; the kill comes first.

Why this reaches the tile: a relayed reading is held in a module-level `Map` at `akasha/readout-system/readout-relay/readout-relay.module.code.ts:32`, and `readout-relay.module.ts:34` states the departure plainly — `A machine that starts again holds no reading`. The relay timer is `*:2/5` with 30s jitter, so a restart is followed by up to 5.5 minutes holding nothing, during which the route answers 503 `No reading` for a reason having nothing to do with Monarch. Both sites run `replicas: 1`, so no second pod can answer.

What I did not establish: why it goes unresponsive. `kubectl top` 54s after the latest restart read 135Mi against a 512Mi limit and 5m CPU against 500m, so it is not starved at rest, and an OOM kill would record 137. A growth curve toward the limit is untested. The call taken: filed rather than fixed, since raising the timeout to quiet the symptom would hide whatever blocks the loop for five seconds.

value.claim: The web container is killed for failing liveness every twenty-two to thirty-four minutes, and the two obvious causes are both ruled out by measurement: it is far below its memory ceiling when killed, and it loses two tenths of a percent of its CPU periods to throttling in steady state. Something makes it unresponsive for a full minute, and what that is remains unmeasured.
value.evidence:
Measured 2026-09-01 18:50Z-19:20Z on pod `web-6f48c47fbc-kg2rc`.

The kill is real and regular: `Killing` counted 6 from 15:54:21Z to 19:17:31Z, each `Container web failed liveness probe, will be restarted`, with `Liveness probe failed ... /api/health: context deadline exceeded` counted 29. Liveness allows 5s and carries `failureThreshold: 6` at `periodSeconds: 10`, so the container is unresponsive for about a minute before each kill rather than missing one unlucky probe.

Not the memory ceiling. `/sys/fs/cgroup/memory.max` is 536870912 and `memory.current` read 148606976 — 141Mi of 512Mi. `kubectl top` caught 320Mi just before a kill, still under the limit, and an OOM kill would record 137 rather than the 139 seen. Memory does grow: 135Mi one minute after a restart, 320Mi about twenty-one minutes later, roughly 8Mi a minute. That is a leak worth its own look, but it is not what ends the container.

Not steady-state CPU throttling. `cpu.stat` read twice, 84 periods apart, held `nr_throttled` at 27 and `throttled_usec` at 3963153 across both. Over a longer window of 497 periods, about fifty seconds, one period throttled and 0.05s accrued — two tenths of a percent. All 3.96s of the throttling landed during startup, and the kills come twenty minutes later.

Not a bare tree walk. Walking the pod's `/app/repo/pages` reached 71,445 files in 93ms warm, so the size of the tree alone stalls nothing.

What is left untested: `readoutCatalog()` does not merely walk that tree, it reads and parses frontmatter across it, and six stoplight routes call it on every request. Whether that parse blocks the loop long enough, and whether the kills line up with widget refresh traffic, was not measured. The call taken: ruled out what could be ruled out cheaply and filed the rest rather than guessing at a cause or quieting the symptom by loosening the probe.

value.claim: Two exported unions are named `BadgeVariant`, and the eight members of the one in `page/core/schema/modules/color-rule-variant` are a strict subset of the eighteen in `utils-narrow/badge-variant`. The eighteen are exactly the eighteen keys of `VARIANT_MAP` in `design/badges/badge`, the table that paints a badge, so the wide union restates the drawing vocabulary and the narrow one holds under half of it. Committed source holds nine declarations spelled `BadgeVariant` rather than two. THE TWO UNIONS, MEMBER BY MEMBER. `utils-narrow/badge-variant/badge-variant.module.code.ts` lines 1-19 declare eighteen: `accent`, `destructive`, `elevation`, `elevation-muted`, `surface`, `normal`, `fine`, `superior`, `epic`, `legendary`, `mythic`, `radiant`, `green`, `blue`, `purple`, `yellow`, `orange`, `red`. `page/core/schema/modules/color-rule-variant/color-rule-variant.module.code.ts` lines 3-14 derive eight from a `BADGE_VARIANTS` array: `accent`, `elevation-muted`, `green`, `blue`, `purple`, `yellow`, `orange`, `red`. All eight are among the eighteen, so the subset is strict and the ten the wide one adds are `destructive`, `elevation`, `surface` and the seven rarity tiers `normal` through `radiant`.

WHO READS WHICH. Ten files import the `BadgeVariant` symbol from `color-rule-variant`: `page/core/modules/resolve-badge-variant` and nine components under `page/ui/components/` (`calendar-time-property-badge`, `date-property-badge`, `instant-property-badge`, `multi-select-popover`, `number-property-badge`, `page-detail-properties-shared`, `progress-property-badge`, `relation-display`, `select-property-badge`). Its twelve category rows at lines 11-22 spell six distinct values — `orange`, `blue`, `green`, `yellow`, `purple`, `red` — and every one of the six is in the narrow union too, so the twelve members only the wide union carries are reached through that type by nothing. Piping the wide one's importer list into a grep for `color-rule-variant` returns nothing, so no file sees both unions.

WHAT THE EIGHTEEN ACTUALLY ARE. `design/badges/badge/badge.module.code.tsx` lines 17-36 hold `VARIANT_MAP` with eighteen keys, in the same order and with the same spellings as the wide union, and line 56 derives a third `BadgeVariant` from it through `VariantProps`. Nothing in the tree proves either copy against the map.

It surfaced when a rename of the `color-rule-variant` module to `badge-variant` was refused for the slug being taken. `utils-narrow/badge-variant/badge-variant.module.ts:6` states `slug: "badge-variant"` on a `module` page, and `color-rule-variant.module.ts:6` is a `module` page too. `page/properties/slug.text-property.ts:13` states `unique: "page-type"` and its invariant at line 17 reads "A slug is unique among the pages of its page type", so the two cannot both be `module/badge-variant`. value.evidence:

The old `pointsBy` at :31 matched `/\brelation(-(?:slug|seq|id|name|address))?\b/` and mapped `-address` to a fourth mode. `akasha/pages-system/pages-access/file-relation/file-relation.module.code.ts:11` carries the same regex with the `address` arm absent, and :30 declares `RelationPoints = "id" | "seq" | "name"`. value.claim: `property-slug` states two rules for spelling the key a page carries, and neither is stated as running before the other. "The key a page carries is this written in camel" camelises the property slug; "A key drops the words its declarer's name already says" takes a word out first. Over `event-types`, `run-seq` and `run-error-message` the dropping rule read first yields `types`, `seq` and `errorMessage`, where the keys the page types carry are `eventTypes`, `runSeq` and `runErrorMessage`. `types` and `errorMessage` are carried by no page type; `seq` is carried by two, neither of them `sync-run`, so the wrong reading of that one lands on a key that exists somewhere else. The two rules resolve opposite ways within one checkout: `calendar-event` drops the repeated word and `sync-run` keeps it.
value.evidence:
Measured 2026-09-05 at HEAD `832fa11720`, read-only.

THE TWO RULES, QUOTED. `page/type/page-property/properties/property-slug.text-property.ts` carries seven invariants. Line 29: "The key a page carries is this written in camel." Line 37: "A key drops the words its declarer's name already says." That line was reworded from "what its declarer's name" to "the words its declarer's name" while I was writing this; I quote it as it is now. A third, line 41, reads "A qualifier only the slug's wider scope needed is not carried into the key", which is the dropping rule again from the other side. The page's definition at line 10 is "the key a page carries this property's value under", and its `nameFormatSlug` is `lower-kebab-case`, so the property slug is kebab and the key is not.

THE THREE PROPERTIES AND THE KEYS THAT ANSWER. `alan/harness/calendar/calendar-events/properties/calendar-event-types.text-property.ts` is slugged `calendar-event-types` at line 8 and states `propertySlug: "event-types"` at line 9; `calendar-event.page-type.ts:28` carries `eventTypes`. `collections/sync-runs/properties/run-seq.number-property.ts:9` states `propertySlug: "run-seq"`; `sync-run.page-type.ts:15` carries `runSeq`. `run-error-message.text-property.ts:9` states `propertySlug: "run-error-message"`; `sync-run.page-type.ts:24` carries `runErrorMessage`. Camelising is what answers in all three.

WHAT THE OTHER ORDER YIELDS. Read the dropping rule first and `event-types` under `calendar-event` loses `event` to give `types`; `run-seq` and `run-error-message` under `sync-run` lose `run` to give `seq` and `errorMessage`. A grep for a page-type member line spelling each, across all 451 `*.page-type.ts` files, matches `types` nowhere and `errorMessage` nowhere. `seq` matches twice: `alan/tracking/session-activities/session-activity.page-type.ts:12` and `story/named-event/named-event.page-type.ts:23`. So of the three wrong keys, two name nothing and one names a real key on two page types that are not the one being asked of. A reader checking whether a key exists anywhere rather than on this page type would pass `seq`.

THE CALENDAR CASE SHOWS THE RULES HAVE NO STOPPING POINT. The dropping rule has already been applied once on that property: the page's slug is `calendar-event-types` and its property slug is `event-types`, with `calendar` dropped because the declarer is `calendar-event`. Applying the same rule again at the next step drops `event` and gives `types`. Nothing in the seven invariants says the rule fires once, and nothing says which of the two runs first. `sync-run` does the opposite on the same shape: `run` is what its declarer's name already says and `run-seq` keeps it, so the key is `runSeq`.

HOW WIDESPREAD THE SHAPE IS. A script over every `*.page-type.ts` took each file's `slug` and each member key of its exported type, dropped the six keys inherited from `page`, and asked whether the key's first word is one of the slug's words. 451 page types carry members; 3911 keys were examined; 220 lead with a word their page type's slug already says. `to-do` carries eight such keys (`toDoDueDate`, `toDoPriority`, `toDoRecurrence` and five more), `monarch-account` four, `calendar-event` one (`eventTypes`). The script matches only on the first word and only against whole slug words, so it undercounts.

THE AMBIGUITY RESOLVING THE OTHER WAY, AND ITS REPAIR. `pages/queries/pages/to-dos-due.page-query.ts` named `due-date` in its `keys` list where `to-do` carries `toDoDueDate`. That is the dropping rule applied where the page type prefixes instead. It is no longer there: commit `0d65191732` of 2026-09-05 11:58:28 -0600 replaced it, and the file now names `toDoDueDate` at line 11. So this half of the brief I was given did not reproduce at HEAD, and I read it out of `git log -p` on that path instead. That commit's own message is the wider measurement: "Eighteen of the sixty-nine page queries name a key their page type declares under no spelling. Twelve refuse outright... Six name the key only in `targetKey`, which nothing checks", and of the eight it repairs, three "each named the bare old key where the page type now prefixes it with the type's own name. Thirteen keys in all." I did not re-measure those counts myself; they are that commit's claim, not mine.

WHAT I DID NOT ESTABLISH. I did not find a written statement of which rule runs first, but I did not read every page under `page/type/` either, so one may be somewhere I did not look. I did not measure how often an agent actually gets this wrong; the 220 figure counts a shape, not a fault, and most of the 220 are correct keys. I did not judge which reading is meant.

value.evidence: Measured 2026-09-03. `tools/lib/surplus-fall/tier.ts:1` declares `TierColor = "black" | "red" | "yellow" | "green" | "blue"`, five members. `akasha/readout-system/readout-tier/readout-tier.module.code.ts:1` declares the same name with six, adding `"orange"` between red and yellow. `Rung` is `{at, color}` in both. value.claim: `akasha inference upscale --host cluster` cannot run, for a reason unrelated to the workstation path it shares a command with. Every cluster precondition is met and the Job schedules onto node-06, which then fails to pull `cluster/upscale-cu121:4bd365d5a65a`, a tag the registry does not hold. `refOf` returns the repository with the hash of the build's inputs, so the tag is a content hash: editing the recipe silently renames the image the Job asks for, and the Job goes on asking for an image nobody built. This is a stale deploy rather than a stale path. Nothing between the recipe edit and the run says so, and the failure surfaces only when someone runs the command, as a pull error naming a tag rather than as anything naming the recipe.
value.evidence:
Run tonight from the workstation, after `5adb5909422` mended the workstation path, to find out whether the cluster route shared that fault. It does not. `runClusterUpscale` composes no filesystem path at all, reaching SeaweedFS over S3 and the cluster over its API, so the two halves of this command are broken in two unrelated ways.

Every precondition holds. Namespace `seaweedfs` is Active, the secret `seaweedfs-creds` is there, and node-06 is Ready with `nvidia.com/gpu: 1` allocatable and the label `alanwalton.com/gpu-vram-usable-min.8gi=true` that the job selects on. The Job was created and scheduled onto node-06 within seconds.

The pod then failed to resolve `registry.registry.svc.cluster.local:5000/cluster/upscale-cu121:4bd365d5a65a`, reported as not found, going ErrImagePull then ImagePullBackOff. The registry answers four tags for that repository: `14565`, `7f1fb56fc0db`, `buildcache` and `serving`. The tag asked for is not among them, and `7f1fb56fc0db` is the same shape, being what was last pushed.

The mechanism is at `image-ref.module.code.ts:12-15`, where `refOf` returns `refFor(build.repository, inputsFor(build).hash)`, so the tag is a content hash over the build's inputs. `upscale-serving-job.module.code.ts:44` takes the image from `refOf(upscaleClusterImage)`. A recipe edit therefore renames the image the Job asks for, with no build triggered and nothing placed to notice the rename. It is the shape this domain already records one layer out: the reference is derived correctly and points at something nobody made.

Mine to own. The command's last error was a 404 from `getJob` at `cluster-fetch.module.code.ts:92`, and that was me rather than the system: I deleted the Job while the command was still polling it. The fault is the pull failure observed before that delete.

Suspicion rather than something established: which commit moved the hash. `82f57c9907a` and `e3586cea426` both touched the cluster-image folder, and whether either changed the hashed inputs was not checked.

Not done here. The image was not built. Building it is a deploy, and whether the recipe as it now is is the one that should be pushed is not settled by the Job asking for it.

value.claim: The audit is what judges a mechanical landing, and which of its checks see that landing depends on when the landing arrives inside the audit's own window.
value.evidence:
`change-mechanical` states `runsChecks: false` and carries the gap `A fault a mechanical change lands is found by the audit`, so the audit is the whole of the compensating control. It is a moving read over a tree other agents are landing into, and a landing that arrives part way through is seen by the checks that have not yet read and missed by the checks that already have.

Measured on one landing. `b9055bc3376` landed five `.d.ts` at `temper/addons/types/eso/generated/` at 2026-09-12T11:22:00Z. The audit that reported them measured between 11:20:25Z and 11:27:16Z, so the landing arrived 95 seconds into a 411-second window. That audit reported 10,680 `typecheck` refusals, zero from `global-declared-once` and zero from `file-has-its-page`.

Both of those checks do refuse these files. Run at HEAD with the five bodies restored, the audit variant of `global-declared-once` returns 5,198 refusals naming them and the audit variant of `file-has-its-page` returns 5. The check-on-change variants return the same 5,198 and 5. They reported nothing only because they had already read the tree when the files arrived.

The cost is in which check survives the race. `global-declared-once` names the cause in one line — `` `ActionBarSlotType` is declared at temper/eso-types/eso-enums-01/eso-enums-01.type-declaration.d.ts:1 and at temper/addons/types/eso/generated/enums.d.ts:8 `` — and `file-has-its-page` names it in five. `typecheck` names it in 10,680, of which about 380 are consequences in addon modules rather than the fault, because a redeclared name stops being typechecked wherever it is read. The two cheap answers were the ones lost, and the expensive one was the only signal the swarm got.

The same window explains three more refusals in that audit that are not faults: two `index-is-level-with-the-pages` and one `lint-clean`, all naming paths that the page moves at 04:47:38 and 05:08:22 local were shifting while the audit read.

value.claim: Working memory keeps no mark of whether a line was verified or inferred, so a later reader cites a guess as an authority.
value.evidence:
An initiative's working memory is prose. A sentence an agent measured and a sentence an agent guessed are written in the same voice, in the same field, with nothing to tell them apart. The next reader has no way to discount the guess, and the page is cheaper to cite than the source is to re-check, so the guess hardens.

The loop closed inside one hour on 2026-09-10, and both ends are in git.

At commit `d85fa643` this seat wrote, into the working memory of the intent "Alan deletes an initiative from the Work Panel's right click menu.":

"The initiative page type states `mortal: true`, so its pages are expected to be deleted, and `akasha change draft` already runs a `remove-page` act, so nothing new has to be written to do the deleting."

The second half was checked by running the act. The first half was an inference drawn from the definition of `mortal`, "whether a page type's pages are expected to be deleted", and was never checked against what mortality does.

A survey agent reading the tree afterwards quoted that sentence back under the heading "The decisive quote for feature #2", citing it by file and line number. It was reading this seat's own guess as settled ground.

The inference is wrong. Per `page/type/properties/mortal.boolean-property.ts`, `mortal` exempts a page only from dangling-reference refusals: a non-mortal page cannot hold a relation to a mortal page, a mortal page naming a page that is not there is not refused, and a name for a mortal page type is not refused for reaching no page. Deletion is gated by none of it, and any page can be removed. `change/guard/pages/import-not-left-hanging/import-not-left-hanging.change-guard.ts:43` states plainly "Mortality exempts no import here." The line was corrected at commit `d95d720c`.

This was the fourth instance in one day of an inference written into a page and later read back as fact by this seat or by an agent it dispatched. The earlier three concerned an AutoFill suppressor, a gap in the health-samples drain, and a count of deep-link literals, where an initiative's working memory said "24 more are allowlists and `.widgetURL` literals", a number this seat had inferred and later cited to Alan as established.

Care does not fix this. The writer of a line often does not know at the time which half of a sentence was measured, and the reader has nothing in the field to go on either way. The mark would have to be in the record rather than in the prose.

value.claim: The solar thread prices in programmes belonging to a utility that does not serve the house. The site is on Provo City Power; six files carry Rocky Mountain Power's rebates, free audit, export programme and reliability figures as though they applied, one making the RMP audit step one of the bid strategy. `scope.md` catches one file, and records that Provo Power's own rebates need research nothing has done. Two files credit ownership with a 30% federal credit the corpus records as terminated.
value.evidence:
Read 2026-08-16 across the 41 files of `alan/book/all-about-alan/projects/solar-power`.

`scope.md`: "Utility: **Provo City Power** — municipal utility, not Rocky Mountain Power." `customer-generation.md` opens the same way.

Where RMP is nonetheless priced in. `envelope/incentives.md` carries "## State — Rocky Mountain Power Wattsmart", "**Status: live**", a rebate table capped at "$1,100 total", a free assessment, and "it's free money for paperwork. Apply it." Its bid strategy step 1: "Free Rocky Mountain Power Wattsmart audit through GreenHome Specialties." `envelope/assessment.md`: "Rocky Mountain Power offers a **free home energy assessment** through the Wattsmart Homes program." `installers/observations.md`: "Rocky Mountain Power's Customer Generation Program credits exports far below retail"; `installers.md` repeats it. `sizing/battery.md` sizes outage ride-through on "Rocky Mountain Power historical reliability, Utah Valley SAIDI is ~90–110 min/yr". `installers/local.md` uses the "Wattsmart Battery partner" tie as a selection criterion.

It names that one file. No file records that research; `customer-generation.md` concludes the other way — "**Net stack for a 2026 owned install at this site: $0 in incentives.**"
